title: pAI-Econ-claude: A Gated Human-in-the-Loop Multi-Agent Architecture for AI-Assisted Economic Theory Development
summary: In many social-science research tasks, such as economics, LLM-based agents must produce outputs for which no cheap, task-complete, machine-readable correctness signal exists. This creates a distinctive reliability problem for multi-agent systems: how should generation, critique, coordination, and human judgment be organized when no component can certify the final result? We address this problem through pAI-Econ-claude, a gated, human-in-the-loop multi-agent architecture for AI-assisted economic theory development. Agents coordinate through a shared workspace of inspectable intermediate records; specialized gates diagnose targeted failure modes and recommend loopbacks without certifying correctness; and human checkpoints retain authority over decisions that are costly to reverse. We evaluate the architecture on five matched economic-theory tasks against an ungated baseline. Two evaluators blinded to configuration agreed on all five pairwise rankings, preferring the gated architecture in four tasks and the baseline in one. Mean failure severity fell from 1.58 to 1.16, while overall usefulness rose from 2.60 to 3.10. The largest observed gain occurred when a reality check rejected a false market-structure premise and a proof review prompted revision of a false welfare claim. The negative case shows that scaffolding can also compress an economically important mechanism too aggressively. The results support a bounded claim: gated oversight improves the auditability of AI-assisted economic theory without substituting for formal verification, and the allocation of irreversible human judgment is a more informative design variable than pure agent autonomy. The workflow is publicly available at https://github.com/maxwell2732/pAI-Econ-claude.

AI.tldr: A gated, human-in-the-loop multi-agent architecture improves reliability in economic theory development by using targeted failure mode checks and human oversight without requiring perfect correctness certification.
AI.motivation: Social science research (like economics) using LLM-based agents faces reliability problems because there's no cheap, task-complete, machine-readable correctness signal available to certify results.
AI.method: pAI-Econ-claude architecture: agents coordinate through inspectable intermediate records; specialized gates diagnose targeted failure modes and recommend loopbacks; human checkpoints retain authority over costly decisions.
AI.result: Evaluation on 5 economic theory tasks: gated architecture preferred in 4/5 tasks; mean failure severity fell from 1.58 to 1.16; overall usefulness rose from 2.60 to 3.10; largest gains from reality checks and proof reviews.
AI.conclusion: Gated oversight improves auditability without substituting for formal verification; allocation of irreversible human judgment is more informative than pure agent autonomy.

title: FedAgentKE: Federated Semantic Knowledge Evolution for Heterogeneous Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based agents increasingly rely on reasoning, tool use, and iterative execution, yet existing agent frameworks still operate largely in isolation. While recent memory-based agent systems improve individual agents through local retrieval and workflow reuse, local experiences remain fragmented across isolated agent frameworks, limiting cross-framework knowledge transfer and collaborative reasoning evolution. We propose FedAgentKE, a lightweight framework for Federated Semantic Knowledge Evolution across heterogeneous agents. FedAgentKE enables distributed agent frameworks to collaboratively evolve transferable reasoning abstractions through iterative semantic knowledge distillation, aggregation, and adaptation without sharing raw reasoning trajectories. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements under both cross-framework and cross-task settings, highlighting the potential of federated semantic knowledge evolution for future collaborative agent ecosystems.

AI.tldr: FedAgentKE is a federated learning framework that enables heterogeneous LLM-based agents across different frameworks to collaboratively evolve and share semantic knowledge without exchanging raw reasoning data.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based agent frameworks operate in isolation with fragmented local experiences, limiting cross-framework knowledge transfer and collaborative reasoning evolution despite agents' increasing reliance on reasoning, tool use, and iterative execution.
AI.method: Proposes FedAgentKE, a lightweight federated framework that enables distributed agent frameworks to collaboratively evolve transferable reasoning abstractions through iterative semantic knowledge distillation, aggregation, and adaptation without sharing raw reasoning trajectories.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements under both cross-framework and cross-task settings, showing the framework's effectiveness in enhancing agent performance through federated semantic knowledge evolution.
AI.conclusion: FedAgentKE highlights the potential of federated semantic knowledge evolution for building future collaborative agent ecosystems where heterogeneous agents can share and evolve reasoning capabilities without compromising privacy through raw data exchange.

title: Workload-Aware Caching for Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Multi-agent systems decompose complex tasks into directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) of specialized agent executions, creating natural opportunities for caching intermediate results across queries. However, existing cache eviction policies treat all cached entries uniformly based on access history, ignoring structural and workload signals uniquely available in agentic execution environments. We present a workload-aware eviction policy that combines three signals, namely recomputation cost, DAG dependency count, and agent invocation frequency, into a unified scoring function that retains the most valuable entries under memory constraints. Evaluated across three multi-agent benchmarks spanning diverse reuse regimes, our policy reduces latency by up to 64.7% relative to the uncached baseline and achieves on average a 31.1% latency reduction over the next best finite-capacity baseline, while approaching the performance of an unbounded cache and maintaining accuracy on par with or exceeding all competing finite-capacity methods. We further show that workload-aware content caching is complementary to other agentic system optimization methods, including plan-level caching and parallel agent execution, with each technique targeting a distinct efficiency bottleneck in multi-agent pipelines.

AI.tldr: A workload-aware cache eviction policy for multi-agent systems that considers recomputation cost, DAG dependencies, and agent invocation frequency to intelligently retain valuable intermediate results, reducing latency by up to 64.7% while maintaining accuracy.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent systems decompose tasks into DAGs where intermediate results can be cached across queries, but existing cache eviction policies treat all entries uniformly based on access history, ignoring structural and workload signals unique to agentic execution environments.
AI.method: Developed a workload-aware eviction policy that combines three key signals: recomputation cost, DAG dependency count, and agent invocation frequency into a unified scoring function to retain the most valuable entries under memory constraints.
AI.result: Across three multi-agent benchmarks spanning diverse reuse regimes, the policy reduces latency by up to 64.7% relative to uncached baseline, achieves average 31.1% latency reduction over the next best finite-capacity baseline, approaches unbounded cache performance, and maintains or exceeds accuracy of competing methods.
AI.conclusion: Workload-aware content caching effectively optimizes multi-agent systems and is complementary to other optimization methods like plan-level caching and parallel execution, each targeting distinct efficiency bottlenecks in multi-agent pipelines.

title: MKEvolve: A Modular Multi-Agent Framework for Kernel Code Generation
summary: Despite rapid progress in LLM-based code generation, writing correct and performant kernels for hardware accelerators remains a key bottleneck in scaling modern ML workloads. We present MKEvolve (Modular Kernel Evolve), a framework that iteratively co-evolves a modular decomposition of complex PyTorch modules and the LLM-generated kernel for each submodule, refining the decomposition by splitting and fusing across iterations while independently improving each subkernel via LLM-driven beam search. The resulting kernels are programmatic compositions of independently verified subkernels, making them configurable (subkernel implementations are swappable), interpretable (errors and speedups are traceable to specific subkernels), and readily adaptable to related model architectures. Experiments with Triton on KernelBench L2 and L3, spanning multi-operator sequences and full model architectures, show that MKEvolve improves both correctness and speedup over end-to-end direct synthesis baselines while reducing LLM token usage by up to 35%.

AI.tldr: MKEvolve is a framework that co-evolves modular kernel decompositions and LLM-generated subkernels for hardware accelerators, improving correctness and performance while reducing token usage by up to 35%.
AI.motivation: Despite LLM progress in code generation, writing correct and performant kernels for hardware accelerators remains a bottleneck in scaling modern ML workloads. End-to-end direct synthesis approaches have limitations in correctness and performance.
AI.method: MKEvolve iteratively co-evolves a modular decomposition of complex PyTorch modules and LLM-generated kernels for each submodule. It refines decompositions by splitting and fusing across iterations while independently improving each subkernel via LLM-driven beam search. The framework produces programmatic compositions of independently verified subkernels.
AI.result: Experiments with Triton on KernelBench L2 and L3 show MKEvolve improves both correctness and speedup over end-to-end direct synthesis baselines while reducing LLM token usage by up to 35%. The kernels span multi-operator sequences and full model architectures.
AI.conclusion: MKEvolve addresses the kernel programming bottleneck by enabling modular, configurable, interpretable, and adaptable kernel generation through co-evolution of decomposition and implementation, offering practical improvements in correctness, performance, and efficiency for hardware accelerator programming.

title: DataPrep-Bench: Benchmarking LLMs as Training Data Preparators
summary: The quality of training data fundamentally determines the capabilities of large language models (LLMs), yet no unified benchmark exists to measure how well LLMs, agents, and data-centric workflows actually prepare training data end to end. We view LLM-driven data preparation as comprising two complementary capabilities: data construction, which transforms raw sources into supervised training data, and data quality evaluation, which predicts the training value of candidate datasets before downstream training; throughout, "quality" refers to downstream training utility rather than surface-level textual properties. We introduce DataPrep-Bench, the first unified benchmark that jointly evaluates both capabilities under a shared downstream-grounded protocol over six domains and multiple base models. For data construction, methods consume identical raw sources and are scored by fine-tuning a base model on their outputs jointly with Dolly-15k; alongside this track we release Data-Construction-Skill, a skill-guided agent that lifts the Dolly-only baseline by nearly 20 points absolute on Llama-3.1-8B Finance and is competitive with the strongest agent- and DataFlow-based methods in knowledge-extraction-dense domains. For data quality evaluation, scoring functions are scored by Pearson correlation with downstream performance on a shared candidate pool; we release the Distributional Alignment Score (DAS), a distribution-based evaluator that uses MMD between a candidate dataset and a domain proxy. DAS attains the strongest cross-model correlation in four of six domains and is the only metric clearing r > 0.70 simultaneously in Math, Science, and Medical, outperforming existing quality-, diversity-, and heuristic-based evaluators. DataPrep-Bench provides a unified, downstream-grounded framework for measuring progress on both capabilities as co-equal targets of LLM-driven data preparation.

AI.tldr: DataPrep-Bench: A unified benchmark for evaluating LLM-driven data preparation capabilities (construction and quality evaluation) across six domains with downstream-grounded assessment.
AI.motivation: No unified benchmark exists to measure how well LLMs, agents, and data-centric workflows prepare training data end-to-end, despite data quality fundamentally determining LLM capabilities. Current approaches lack a downstream-grounded evaluation framework that considers training utility rather than surface-level textual properties.
AI.method: Introduces DataPrep-Bench with two complementary evaluation tracks: 1) Data Construction - methods transform raw sources into supervised training data and are scored by fine-tuning base models on outputs jointly with Dolly-15k; 2) Data Quality Evaluation - scoring functions are evaluated by Pearson correlation with downstream performance on shared candidate pools. Proposes Data-Construction-Skill agent and Distributional Alignment Score (DAS) using MMD between candidate datasets and domain proxies.
AI.result: Data-Construction-Skill agent lifts Dolly-only baseline by nearly 20 points absolute on Llama-3.1-8B Finance and is competitive with strongest methods. DAS achieves strongest cross-model correlation in 4/6 domains and is only metric clearing r > 0.70 simultaneously in Math, Science, and Medical, outperforming existing evaluators.
AI.conclusion: DataPrep-Bench provides a unified, downstream-grounded framework for measuring progress on both data construction and quality evaluation capabilities as co-equal targets of LLM-driven data preparation, enabling comprehensive assessment of data-centric workflows.

title: AINTMA: Agentic AI Architecture for Autonomous Test Management with Generative Intelligence, Secure Cloud Communication and Adaptive Quality Analytics
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables, Submitted to AICCONS (AIP Conference Proceedings format)
summary: Modern software quality assurance demands intelligent, autonomous systems capable of adaptive decision-making across distributed cloud environments. This paper presents AINTMA (Agentic Intelligent Test Management Architecture), a multi-agent agentic AI system that transforms traditional test management into an autonomous quality intelligence ecosystem. AINTMA deploys six specialized AI agents (Test Discovery, Risk Assessment, Reinforcement Learning Prioritization, Execution Orchestration, Generative Quality Intelligence, and Cloud Security Monitor) coordinated through a secure multi-agent communication framework over a cloud-native microservices infrastructure. The Generative Quality Intelligence agent employs large language models to produce plain language quality narratives, defect risk summaries, and data-augmented test recommendations. The RL Prioritization agent models test selection as a Markov Decision Process, learning contextual policies from large-scale historical test execution data (47 features, rolling 36-month window). Secure cloud communication is enforced through a zero-trust API gateway with OAuth2/JWT authentication, encrypted inter-agent messaging, and multi-tenant isolation. Evaluation across 12 heterogeneous software projects over 18 months demonstrates: 88.4% test prioritization accuracy (APFD, vs. 51.2% random, 82.1% best commercial baseline); 43% test cycle time reduction; defect escape rate reduced from 8.3% to 2.1%; 340% ROI at 9-month payback. The agentic architecture scales to 50,000+ test cases with sub-400ms response time, and the generative intelligence module achieves 4.3/5.0 developer usefulness rating. AINTMA demonstrates that agentic AI, combining autonomous multi-agent coordination, generative intelligence and secure smart connectivity, can fundamentally advance software quality management in cloud-scale enterprise environments.

AI.tldr: AINTMA is an agentic AI system that transforms test management into an autonomous quality intelligence ecosystem using six specialized AI agents with secure cloud communication, achieving significant improvements in test prioritization, cycle time reduction, and defect escape rates.
AI.motivation: Modern software quality assurance needs intelligent, autonomous systems for adaptive decision-making across distributed cloud environments, moving beyond traditional test management approaches.
AI.method: Deploys six specialized AI agents coordinated through secure multi-agent communication over cloud-native microservices: Test Discovery, Risk Assessment, RL Prioritization (MDP modeling with 47 features from 36-month historical data), Execution Orchestration, Generative Quality Intelligence (LLMs for narratives), and Cloud Security Monitor with zero-trust API gateway.
AI.result: 88.4% test prioritization accuracy (vs. 51.2% random, 82.1% baseline), 43% test cycle time reduction, defect escape rate reduced from 8.3% to 2.1%, 340% ROI at 9-month payback, scales to 50,000+ test cases with sub-400ms response, and 4.3/5.0 developer usefulness rating.
AI.conclusion: Agentic AI combining autonomous multi-agent coordination, generative intelligence, and secure smart connectivity can fundamentally advance software quality management in cloud-scale enterprise environments.

title: AppWorld-UL: Benchmarking Diverse Agent-User Interactions for Tool-Use
summary: Tool-use agents that address day-to-day digital tasks such as ordering groceries must not only operate applications, but also interact with the user, e.g., to ask clarification questions, prompt for confirmation, and inform the user when the instruction is infeasible. However, current benchmarks for evaluating agent-user interactions do not capture the diversity of such interactions. Further, they operate in small environments with few, often non-state-changing, APIs. To address this gap, we introduce AppWorld-UL, a ``user-in-the-loop'' benchmark of 516 challenging tasks requiring diverse agent-user interactions. Building upon the AppWorld framework with 9 popular simulated apps like Amazon and Spotify, we systematically modify original tasks to introduce ambiguities and constraints that necessitate various types of agent-user interaction. User behavior is simulated by an LLM prompted to respond with carefully designed knowledge boundaries, offering more reliable simulation than the unconstrained or overly rigid alternatives used in prior work. Our evaluation reveals that a state-of-the-art LLM, Claude Opus 4.7, achieves only 48.6% success on AppWorld-UL, and only 35.7% on the harder, compositional subset. On the stricter, scenario-level metric, compositional task performance drops to only 21.3%. Our analysis reveals that correct user-interaction is crucial for success. This demonstrates the benchmark's difficulty and its potential to advance research on user-in-the-loop tool-use agents.

AI.tldr: AppWorld-UL is a new benchmark for evaluating user-in-the-loop tool-use agents that require diverse agent-user interactions during digital tasks, featuring 516 challenging tasks across 9 simulated apps with LLM-simulated user behavior.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks for evaluating agent-user interactions are limited in capturing the diversity of real-world interactions and operate in small environments with few APIs, failing to address the complexity of day-to-day digital tasks that require agent-user interactions like clarification questions and confirmations.
AI.method: The authors built upon the AppWorld framework with 9 popular simulated apps (like Amazon and Spotify), systematically modifying original tasks to introduce ambiguities and constraints requiring agent-user interactions. They simulated user behavior using an LLM with carefully designed knowledge boundaries for more reliable simulation than prior approaches.
AI.result: The benchmark reveals significant performance gaps: state-of-the-art LLM Claude Opus 4.7 achieves only 48.6% success on AppWorld-UL, 35.7% on the harder compositional subset, and only 21.3% on the stricter scenario-level metric for compositional tasks. Analysis shows correct user interaction is crucial for success.
AI.conclusion: AppWorld-UL represents a difficult and valuable benchmark that demonstrates the limitations of current agents in handling diverse user interactions during digital tasks, with potential to advance research on user-in-the-loop tool-use agents by addressing real-world complexities.

title: PhantomFill: When the Form Demands an Answer, Language Models Invent One
summary:
Language models in production do not write prose. They fill forms: JSON fields, function arguments, extraction templates. We show that the form itself causes hallucination.
  We ask thirteen models the same question about the same input and change only the answer format. The inputs are built so the question cannot be answered: a viral post showing 12,400 likes but no visible replies, a support ticket whose call was never transcribed. In free text, GPT-5.5 answers honestly. It says there is no reply data, 98% of the time. Given a required JSON field for sentiment, the same model invents an answer 40 times out of 40. It fabricates the mood of crowds it never saw and quotes customers it never heard.
  The pattern holds with force. Required fields drive fabrication to 100% in ten of thirteen models. An explicit "insufficient evidence" option rescues only the frontier: all nine open-weight models ignore it. A direct instruction, do not infer sentiment, is overridden by the schema in four of six models. Resistance does not come with scale: within a single model family, the smallest model refuses, the mid-sized model fabricates, the largest refuses again. Honesty under format pressure is a training outcome that no one is measuring.
  The fabrication hides exactly where hedging is impossible: in required enums and minimum-count arrays, fields where no disclaimer fits. We release PhantomFill, a benchmark with deterministic scoring and two reportable numbers: the Coerced Fabrication Rate and the Escape Utilization Rate. The fix we test is one line of schema. The failure we measure is everywhere.

AI.tldr: Language models hallucinate when forced to fill structured formats like JSON fields, even when they honestly answer "I don't know" in free text - required fields drive fabrication to 100% in most models.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates how production language models are increasingly used to fill structured forms (JSON fields, function arguments, extraction templates) rather than generate prose, and examines how these structured formats themselves cause hallucination.
AI.method: The researchers tested 13 models with the same unanswerable questions (e.g., viral post with likes but no replies, support ticket without transcription) while varying only the answer format. They measured fabrication rates when models were forced to fill required fields in structured formats versus free text responses.
AI.result: Required fields drive fabrication to 100% in 10 of 13 models. GPT-5.5 answers honestly 98% of the time in free text but fabricates 40/40 times when required to fill JSON sentiment fields. Even with explicit "insufficient evidence" options, 9 of 13 open-weight models ignore it. Direct instructions not to infer sentiment are overridden by schema requirements in 4 of 6 models.
AI.conclusion: The study reveals that honesty under format pressure is an unmeasured training outcome. Fabrication hides where hedging is impossible - in required enums and minimum-count arrays. The researchers introduce PhantomFill benchmark to measure Coerced Fabrication Rate and Escape Utilization Rate, finding this failure pattern is widespread and requires schema-level fixes.

title: Marking the Wrong Symptoms: Evaluating LLM Watermarks in Medical Texts
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into clinical workflows, stressing the need for reliable traceability of model-generated output with watermarking. Yet, most watermarks are evaluated on general-purpose benchmarks, leaving domains like medicine, where small token-level perturbations can result in significant semantic changes, underexplored. In this work, we present the first rigorous study of how LLM watermarks affect medical performance, benchmarking 5 watermarking schemes across 11 LLMs and 7 VLMs on various tasks spanning unimodal and multimodal clinical reasoning. Importantly, we complement existing evaluations by introducing a human-expert-validated pipeline for systematically auditing medical reasoning quality, terminological precision, and induced hallucinations. Our results reveal that watermarking can induce substantial degradation across multiple failure modes, including lexical corruption, hallucinated terminology, and amplified misattribution or omission of image findings. Notably, we find that the absence of domain-specific analyses, combined with aggregate metrics that miss failures inherent to clinical text, can systematically obscure practical watermark-induced degradations. Our findings establish domain-specific evaluation as a prerequisite for the safe deployment of watermarked models in medicine, where current benchmarks can otherwise mask clinically consequential failures.

AI.tldr: LLM watermarks degrade medical performance significantly across multiple failure modes, highlighting the need for domain-specific evaluation beyond general benchmarks for safe clinical deployment.
AI.motivation: Large language models are being integrated into clinical workflows, requiring reliable traceability via watermarking. However, most watermark evaluations use general-purpose benchmarks, leaving medicine underexplored despite the critical nature of medical text where small token-level perturbations can cause significant semantic changes.
AI.method: First rigorous study benchmarking 5 watermarking schemes across 11 LLMs and 7 VLMs on various tasks spanning unimodal and multimodal clinical reasoning. Introduced a human-expert-validated pipeline for systematically auditing medical reasoning quality, terminological precision, and induced hallucinations.
AI.result: Watermarking induces substantial degradation across multiple failure modes: lexical corruption, hallucinated terminology, and amplified misattribution or omission of image findings. Aggregate metrics miss failures inherent to clinical text, systematically obscuring practical watermark-induced degradations.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific evaluation is a prerequisite for safe deployment of watermarked models in medicine, as current benchmarks can mask clinically consequential failures. The absence of domain-specific analyses combined with aggregate metrics can systematically obscure practical degradations.

title: Bayesian uncertainty estimation improves clinical decision making in medical AI agents
summary: Machine learning models for medical image analysis typically lack a reliable measure of confidence, limiting their use in ambiguous or atypical cases. Here we show that Monte Carlo dropout, applied to a multi-task chest-radiograph classifier (eight thoracic findings, 137,593 training images), provides an epistemic uncertainty signal that tracks generalisation across training-set scales and flags confident yet error-prone predictions. Adding this signal to the point prediction raised error-detection AUROC from 0.74 to 0.77 ($Δ$AUROC +0.023, 95% CI [+0.014, +0.033]). In a controlled 2x2 factorial experiment, a clinical-decision-support agent exploited this uncertainty only when it was delivered as a binary error-risk flag rather than as raw scores, cutting confident misdiagnoses on unreliable findings from 8.5% to 2.7%. Epistemic uncertainty estimation thus carries decision-relevant information beyond point predictions, but its value for downstream agents depends on how it is communicated.

AI.tldr: Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty estimation improves error detection in chest X-ray classification and reduces misdiagnoses when communicated as binary error-risk flags rather than raw scores.
AI.motivation: Medical image analysis models lack reliable confidence measures, limiting their use in ambiguous or atypical cases where uncertainty is high.
AI.method: Applied Monte Carlo dropout to a multi-task chest radiograph classifier (8 findings, 137,593 training images) to obtain epistemic uncertainty signals, then tested how different uncertainty communication formats affect clinical decision support.
AI.result: Uncertainty signal improved error-detection AUROC from 0.74 to 0.77. In a factorial experiment, presenting uncertainty as binary error-risk flags (vs raw scores) reduced confident misdiagnoses from 8.5% to 2.7% for unreliable findings.
AI.conclusion: Epistemic uncertainty estimation provides decision-relevant information beyond point predictions, but its downstream clinical value depends critically on how it's communicated to users - binary flags work better than raw scores.

title: The Active Ingredient in Muon's Grokking
summary: The Muon optimizer reaches the grokking threshold on modular arithmetic faster than AdamW. Prior work attributes this to "spectral-norm constraints plus orthogonalized momentum" but does not isolate which mechanism matters. To better understand Moun's behavior, we run multi-seed and multi-learning-rate sweeps to decompose and stress-test the effect. First, an ablation shows the speedup comes from orthogonalization (the Newton-Schulz iteration): orthogonalize-only matches full Muon, whereas spectral-only is no faster than AdamW and is unreliable, and this verdict holds across learning rates. Second, a mechanistic analysis finds that orthogonalizing optimizers reach generalization at roughly 3x lower spectral norm and, controlling for how much the embedding actually moves, settle into a lower-norm solution rather than simply perturbing the embedding less. Third, reducing the Newton-Schulz iteration count from five to one accelerates reaching the threshold but makes the grokked solution fragile, prone to transient collapse, with fragility that grows with learning rate; a single iteration is fast and stable only at small learning rate, while the canonical five iterations are the learning-rate-robust choice. We also show spectral scaling can be dropped at no measured cost. A methodological thread runs throughout: under a stability-aware metric, "faster" claims about grokking optimizers can invert, so we report both first-crossing and sustained-grok times. To support reproducibility, we release our full training and analysis code at https://github.com/louiswang524/muon-grokking-frontier

AI.tldr: Muon optimizer outperforms AdamW on modular arithmetic grokking due to orthogonalization, not spectral constraints; single iteration orthogonalization is fast but fragile, while 5 iterations are robust; spectral scaling is unnecessary.
AI.motivation: Prior work attributes Muon's superiority over AdamW to "spectral-norm constraints plus orthogonalized momentum" but doesn't isolate which mechanism matters, motivating a detailed decomposition study.
AI.method: Multi-seed and multi-learning-rate sweeps with ablation studies: comparing orthogonalize-only vs spectral-only vs full Muon; mechanistic analysis of spectral norms; testing different Newton-Schulz iteration counts; stability-aware metrics with first-crossing and sustained-grok times.
AI.result: Speedup comes from orthogonalization (Newton-Schulz iteration), not spectral constraints; orthogonalizing reaches generalization at 3x lower spectral norm; single iteration accelerates threshold but causes fragile solutions; 5 iterations are learning-rate-robust; spectral scaling can be dropped without cost.
AI.conclusion: Orthogonalization is the key mechanism in Muon's grokking superiority; careful iteration count selection balances speed vs stability; spectral constraints are unnecessary; methodological care needed when measuring optimizer performance on grokking tasks.

title: ClickGuard: Detecting and Spoiling Clickbait News with Informativeness Measures and Large Language Models
summary: This paper presents an AI-driven browser extension that identifies clickbait to help users avoid misleading Internet articles. Moving beyond traditional detection, the application employs a hybrid machine learning architecture that combines transformer-based embeddings with linguistically motivated features and a custom "baitness" score. After evaluating various natural language processing techniques -- from classic vectorizers to large language model (LLM) embeddings -- an XGBoost-based model was developed that achieves an F1-score of 91% on the open combined dataset. Most importantly, the tool can warn users before and after they access a clickbait article. After opening an article, the user receives a percentage score indicating the likelihood that it is clickbait. The prediction is explained based on the analyzed metrics, including those specifically developed within the proposed system. The browser extension also provides a clickbait spoiler -- a one- to two-sentence summary of the entire article. Demo video:https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJ1gkQV82C4}{https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJ1gkQV82C4

AI.tldr: An AI-powered browser extension that detects clickbait articles using a hybrid ML approach, achieving 91% F1-score, and provides real-time warnings and article summaries to users.
AI.motivation: To help users avoid misleading clickbait articles on the Internet by developing a practical tool that goes beyond traditional detection methods and provides real-time protection.
AI.method: A hybrid machine learning architecture combining transformer-based embeddings with linguistically motivated features and a custom "baitness" score. The system evaluates various NLP techniques including classic vectorizers and LLM embeddings, ultimately developing an XGBoost-based model for classification.
AI.result: Achieves 91% F1-score on an open combined dataset. The browser extension successfully warns users before and after accessing clickbait articles, provides percentage scores indicating clickbait likelihood, offers explanations based on analyzed metrics, and generates clickbait spoilers (1-2 sentence summaries).
AI.conclusion: The paper presents a practical, high-performance AI-driven browser extension that effectively identifies clickbait articles with explainable predictions, providing users with both preventive warnings and post-access information, thereby enhancing online content consumption.

title: HiMe: Real-Time Self-Hosted Personal Agent Platform for Health Insights with Wearable Devices
summary: Traditional approaches to wearable health signal analysis, such as smartwatches, are constrained by rigid analytical frameworks and limited personalisation. The emergence of LLM agents creates a new opportunity for Personal Health Agentic Analysis, where health insights can be generated adaptively and in context. However, currently there is no open-source locally deployable platform capable of processing personal health data in real time while preserving privacy. We present HiMe, a locally deployable, privacy-first agent platform that is fully compatible with real-time health data ecosystems across a wide range of wearable devices. HiMe is guided by three design principles. The database is treated as a first-class component. Effectiveness and efficiency are jointly optimised to achieve a low-cost Pareto-optimal balance. Data are processed in real time while the user is modelled over the long term. Together, these principles make it practical for individuals to harness Personal Health Agents for continuous, personalised health monitoring for better wellbeing.

AI.tldr: HiMe is an open-source, locally deployable privacy-first agent platform for real-time personal health data analysis from wearables using LLM agents, designed for continuous personalized health monitoring.
AI.motivation: Traditional wearable health analysis is constrained by rigid frameworks and limited personalization. While LLM agents offer opportunities for adaptive Personal Health Agentic Analysis, there's currently no open-source locally deployable platform that processes health data in real-time while preserving privacy.
AI.method: HiMe follows three design principles: 1) Treating database as first-class component, 2) Jointly optimizing effectiveness and efficiency for low-cost Pareto-optimal balance, and 3) Processing data in real-time while modeling users over the long term. It's a locally deployable, privacy-first agent platform fully compatible with real-time health data ecosystems across various wearable devices.
AI.result: HiMe presents a practical platform that enables individuals to harness Personal Health Agents for continuous, personalized health monitoring for better wellbeing by processing data locally in real-time while preserving privacy.
AI.conclusion: HiMe addresses the gap for open-source locally deployable health agent platforms, making personal health agentic analysis practical for individuals through its privacy-first, real-time processing approach with long-term user modeling.

title: Scaling Closed-Loop Feature Channel Configuration with LLMs
summary: Promising initial results in closed-loop large-language-model-based channel-configuration search demonstrated that neural-network widths can be optimized directly through executable code generation and accuracy feedback. However, those results were obtained from a relatively sparse set of valid evaluations, leaving open whether the observed optimization behavior transfers to a denser sampling regime and whether additional architectural regularities emerge when more generated networks are evaluated. To test this, the same search setting is scaled to 250 candidate networks per fine-tuning cycle. The analysis covers 2000 generated candidates from 8 complete cycles, yielding 462 verified CIFAR-100 evaluations after task and metadata filtering. Per-cycle mean accuracy exhibits a positive linear trend with slope 9.87e-4 (p=0.043), while the high-performing frontier improves more strongly: the best observed accuracy increases from 0.3144 to 0.3676, and both the top-5 and top-10 cycle-level means exhibit positive trends. The scaled run also reveals improved parameter efficiency. The best model reaches 0.3676 with 11.8M parameters, compared with an early high-performing model at 0.3144 with 166.5M parameters. Beyond accuracy, the larger sample exposes architectural regularities that were difficult to assess from sparse observations. Non-power-of-two channel widths occur in 41.8% of verified candidates, and the strongest models share structured channel-allocation patterns characterized by moderate early widths and expanded middle or later blocks. These findings indicate that the channel-search signal observed in the initial study transfers

AI.tldr: Scaling up neural architecture search with LLM-based channel configuration generation from sparse to dense sampling reveals positive accuracy trends, improved parameter efficiency, and architectural regularities in network designs.
AI.motivation: Previous work showed promising results for LLM-based channel configuration search through code generation and accuracy feedback, but results were based on sparse evaluations. The authors wanted to test if the optimization behavior transfers to denser sampling and if additional architectural patterns emerge with more generated networks.
AI.method: Scaled the same search setting to evaluate 250 candidate networks per fine-tuning cycle. Analyzed 2000 generated candidates from 8 complete cycles, with 462 verified CIFAR-100 evaluations after filtering. Used LLM-based executable code generation and accuracy feedback to optimize neural network widths.
AI.result: Found positive linear trend in per-cycle mean accuracy (slope 9.87e-4, p=0.043). Best accuracy improved from 0.3144 to 0.3676. Parameter efficiency improved dramatically: best model reached 0.3676 with 11.8M parameters vs early model's 0.3144 with 166.5M parameters. Non-power-of-two widths occurred in 41.8% of candidates. Strongest models showed structured patterns with moderate early widths and expanded middle/later blocks.
AI.conclusion: The channel-search signal from initial studies transfers well to denser sampling. Denser evaluation reveals architectural regularities and yields more parameter-efficient models, confirming the viability of LLM-based neural architecture search for channel configuration optimization.

title: Stochastic Sampling is Epistemically Shallow: The Dimensionality Gap Between Temperature Variation and Model Diversity in LLMs
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at EIML@ICML 2026
summary: When a language model gives different answers on repeated runs, does that variation reveal what it does not know? Self-consistency turns the variation into a per-question uncertainty estimate via majority voting. But does the same variation reveal cross-question structure -- related questions flipping together, the way a diverse ensemble does? We compare two regimes on the same questions: one model run $100$ times at $τ=1$ versus an ensemble of $24$ LLMs run once each at $τ=0$. A Marchenko--Pastur random-matrix test separates signal from sampling noise on both sides. Within any single model, at most one dimension rises above noise across five families and three benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K). Across the ensemble, four eigenvalues clear the noise edge, while a matched-difficulty Bernoulli null produces at most one in $500$ Monte Carlo draws. Self-consistency gives accurate per-question uncertainty but no detectable cross-question structure; only a diverse ensemble surfaces what a model does not know.

AI.tldr: Self-consistency methods provide per-question uncertainty estimates but lack detectable cross-question structure, while diverse ensembles of different LLMs reveal what models don't know through correlated patterns across questions.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates whether the variation in language model outputs across repeated runs reveals not just per-question uncertainty but also cross-question structure - whether related questions flip together in a consistent pattern, similar to how diverse ensembles behave.
AI.method: The researchers compare two regimes: (1) one model run 100 times at temperature τ=1, and (2) an ensemble of 24 different LLMs each run once at τ=0. They use a Marchenko-Pastur random-matrix test to separate signal from sampling noise across five families and three benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K).
AI.result: Within any single model, at most one dimension rises above noise, while across the diverse ensemble, four eigenvalues clear the noise edge. A matched-difficulty Bernoulli null produces at most one eigenvalue above noise in 500 Monte Carlo draws. Self-consistency provides accurate per-question uncertainty but no detectable cross-question structure.
AI.conclusion: Self-consistency methods are effective for estimating per-question uncertainty but cannot reveal cross-question structure; only diverse ensembles of different language models can surface what a model does not know through correlated patterns across questions.

authors: Elderly People with Frailty or Dementia Azul Debenedetti
title: SafeStep: AI-powered Travel Assistance for Elderly People with Frailty or Dementia
summary: More than a million people in the UK suffer from frailty or dementia, which severely compromise their ability to travel in urban environments. This paper presents SafeStep, an AI-driven travel system that assists elderly users with their journeys. At the core of SafeStep is a novel travel graph representation, which integrates route planning with predictive modelling. For each stage of a journey, the system (i) generates personalized failure scenarios using a combi-nation of LLMs and the Anticip8 behavioral prediction engine, (ii) proposes targeted interventions, and (iii) estimates the impact of interventions on out-come probabilities. This enables SafeStep to select interventions that maximize the likelihood of the person reaching their destination. SafeStep was evaluated through experiments on travel graph generation and a field study involving 26 real-world journeys. Results showed that combining Anticip8 for failure pre-diction with GPT-based models for intervention evaluation yields the most re-liable performance. User feedback indicated that SafeStep improves confidence and perceived safety during travel, although interface usability needs to be im-proved for the target demographic. In the future, we would like to improve and release SafeStep. The AI system that was developed for SafeStep could be ap-plied in other areas, such as mental health, career coaching and addiction treatment.

AI.tldr: SafeStep is an AI-driven travel assistance system for elderly users with frailty/dementia that uses a travel graph representation to predict journey failure scenarios, propose interventions, and maximize successful travel outcomes.
AI.motivation: Over a million people in the UK suffer from frailty or dementia, severely compromising their ability to travel in urban environments. There's a need for systems that can assist elderly users with safe and confident travel.
AI.method: The system uses a novel travel graph representation integrating route planning with predictive modeling. For each journey stage, it: (1) generates personalized failure scenarios using LLMs + Anticip8 behavioral prediction engine, (2) proposes targeted interventions, and (3) estimates intervention impact on outcome probabilities to select optimal interventions.
AI.result: Experiments on travel graph generation and a field study with 26 real-world journeys showed that combining Anticip8 for failure prediction with GPT-based models for intervention evaluation yields the most reliable performance. User feedback indicated improved confidence and perceived safety, though interface usability needs improvement for the elderly demographic.
AI.conclusion: SafeStep demonstrates effective AI-assisted travel support for elderly users. The authors plan to improve and release the system, and note that the underlying AI approach could be applied to other domains like mental health, career coaching, and addiction treatment.

title: Multimodal CoLRAG-TF: Triple-Filtered Retrieval for Complex PDFs
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over heterogeneous PDF collections remains challenging due to multimodal content, domain-specific terminology, and the need for multi-hop reasoning across dispersed evidence. We present Multimodal CoLRAG-TF, a four-axis fusion architecture that integrates dense text embeddings, BM25 keyword matching, knowledge-graph triple filtering, and image-based similarity for robust retrieval over complex documents. Our system constructs a multimodal index of 2,403 blocks extracted from 43 Japanese disaster lesson PDFs, supported by a hybrid OCR pipeline and LLM-based caption generation. To enhance compositional reasoning, we extract 11,414 OpenIE triples and index them with FAISS, enabling sub-second triple lookup and hierarchical propagation of relevance signals. A HippoRAG2-inspired coarse-to-fine retriever (volume $\to$ chapter $\to$ block) narrows the search space before final fusion scoring. Bayesian optimization over fusion weights reveals that the triple axis must dominate ($α_\text{triple} = 0.44$) to counteract lexical bias and sustain multi-hop retrieval quality. Evaluated on a 457-pair benchmark, Multimodal CoLRAG-TF achieves a Retrieval Recall of 0.9909 and a 71.6$\%$ improvement in multi-hop answer similarity over single-hop queries. An image-to-lesson pipeline using a vision LLM further demonstrates the applicability of the approach to visual inputs. These results show that triple-filtered multimodal fusion is essential for structured reasoning over noisy, heterogeneous PDFs and provides a general framework applicable beyond the disaster domain.

AI.tldr: Multimodal CoLRAG-TF is a four-axis fusion architecture for RAG that combines text embeddings, keyword matching, knowledge-graph triple filtering, and image similarity to enable robust retrieval and multi-hop reasoning over heterogeneous PDF documents.
AI.motivation: Retrieval-augmented generation over heterogeneous PDF collections is challenging due to multimodal content, domain-specific terminology, and the need for multi-hop reasoning across dispersed evidence, especially in complex domains like disaster lessons.
AI.method: 1) Builds multimodal index of 2,403 blocks from 43 Japanese disaster PDFs using hybrid OCR and LLM-based caption generation. 2) Extracts 11,414 OpenIE triples and indexes them with FAISS for sub-second lookup. 3) Uses HippoRAG2-inspired coarse-to-fine retriever (volume→chapter→block). 4) Implements four-axis fusion: dense text embeddings, BM25 keyword matching, knowledge-graph triple filtering, and image similarity. 5) Uses Bayesian optimization to determine optimal fusion weights.
AI.result: Achieves Retrieval Recall of 0.9909 on 457-pair benchmark, with 71.6% improvement in multi-hop answer similarity over single-hop queries. Bayesian optimization shows triple axis must dominate (α_triple = 0.44) to counteract lexical bias. Image-to-lesson pipeline further demonstrates applicability to visual inputs.
AI.conclusion: Triple-filtered multimodal fusion is essential for structured reasoning over noisy, heterogeneous PDFs and provides a general framework applicable beyond the disaster domain, effectively addressing challenges of multi-modal content and multi-hop reasoning.

title: JAXBench: Benchmarking Autonomous TPU Kernel Optimization
summary: Rigorous benchmarks have driven progress in autonomous GPU kernel performance optimization by establishing a shared target to hillclimb on, but no equivalent exists for TPUs. We present JAXBench, a TPU-native benchmark suite for AI-generated kernel optimization on Google Cloud TPUs. JAXBench comprises 50 JAX workloads that are both relevant and provide headroom for optimization. We extract 17 production ML operators from architectures in the public MaxText library such as Llama-3.1, DeepSeek-V3, Mixtral, Mamba-2, and AlphaFold2, and translate 33 operators from KernelBench that are validated for correctness and set with new problem sizes that achieve high TPU v6e MXU utilization. Eight of the 17 production operators ship with hand-optimized Pallas kernels from the public Tokamax library and block-size tuned to establish an expert upper-bound baseline. We evaluate four feedback-driven methods on generating candidate Pallas kernels for JAXBench. Across the full suite with Gemini 3 Flash, we find that target-specific context matters more than model scale on a sparsely-documented DSL like Pallas. Conditioning on curated TPU documentation raises per-sample correctness from 5.8% to 37.3% and solves 48 of 50 benchmarks at a 1.28x geomean speedup. Search structure yields significant gains once correctness is achieved, with Autocomp's beam-search pipeline reaching a 1.36x geomean speedup over XLA. On the 8 hand-tuned kernels, Autocomp reaches 1.60x geomean over XLA, recovering most of the 2.08x Tokamax upper bound but trailing on the specialized paged and ragged attention operators. High-quality TPU kernel optimization remains a challenging task, and we release the JAXBench benchmark, evaluation harness, and baseline results to support open source contributions.

AI.tldr: JAXBench is a new benchmark suite for AI-generated kernel optimization on Google Cloud TPUs, featuring 50 JAX workloads with production ML operators, establishing baselines and evaluating AI-driven optimization methods.
AI.motivation: While rigorous benchmarks exist for GPU kernel optimization, no equivalent benchmark suite exists for TPUs, creating a gap in measuring progress for AI-generated kernel optimization on TPU hardware.
AI.method: The authors created JAXBench with 50 JAX workloads: 17 production ML operators from MaxText library architectures and 33 operators from KernelBench adapted for TPU. They established expert baselines using hand-optimized Pallas kernels and evaluated four feedback-driven methods for generating candidate Pallas kernels, testing Gemini 3 Flash with various conditioning approaches.
AI.result: Target-specific context proved more important than model scale for Pallas DSL, with curated TPU documentation raising correctness from 5.8% to 37.3% and solving 48/50 benchmarks at 1.28x geomean speedup. Autocomp's beam-search pipeline achieved 1.36x geomean over XLA, and on hand-tuned kernels reached 1.60x geomean, recovering most of the 2.08x expert upper bound.
AI.conclusion: High-quality TPU kernel optimization remains challenging but achievable with proper context and search methods. The authors release JAXBench as an open benchmark to support progress in this field.

title: Compact Latent Coordination for Autonomous Vehicles at Unsignalized Intersections
summary:
Coordinating autonomous vehicles at unsignalized intersections remains a critical challenge for multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) systems, which typically struggle with combinatorial action spaces, reliance on privileged information, or rigid agent designs. We propose Master-Agent Proto-plan System (MAPS), a hierarchical deep reinforcement learning (DRL) architecture in which a centralized Master agent generates a compact, continuous embedding, denoted as proto-plan, that encodes a global coordination strategy. Decentralized Worker agents integrate this embedding with local observations to execute vehicle-specific control, decoupling strategic intent from tactical execution and enabling independent optimization of each module.
  As a proof-of-concept evaluation of this coordination mechanism, we test MAPS across 72 intersection configurations in HighwayEnv. MAPS achieves collision-free navigation while significantly reducing average travel time, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. The learned proto-plans further exhibit robust generalization: a system trained with three agents achieves a 94% success rate when deployed zero-shot to five-agent scenarios, confirming that proto-plan-based hierarchical learning provides a promising framework for multi-vehicle coordination.

AI.tldr: MAPS uses a hierarchical DRL approach with a Master agent generating global coordination embeddings (proto-plans) that decentralized Worker agents use for vehicle-specific control, achieving superior performance in unsignalized intersection coordination.
AI.motivation: Current MARL systems for autonomous vehicle coordination at unsignalized intersections have critical limitations including combinatorial action spaces, reliance on privileged information, and rigid agent designs that hinder effective multi-agent coordination.
AI.method: Proposes MAPS - a hierarchical deep reinforcement learning architecture where a centralized Master agent generates continuous embeddings (proto-plans) encoding global coordination strategies, which decentralized Worker agents integrate with local observations to execute vehicle-specific control, decoupling strategic intent from tactical execution.
AI.result: MAPS achieves collision-free navigation while significantly reducing average travel time across 72 intersection configurations in HighwayEnv, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. The system demonstrates strong generalization with 94% success rate when deployed zero-shot from 3-agent to 5-agent scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Proto-plan-based hierarchical learning provides a promising framework for multi-vehicle coordination, offering robust generalization and effective decoupling of strategic coordination from tactical execution in autonomous vehicle systems.

title: Adaptive Depth in Looped Transformers: Diagnosing Learned Halting Gates and Trajectory Readouts
summary: Looped Transformers increase test-time computation by repeatedly applying a shared recurrent block. Learned halting objectives in looped Transformers typically use a single exit distribution both as the inference-time stopping rule and as the training-time weighting of per-depth losses. This entangles exit selection with trajectory formation: the gate not only chooses which recurrent state to use, but also determines how strongly each intermediate state is supervised. Consequently, poor adaptive-compute performance can arise from the readout, the induced trajectory, or their interaction. We study adaptive depth in looped Transformers through this trajectory--readout lens, across controlled synthetic tasks (modular arithmetic and binary parity) and large-scale Ouro-1.4B and 2.6B checkpoints. We find that fixed-prior depth supervision, which shapes the trajectory without an input-dependent halting policy, produces difficulty-aware trajectories whose intermediate states expose useful stopping signals, and that simple post-hoc confidence readouts often match or outperform learned linear and MLP gates. Fitting gates on frozen trajectories localizes the failure: it appears to stem mainly from the trajectory induced by joint gate training rather than from limited gate expressivity. The same pattern is present in Ouro evaluations, where pretrained ponder gates are competitive but not uniformly Pareto-optimal, and measured latency confirms that the resulting reductions in average exit depth translate into practical inference-time savings. Our systematic diagnostic evaluation reframes adaptive depth in looped Transformers as a joint problem of trajectory formation and exit readout, rather than gate learning alone, highlighting a distinction that prior learned-halting work has often left implicit.

AI.tldr: Looped Transformers with learned halting objectives often underperform due to entangling exit selection with trajectory formation. Using fixed-prior depth supervision produces better difficulty-aware trajectories, and simple confidence-based readouts can match or outperform learned gates.
AI.motivation: Current learned halting objectives in looped Transformers use a single exit distribution for both inference-time stopping and training-time loss weighting, which entangles exit selection with trajectory formation. This coupling can lead to poor adaptive-compute performance that's difficult to diagnose.
AI.method: The authors study adaptive depth through a trajectory-readout lens, using controlled synthetic tasks (modular arithmetic, binary parity) and large-scale models (Ouro-1.4B/2.6B). They implement fixed-prior depth supervision to shape trajectories independently, then evaluate simple post-hoc confidence readouts versus learned linear/MLP gates. They also fit gates on frozen trajectories to isolate trajectory vs. gate effects.
AI.result: Fixed-prior depth supervision produces difficulty-aware trajectories with useful stopping signals. Simple confidence readouts often match or outperform learned gates. Failure mainly stems from trajectories induced by joint gate training rather than limited gate expressivity. In Ouro evaluations, pretrained ponder gates are competitive but not uniformly Pareto-optimal, with latency savings confirming practical inference benefits.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive depth in looped Transformers should be framed as a joint problem of trajectory formation and exit readout, not just gate learning. The distinction between trajectory shaping and exit selection is crucial and often implicit in prior work. Fixed-prior supervision with simple readouts can be effective.

title: DC-Leap: Training-Free Acceleration of dLLMs via Draft-Guided Contiguous Leaping Decoding
summary: While parallel decoding is central to the efficiency of Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs), current strategies are often hindered by overly conservative confidence thresholds. These thresholds, necessitated by the Joint Probability Dependence Error (JPDE), result in redundant denoising iterations and suboptimal inference speeds. To overcome this, we propose DC-Leap, a training-free framework that enables reliable acceleration of dLLMs in the moderate-confidence regime. DC-Leap introduces a Dynamic Contiguous Verification strategy that integrates strictly-ordered causal constraints into the parallel decoding process. By progressively validating token dependencies, this mechanism effectively neutralizes the JPDE, enabling reliable acceleration with comparable performance. Furthermore, DC-Leap incorporates the draft-guided decoding mechanism, where the draft helps extend the context by leaping forward across multiple tokens, providing look-ahead context and retaining the structural benefits of bidirectional attention during inference. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that DC-Leap achieves substantial speedups, up to 53.19x on MBPP for long-sequence generation, and up to 105.02x when combined with KV-Cache with comparable generation quality. Code is available at https://github.com/ffh-wyls/DC-Leap .

AI.tldr: DC-Leap is a training-free framework that accelerates diffusion large language models (dLLMs) through dynamic contiguous verification and draft-guided decoding, achieving up to 105x speedup while maintaining generation quality.
AI.motivation: Current parallel decoding strategies for dLLMs are hindered by overly conservative confidence thresholds needed to avoid Joint Probability Dependence Error (JPDE), resulting in redundant denoising iterations and suboptimal inference speeds.
AI.method: Introduces Dynamic Contiguous Verification strategy that integrates strictly-ordered causal constraints into parallel decoding, progressively validating token dependencies to neutralize JPDE. Also incorporates draft-guided decoding where draft tokens provide look-ahead context and retain bidirectional attention benefits.
AI.result: Achieves substantial speedups up to 53.19x on MBPP for long-sequence generation, and up to 105.02x when combined with KV-Cache, while maintaining comparable generation quality.
AI.conclusion: DC-Leap enables reliable acceleration of dLLMs in moderate-confidence regimes without retraining, overcoming JPDE limitations and achieving significant inference speed improvements.

title: Toward Continuous Assurance for the Democratization of AI Agent Creation in Industry
summary: AI agents are increasingly created inside organizations by non-engineering users through low-code, no-code, and conversational development environments. This democratization enables rapid local innovation, but it also creates a reliability gap: agents that appear to users as simple productivity artifacts may depend on changing models, tools, retrieval sources, permissions, prompts, schedules, and external services. These dependencies can cause silent degradation long after deployment, even when no user directly modifies the agent. This paper identifies the reliability challenge created by democratized AI agent creation and proposes a lightweight continuous-assurance framework for citizen-created organizational agents. The framework combines dependency mapping, readiness contracts, scheduled checks, diagnostics, and lifecycle governance to assess whether an agent remains operationally ready under expected conditions. We also present an initial prototype auditor and scenario-based assessment showing how the proposed taxonomy can be translated into practical checks and actionable remediation guidance.

AI.tldr: A framework for ensuring reliability of AI agents created by non-technical users in organizations through lightweight continuous assurance with dependency tracking and readiness checks.
AI.motivation: The democratization of AI agent creation through low-code/no-code platforms enables rapid innovation but creates reliability challenges due to silent degradation from changing dependencies (models, tools, permissions, external services) even without direct user modifications.
AI.method: Proposes a lightweight continuous-assurance framework combining dependency mapping, readiness contracts, scheduled checks, diagnostics, and lifecycle governance to assess agent operational readiness.
AI.result: Presents an initial prototype auditor and scenario-based assessment demonstrating how the proposed taxonomy can be translated into practical checks and actionable remediation guidance.
AI.conclusion: Addresses the reliability gap in democratized AI agent creation by providing a systematic approach to maintain agent operational readiness despite changing dependencies and environments.

title: Generative Bayesian Filtering for State Estimation
summary: The state of a dynamic system evolves over time, switching among several latent modes that govern its observable behavior. Filtering methods infer the latent state from observations. Classical filtering approaches, including Kalman filters, typically rely on simple observation models, such as linear-Gaussian models, that are incapable of characterizing the increasingly nonlinear and heterogeneous patterns in high-dimensional sensor signals. To tackle the challenge, we propose Generative Bayesian Filtering (GBF), a filtering framework that replaces restrictive observation models with pretrained conditional generative models parametrized by conditional variational autoencoders (CVAE). For online inference, GBF performs a Bayesian prediction-update recursion in which the measurement update is formulated as a posterior sampling problem that combines the dynamical prior with the CVAE-induced likelihood. The resulting filtering problem is then transformed into a score-based sampling problem, which naturally inherits the flexibility from generative models and the uncertainty quantification capabilities from ensembling. Experiments on synthetic datasets and real-world applications involving manufacturing system monitoring and arrhythmia diagnosis demonstrate that GBF improves state estimation accuracy and robustness relative to baseline approaches.

AI.tldr: GBF is a new filtering framework that replaces traditional simple observation models with pretrained conditional generative models (CVAEs) for better handling of nonlinear, high-dimensional sensor signals.
AI.motivation: Classical filtering approaches (like Kalman filters) rely on simple observation models (linear-Gaussian) that can't characterize increasingly nonlinear and heterogeneous patterns in high-dimensional sensor signals from dynamic systems with multiple latent modes.
AI.method: Replaces restrictive observation models with pretrained conditional generative models (CVAEs). Uses Bayesian prediction-update recursion where the measurement update is formulated as a posterior sampling problem combining dynamical prior with CVAE-induced likelihood, then transformed into a score-based sampling problem.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic datasets and real-world applications (manufacturing system monitoring and arrhythmia diagnosis) demonstrate improved state estimation accuracy and robustness compared to baseline approaches.
AI.conclusion: GBF successfully addresses limitations of classical filtering by leveraging generative models for flexible nonlinear pattern handling while maintaining uncertainty quantification through ensembling, making it effective for real-world dynamic systems with complex sensor signals.

title: InferenceBench: A Benchmark for Open-Ended LLM Inference Optimization by AI Agents
summary: AI agents are increasingly used to automate research and development tasks, yet existing benchmarks typically evaluate them on prescribed workflows or narrow action spaces. Even nominally open-ended tasks can often be solved by retrieving a well-known recipe and tuning a few hyperparameters, making it unclear whether strong results reflect genuine optimization or memorized solutions. We introduce InferenceBench, where an agent must deploy an OpenAI-compatible inference server and optimize the speed of LLM inference. Each agent receives a target LLM, one H100 GPU, an optimization scenario, and a wall-clock time budget of two hours. Three optimization scenarios isolate distinct bottlenecks of inference (prefill latency, decode latency, and concurrent request throughput) and a fourth balances all three at the same time. Across 15 frontier agent configurations, agents reliably improve over a naive PyTorch baseline (up to $8.08\times$) and often match or exceed serving engines with default settings ($4.05\times$ for vLLM), but still fall below a simple hyperparameter search under the same time budget (up to $11.53\times$). Qualitative analysis of agent trajectories shows that although agents enumerate many relevant optimization techniques, they overwhelmingly converge on a single inference framework. They test only a few distinct configurations and spend the remaining budget re-measuring, repairing, or optimizing hyperparameters rather than exploring substantially different strategies. This suggests the bottleneck is not domain knowledge, but the ability to propose diverse configurations, evaluate them systematically, and submit the best identified solution. Overall, InferenceBench reflects the ability of agents to operate in an open-ended AI engineering setting, where memorized solutions lead to limited improvements.

AI.tldr: InferenceBench is an open-ended benchmark for evaluating AI agents on optimizing LLM inference server performance across different optimization scenarios, revealing that agents often converge on limited strategies rather than exploring diverse solutions.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks evaluate AI agents on prescribed workflows or narrow action spaces, often allowing them to succeed by retrieving known recipes and tuning hyperparameters. It's unclear whether strong results reflect genuine optimization or memorized solutions.
AI.method: Introduced InferenceBench where agents must deploy an OpenAI-compatible inference server and optimize LLM inference speed. Each agent receives a target LLM, one H100 GPU, an optimization scenario, and a 2-hour time budget. Four scenarios isolate different inference bottlenecks: prefill latency, decode latency, concurrent request throughput, and a balanced scenario combining all three.
AI.result: Across 15 frontier agent configurations, agents reliably improved over naive PyTorch baselines (up to 8.08×) and often matched or exceeded serving engines with default settings (4.05× for vLLM). However, they still fell below simple hyperparameter search (up to 11.53×). Agents overwhelmingly converged on a single inference framework, tested few configurations, and spent remaining budget re-measuring/repairing rather than exploring diverse strategies.
AI.conclusion: The bottleneck for AI agents in open-ended AI engineering settings isn't domain knowledge, but rather the ability to propose diverse configurations, evaluate them systematically, and submit the best solution. Memorized solutions lead to limited improvements in such settings.

title: The Boundaries of Automation: A Theory of Persistent Human Participation
summary: The rapid progress of AI has intensified the long-standing pursuit of automation: replacing human participation with algorithms wherever possible. Implicit in this pursuit is the assumption that humans remain in the loop only because current AI systems are not yet sufficiently capable. This paper challenges that assumption. Rather than asking how far automation can extend, we ask where its conceptual limits lie and argue that human participation may persist even with highly capable AI systems for three distinct reasons. Technical or complementarity grounds arise when humans contribute capabilities or perspectives unavailable to AI. Normative or developmental grounds arise when participation itself is valuable for human agency or learning. Most importantly, emergence grounds arise from target emergence: in some activities, the target is not fully specified in advance but instead emerges through the interaction itself. In these cases, human participation is not merely a means of improving execution but is constitutive of the target being produced. Human--AI co-construction, understood as the joint production of outcomes by humans and AI systems, is therefore not simply a temporary response to imperfect AI, but a persistent feature of activities whose objectives emerge through participation. This perspective has important implications for the limits of automation and for the design, evaluation, and ethics of future AI systems.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the assumption that human participation in AI systems is only temporary until AI becomes capable enough to fully automate tasks. It argues that human participation will persist even with advanced AI for technical, normative, and emergent reasons, particularly when objectives emerge through interaction.
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by challenging the dominant assumption in AI automation research that humans remain in the loop only because AI systems are not yet sufficiently capable. The authors want to question this pursuit of full automation and explore where the conceptual limits of automation actually lie.
AI.method: The paper uses conceptual analysis and philosophical reasoning rather than empirical research. It proposes a framework for understanding persistent human participation through three distinct grounds: technical/complementarity, normative/developmental, and emergence grounds.
AI.result: The paper identifies three reasons why human participation will persist even with highly capable AI systems: (1) technical complementarity where humans provide capabilities AI lacks, (2) normative/developmental reasons where participation itself is valuable for human learning and agency, and (3) emergence grounds where objectives emerge through interaction rather than being predetermined.
AI.conclusion: Human-AI co-construction is not just a temporary response to imperfect AI but a persistent feature of activities where objectives emerge through participation. This perspective has important implications for automation limits, AI system design, evaluation, and ethics.

title: Do Active SAE Feature Planes Carry More Holonomy? A Preregistered Reversal in Gemma
comment: 23 pages, 5 figures. Preregistered confirmatory study; frozen experiment record archived at Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.20960027
summary: This paper tests whether holonomy concentrates on active sparse-autoencoder (SAE) feature planes in Gemma 2 2B, a concrete operationalization of the broader semantic-concentration prediction. Holonomy is measured at the final-token layer-12 to layer-13 residual-stream readout by carrying a local frame around small loops using the instrument's restricted-Jacobian transport rule, then normalizing the resulting rotation by enclosed area. The design, materiality threshold, analysis, and verdict rules were preregistered and frozen before the analysed measurements were inspected. The prediction was falsified in reverse: active-feature planes carried less holonomy than matched mixed-feature controls, with an adjusted log contrast of -0.29439 and 95% interval [-0.43989, -0.14889]. A magnitude-only explanation was not supported in this design, while the three-way ordering across random, mixed-feature, and active-feature planes was undefined at matched magnitude because common support failed. Post-freeze diagnostics at the same readout supported the area law on a small validation subset, bounded matched-center displacement under a simple paired regression, and identified transport distortion as a live mechanism or confound. The result is therefore a narrow, auditable operational reversal, not a causal claim that meaning suppresses holonomy. The cause remains open, with activation-strength geometry, degree of feature engagement, dictionary geometry, matched-center displacement, activation-manifold proximity, and transport shear as live alternatives.

AI.tldr: The study tested whether holonomy (geometric rotation in neural network feature spaces) concentrates on active sparse-autoencoder feature planes in the Gemma 2 2B model. Contrary to the hypothesis, active features showed LESS holonomy than mixed-feature controls, with a significant negative log contrast of -0.29439. This represents a falsification of the original semantic-concentration prediction.
AI.motivation: To test the broader prediction that meaning/semantics concentrates geometric holonomy in neural network representations. The researchers wanted to operationalize whether active sparse-autoencoder feature planes (which presumably capture meaningful semantic features) would exhibit higher holonomy compared to mixed or random features.
AI.method: Used preregistered experimental design with frozen analysis rules. Measured holonomy at the final token between layers 12-13 of Gemma 2 2B by transporting local frames around small loops using restricted-Jacobian transport, then normalizing rotation by enclosed area. Compared holonomy on active sparse-autoencoder feature planes versus matched mixed-feature controls.
AI.result: Reverse falsification: active feature planes showed SIGNIFICANTLY LESS holonomy than mixed-feature controls (adjusted log contrast: -0.29439, 95% CI: [-0.43989, -0.14889]). No support for magnitude-only explanation. Post-analysis diagnostics validated area law, bounded matched-center displacement, and identified transport distortion as a potential mechanism/confound.
AI.conclusion: The result represents a narrow, auditable operational reversal rather than a causal claim that meaning suppresses holonomy. The cause remains open, with multiple live alternatives including activation-strength geometry, degree of feature engagement, dictionary geometry, and transport shear. The study demonstrates rigorous preregistration but yields counterintuitive results requiring further investigation.

title: DecodeShare: Tracing the Shared Subspace of LLM Decode-Time Decisions
summary: Large language models (LLMs) handle many tasks with one set of parameters, but under KV-cached inference it is unclear what task-general structure, if any, is used at decode time rather than during prefill. We propose DecodeShare, a protocol that identifies a low-dimensional subspace consistently shared across tasks in decode-time hidden states, and then tests its causal role by removing that subspace only during decoding. In our experiments, disturbing the discovered shared subspace degrades decision performance far more than disturbing either a prefill-derived or random subspace under the same intervention budget. We further show this decode-shared subspace has practical consequences for activation steering: common steering directions can overlap the task-general decode channel. Projecting out this shared subspace directly separates the functional roles of the two components, while evaluating steering vectors at decode-time yields more reliable signal for downstream deployment than prefill-based proxies. Despite its compactness, the shared subspace can serve as a high-leverage causal channel at decode time. Code is available at: https://github.com/Zishan-Shao/decodeshare.git.
