AI.tldr: LLMs have a low-dimensional task-general subspace that consistently activates during decoding across different tasks, and disturbing this decode-shared subspace significantly degrades performance more than disturbing prefill or random subspaces.
AI.motivation: While LLMs handle multiple tasks with a single parameter set, it's unclear what task-general structure operates specifically during KV-cached inference (decode time) rather than during prefill. The researchers want to identify and understand the causal role of decode-time shared representations.
AI.method: Proposed DecodeShare protocol: 1) identifies a low-dimensional subspace consistently shared across tasks in decode-time hidden states, 2) tests its causal role by removing that subspace only during decoding using intervention techniques, 3) compares effects against prefill-derived and random subspaces under same intervention budgets.
AI.result: Disturbing the discovered shared subspace degrades decision performance much more than disturbing either prefill-derived or random subspaces. The decode-shared subspace overlaps with common activation steering directions, and projecting out this subspace separates functional roles. Steering vectors evaluated at decode-time yield more reliable signals than prefill-based proxies.
AI.conclusion: Despite being compact, the shared subspace serves as a high-leverage causal channel specifically at decode time, providing insights into how LLMs handle task-general computations during inference separate from prefill processing.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Trust Estimation for Multi-LLM Systems via Structured Expert Judgement
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) ensembles are increasingly used to improve reliability by combining predictions from multiple LLMs. However, existing aggregation methods typically assume that all models are equally trustworthy, overlooking differences in uncertainty quality. This assumption is poorly suited to heterogeneous LLMs, whose reliability and capability vary significantly, making naive aggregation vulnerable to unreliable or adversarial experts. In this work, we formulate multi-LLM aggregation as a problem of uncertainty-aware trust estimation. We adapt structured expert judgment from decision theory, using context-aware calibration questions to estimate expert reliability based on the quality of its probabilistic predictions. Specifically, we employ Cooke-style log weighting, which penalises overconfident incorrect predictions and favours well-calibrated experts. We evaluate our approach on MMLU and MMLU-Pro across homogeneous, heterogeneous, and contaminated expert panels. Results show that while aggregation methods perform similarly in homogeneous settings, Cooke weighting becomes critical under heterogeneity and contamination. It achieves a superior accuracy-reliability balance and remains robust when unreliable experts are introduced. These findings suggest that Multi-LLM aggregation requires not just combining predictions, but calibrating trust under uncertainty.

AI.tldr: Cooke-style log weighting for LLM ensembles outperforms naive aggregation by calibrating trust based on uncertainty quality, especially in heterogeneous and adversarial settings.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM ensemble aggregation methods assume equal trustworthiness of all models, which fails in heterogeneous settings where model reliability and capability vary significantly, making naive aggregation vulnerable to unreliable or adversarial models.
AI.method: Formulate multi-LLM aggregation as uncertainty-aware trust estimation using structured expert judgment from decision theory. Employ Cooke-style log weighting that penalizes overconfident incorrect predictions and favors well-calibrated experts, using context-aware calibration questions to estimate reliability based on probabilistic prediction quality.
AI.result: On MMLU and MMLU-Pro benchmarks across homogeneous, heterogeneous, and contaminated expert panels: while aggregation methods perform similarly in homogeneous settings, Cooke weighting becomes critical under heterogeneity and contamination, achieving superior accuracy-reliability balance and remaining robust when unreliable experts are introduced.
AI.conclusion: Multi-LLM aggregation requires not just combining predictions, but calibrating trust under uncertainty. Cooke weighting provides an effective framework for uncertainty-aware trust estimation in heterogeneous LLM ensembles.

title: PlanE: Meta Planning of Data, Tuning, and Inference for Extractive-based LLMs
summary: Enhancing the task-specific capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) primarily requires substantial instruction-tuning datasets. However, the sheer volume of such data imposes a considerable annotation cost, and a lack of optimization methods for tailoring LLMs to specific tasks. To address the above issues, we propose a \textbf{Plan}ning framework for constructing \textbf{E}xtractive-based LLMs called \textbf{PlanE}, which includes data decomposition, instruction tuning, and prompt inference. Additionally, we introduce a Data-Tuning-Inference (DTI) planner, aimed at selecting the optimal base-LLM and its DTI combinations for specific datasets to improve construction efficiency. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our PlanE from two views: (1) across different datasets using the same base-LLM, and (2) on the same dataset using different base-LLMs. Furthermore, we validate the generalizability of the proposed DTI planner under different optimization objectives. The codes are publicly available at https://github.com/gugugu-469/PlanE.

AI.tldr: PlanE is a framework that uses planning to construct extractive-based LLMs with data decomposition, instruction tuning, and prompt inference, plus a DTI planner to optimize LLM selection for specific tasks.
AI.motivation: Traditional instruction-tuning for LLMs requires large annotated datasets which are costly, and lacks optimization methods for tailoring LLMs to specific extractive tasks.
AI.method: Proposes PlanE framework with three components: data decomposition, instruction tuning, and prompt inference. Also introduces a Data-Tuning-Inference (DTI) planner that selects optimal base-LLM and DTI combinations for specific datasets.
AI.result: Experimental results show PlanE's effectiveness across different datasets using same base-LLM and on same dataset using different base-LLMs. DTI planner demonstrates generalizability under different optimization objectives.
AI.conclusion: PlanE provides an efficient framework for constructing extractive-based LLMs with reduced annotation costs and optimized LLM selection for specific tasks through systematic planning.

title: CLOE: Christoffel Loss Autoencoder for Anomaly Detection
summary: Semi-supervised anomaly detection plays a key role in diverse fields such as process monitoring, healthcare, and finance. However, lightweight methods often struggle with high-dimensional data and typically require careful tuning of multiple hyperparameters. Among existing approaches, Christoffel Function--based methods are attractive due to their simplicity, requiring at most a single hyperparameter. They also benefit from a well-established theoretical foundation that yields several interesting results for data science. However, their main limitation is poor scalability to high-dimensional settings. In this paper, we introduce CLOE, a new method that combines an autoencoder for dimensionality reduction with a Christoffel Function--based detector applied in the latent space. To better align representation learning with anomaly detection, we design a novel loss function that leverages the Christoffel Function to guide the autoencoder toward representations that better capture the support of the normal data distribution. We further propose a principled procedure to set the detection threshold and an efficient strategy to tune the single remaining hyperparameter. Experiments on multiple high-dimensional tabular anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that CLOE achieves superior performance compared to existing methods, while preserving the lightweight and low-tuning advantages of Christoffel Function--based approaches.

AI.tldr: CLOE is a new semi-supervised anomaly detection method that combines an autoencoder for dimensionality reduction with Christoffel Function-based detection in latent space, achieving superior performance on high-dimensional data while maintaining low tuning requirements.
AI.motivation: Lightweight anomaly detection methods struggle with high-dimensional data and require careful hyperparameter tuning. While Christoffel Function-based methods are attractive due to simplicity and strong theoretical foundation, they have poor scalability to high-dimensional settings.
AI.method: CLOE combines an autoencoder for dimensionality reduction with Christoffel Function-based detection in the latent space. It introduces a novel loss function that uses the Christoffel Function to guide the autoencoder to better capture the support of normal data distribution. Also includes principled threshold setting and efficient hyperparameter tuning.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple high-dimensional tabular anomaly detection benchmarks show CLOE achieves superior performance compared to existing methods while preserving the lightweight and low-tuning advantages of Christoffel Function-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: CLOE successfully addresses the scalability limitations of Christoffel Function-based methods for high-dimensional data while maintaining their desirable properties of simplicity and minimal hyperparameter tuning, making it an effective solution for semi-supervised anomaly detection.

title: Benchmarking the Personalization Capabilities of Large Language Models
summary: Personalization, the act of varying a message to induce action from a specific receiver while keeping sender, channel, and time fixed, has a long tradition in psychology and marketing as a two-party problem in which sender and receiver have independent objectives. Large language models remove the bounded-inventory constraint of classical retrieval-and-ranking approaches by generating a continuum of message variants conditioned on inferred receiver state, raising the question of how well current models perform personalization in the classical sense. Existing LLM personalization benchmarks measure sender-side adaptation, in which the receiver is the same user the model is serving. The two-party question, whether a generated message induces its intended action in a third party, has been investigated only through A/B tests and small-scale human studies that cannot be re-run against a new model on demand. We adapt the Bayesian Persuasion framework of Kamenica and Gentzkow (2011) to generative agents and instantiate the formulation in sales, where receiver actions are routinely logged against the outreach that induced them. We release SDR-Bench, a public corpus of 6,279 customer success stories spanning 22 industries and approximately 200 enterprises, served through a temporally constrained simulation that prevents future-data leakage. Across frontier LLMs and deep-research agents, we observe a consistent personalization plateau and on a Fortune 100 tech cohort no model statistically separates successful from unsuccessful outreach. A field deployment with 12 professional sales representatives validates the framework, with 48 percent of model-generated content rated immediately useful and senior-expert agreement at Pearson 0.82. We release SDR-Arena and SDR-Bench publicly to support reproducible study of generative personalization at scale.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SDR-Bench, a new benchmark for evaluating LLM personalization in two-party scenarios (like sales outreach), finding that current models show a personalization plateau and fail to separate successful from unsuccessful outreach.
AI.motivation: Current LLM personalization benchmarks only measure sender-side adaptation where the model serves the same user as receiver. There's a lack of benchmarks for the classical two-party personalization problem where a message aims to induce action in a third party, which is important for applications like sales outreach.
AI.method: Adapt the Bayesian Persuasion framework to generative agents and create SDR-Bench - a corpus of 6,279 customer success stories across 22 industries with temporal constraints to prevent future-data leakage. Also develop SDR-Arena for testing, validated through field deployment with 12 professional sales representatives.
AI.result: Across frontier LLMs and deep-research agents, there's a consistent personalization plateau. No model statistically separates successful from unsuccessful outreach on a Fortune 100 tech cohort. Field deployment shows 48% of model-generated content rated immediately useful with senior-expert agreement at Pearson 0.82.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs have significant limitations in true two-party personalization despite generating message variants. The paper provides public benchmarks (SDR-Bench and SDR-Arena) to support reproducible study of generative personalization at scale, highlighting the need for better evaluation frameworks.

title: Position: Stop Reactively Patching Your Model Every Time and Start Proactive Test-Driven AI Development
comment: Accepted at ICML 2026 Position Paper Track. 18 pages
summary: Many modern AI systems are designed to operate under diverse, open-ended, use-cases. To help generalize deployed systems, many deployed-system maintenance pipelines use a reactive AI flywheel that observes emerging feedback from user behavior (errors) and patches the model accordingly. However, when used as the primary maintenance mechanism, these flywheels often ignore the broader context of these errors within the system's objectives, failing to preempt potential future edge cases, which leads to more unnecessary flywheel iterations. Also, it is statistically increasingly difficult to collect remaining errors due to the long-tail nature of open-world use-cases. This position paper argues that a proactive test-driven flywheel is required to address reactive flywheel's limitations and to approach a generalizable system. We advocate for creating a "test space" to technically map feedback data to task objectives, evolving the flywheel from reactive to proactive. We augment our position by mathematically proving a proactive one achieves better long-term scaling with fewer iterations than the reactive flywheel.

AI.tldr: The paper argues for replacing reactive AI flywheels with proactive test-driven flywheels to improve generalization and reduce iterations in deployed AI systems.
AI.motivation: Current reactive AI flywheels that patch models based on observed user errors have limitations: they ignore broader context, fail to preempt future edge cases, and struggle with long-tail open-world use cases where collecting remaining errors becomes statistically difficult.
AI.method: Propose creating a "test space" to technically map feedback data to task objectives, evolving the flywheel from reactive to proactive. This involves systematically testing for potential issues before deployment rather than just reacting to observed errors.
AI.result: Mathematically proves that a proactive test-driven flywheel achieves better long-term scaling with fewer iterations compared to reactive flywheels, addressing the statistical challenges of error collection in long-tail distributions.
AI.conclusion: A proactive test-driven flywheel approach is necessary to address reactive flywheel limitations and approach truly generalizable AI systems, with mathematical evidence supporting its superiority for long-term scaling.

title: Robust Critics: Defending LLMs Against Multi-Turn Attacks
summary:
When a user asks a language model something harmful, is it a genuine attack or a misunderstood but well-meaning question? This ambiguity is one of the central challenges of LLM safety. A model that assumes the worst harms legitimate users; one that assumes the best is easily exploited. The problem is compounded in multi-turn dialogue, where an attacker's true intent may only reveal itself gradually across many exchanges, yet existing safety frameworks apply a contextual bandit treatment, ignoring the trajectory of the conversation.
  To that end, we propose Dialogue Critic Guided Sampling (DCGS), a framework that addresses this by inferring user intent at every turn of dialogue. Instead of applying a fixed rule about what is or is not safe, DCGS learns what the user's intent is likely to be based on the full conversational history and generates responses accordingly. Formally, we model adversarial dialogue as a Markov Decision Process and learn value and regret-based critics at both the individual token and utterance (full response) levels, scoring candidate responses via an action-value critic. We prove that this inference-time reweighting approximates exponential tilting of the base policy, guaranteeing improvement in expected return for any finite candidate pool, a property that group-relative objectives do not exhibit. Evaluated on CARES-18k, WildJailbreak, Redbench, and Harmbench, DCGS outperforms strong robust baselines and frontier models on adversarial dialogue tasks. DCGS also transfers to frontier models, improving their robustness without fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: DCGS (Dialogue Critic Guided Sampling) is a framework that infers user intent at every dialogue turn to improve LLM safety in adversarial multi-turn conversations, using value-based critics to guide response generation without compromising legitimate user interactions.
AI.motivation: Current LLM safety frameworks struggle with ambiguity between genuine harmful attacks and misunderstood but well-meaning questions. Existing approaches use contextual bandit treatments that ignore conversation trajectories, causing models to either harm legitimate users by assuming the worst or become easily exploited by assuming the best, especially problematic in multi-turn dialogues where intent reveals gradually.
AI.method: Models adversarial dialogue as a Markov Decision Process and learns value and regret-based critics at both token and utterance levels. Uses an action-value critic to score candidate responses, applying inference-time reweighting that approximates exponential tilting of the base policy. Framework learns user intent based on full conversational history rather than applying fixed safety rules.
AI.result: Outperforms strong robust baselines and frontier models on adversarial dialogue tasks across CARES-18k, WildJailbreak, Redbench, and Harmbench benchmarks. Demonstrates transfer capability to frontier models, improving their robustness without requiring fine-tuning. Theoretical proof shows the approach guarantees improvement in expected return for any finite candidate pool.
AI.conclusion: DCGS effectively addresses the fundamental ambiguity problem in LLM safety by dynamically inferring user intent across dialogue trajectories, providing a theoretically grounded approach that balances safety and utility while being transferable to existing models without additional training.

title: Grounding Investor Views: Neural Predicates in the Black-Litterman Model
summary: Portfolio construction under the Black-Litterman model requires investors to specify views on asset returns alongside explicit uncertainty estimates -- a process that remains largely subjective and difficult to scale. We propose a formal approach in which neural predicates serve as a structured, probabilistic mechanism for view generation. In our formulation, structured financial analysis data is processed through a compositional hierarchy of neural predicates whose outputs -- probability distributions over market stances -- are mapped to the pick matrix $\mathbf{P}$, the view return vector $\mathbf{q}$, and the view uncertainty matrix $\boldsymbolΩ$ of the Black-Litterman model. View confidence is derived from predicate output distributions, providing a data-driven alternative to subjective uncertainty elicitation. The resulting approach is interpretable, in the sense that any portfolio weight can be traced back through the predicate's logical chain to the underlying data, and fully differentiable, enabling end-to-end learning.

AI.tldr: Neural predicates provide a structured, probabilistic mechanism for generating Black-Litterman model views, replacing subjective uncertainty with data-driven estimates while maintaining interpretability and enabling end-to-end learning.
AI.motivation: Current portfolio construction using the Black-Litterman model requires subjective specification of views on asset returns and uncertainty estimates, which is difficult to scale and lacks objectivity.
AI.method: Process structured financial data through a compositional hierarchy of neural predicates that output probability distributions over market stances. These distributions map to the Black-Litterman model parameters (pick matrix P, view return vector q, and uncertainty matrix Ω), with confidence derived from predicate output distributions.
AI.result: Creates a data-driven alternative to subjective uncertainty elicitation that is interpretable (portfolio weights traceable through logical chains to underlying data) and fully differentiable for end-to-end learning.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach provides a formal, scalable, and interpretable method for view generation in Black-Litterman portfolio construction by using neural predicates to replace subjective judgment with structured probabilistic reasoning.

title: Incomplete Prompt Jailbreaks in Large Language Models
comment: Accepted to ACL 2026 Findings. 15 pages (9 pages for main body), 13 figures
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly released as open-weight models with safeguards against harmful requests. Nevertheless, sentence completion remains vulnerable to incomplete harmful prompts. In this work, we formalize this phenomenon as incomplete prompt jailbreaks (IPJ) and provide a systematic empirical characterization of when and how incomplete prompts elicit harmful continuations. We analyze diverse attractor types associated with incomplete sentence continuation and show that LLMs systematically delay refusal until sentence termination. We further demonstrate that training models to refuse incomplete harmful prompts via parameter tuning is insufficient, failing to generalize across both content domains and attractor types. To enable fine-grained control, we identify two functional neurons: termination and continuation neurons. By clarifying their roles in sentence completion, we highlight the potential of neuron-level interventions for more precise and robust IPJ defenses.

AI.tldr: LLMs remain vulnerable to incomplete harmful prompts (IPJ) despite safeguards; systematic analysis reveals refusal delays and insufficient training defenses, pointing to neuron-level interventions as a promising solution.
AI.motivation: Open-weight LLMs have safeguards against harmful requests, but sentence completion remains vulnerable to incomplete harmful prompts, creating a security gap that needs systematic investigation.
AI.method: Systematic empirical characterization of IPJ, analysis of diverse attractor types in incomplete sentence continuation, investigation of LLM refusal patterns, parameter tuning experiments, and identification of functional neurons (termination and continuation neurons).
AI.result: LLMs systematically delay refusal until sentence termination; training models to refuse incomplete harmful prompts via parameter tuning fails to generalize across content domains and attractor types; two functional neurons (termination and continuation) identified with distinct roles.
AI.conclusion: Neuron-level interventions offer more precise and robust defenses against incomplete prompt jailbreaks, as current training approaches are insufficient; understanding termination and continuation neurons provides a pathway for fine-grained control.

title: A Graph Neural Network approach to zero-shot Digital Twins
summary: Traditional Predictive Digital Twins often remain geometrically rigid, requiring extensive retraining or fine-tuning whenever the underlying physical domain or boundary conditions change. To overcome this limitation, we present a novel framework for \textit{Zero-Shot Digital Twins} that seamlessly couples real-time visual perception with a geometry-agnostic, physics-informed reasoning engine. At the core of our architecture is the Thermodynamics-Informed Graph Neural Network architecture, a Geometric Deep Learning solver grounded in a metriplectic thermodynamic formalism that enforces energy conservation and non-negative entropy production locally through graph message passing. The framework integrates an auxiliary Graph Neural Network to infer unobservable fields (such as stress tensors or velocity and energy distributions) directly from sparse initial visual boundaries, mitigating numerical start-up transients. To bridge the sim-to-real gap, we implement a continuous closed-loop data assimilation mechanism; the pipeline tracks macroscopic deformations and free-surface fluid boundaries in real-time using deep segmentation networks combined with sparse optical flow, dynamically correcting the autoregressive simulation rollout and eliminating numerical drift. To test the validity of our approach, we demonstrate the extreme generalization capabilities of our approach across two disparate physical regimes: the large deformations of a viscoelastic beam and the non-linear sloshing of a viscous fluid. In both scenarios, the unified framework instantiates physically accurate simulations on novel, unseen geometries without case-specific retraining, operating well within real-time latency budgets (approximately 25 ms per frame) and enabling the direct projection of latent mechanical variables via Augmented Reality.

AI.tldr: Zero-Shot Digital Twins framework that integrates real-time visual perception with physics-informed GNNs for geometry-agnostic simulation without retraining, validated on viscoelastic beams and fluid sloshing.
AI.motivation: Overcome limitations of traditional Predictive Digital Twins that require extensive retraining when physical domains or boundary conditions change, enabling adaptive simulations without case-specific fine-tuning.
AI.method: Thermodynamics-Informed Graph Neural Network (GNN) architecture with metriplectic thermodynamic formalism for energy conservation and entropy production; auxiliary GNN for inferring unobservable fields; continuous closed-loop data assimilation with deep segmentation and optical flow; dynamic correction of autoregressive simulations.
AI.result: Extreme generalization across two disparate physical regimes (viscoelastic beam large deformations and viscous fluid sloshing) with physically accurate simulations on novel geometries without retraining, operating at ~25 ms per frame real-time latency, enabling AR projection of latent mechanical variables.
AI.conclusion: Proposed Zero-Shot Digital Twins framework enables geometry-agnostic, physics-informed simulation with real-time visual perception integration, demonstrating robust generalization across different physical domains while maintaining computational efficiency for practical applications.

title: VeriSimpl: Robust Optimization Modeling from Natural Language using Simplification-based Verification
summary: Natural language interfaces can greatly benefit the accessibility and usability of optimization modeling, and recent advances in large language models (LLMs) show promise in automatically translating textual problem descriptions into executable solver formulations. However, a key challenge for existing approaches is to ensure that the inferred formulation correctly implements the intended task, even if it may execute without errors. We introduce VeriSimpl, a solver LLM framework for robust natural-language-to-optimization formalization. Our approach is based on the idea of simplification-based verification, where the optimization solver is leveraged to generate simplified diagnostic queries about a candidate formulation to allow the LLM to tractably reason about the correctness of the formulation with respect to the task description. We present such simplification strategies along different dimensions with respect to problem constraints and decision variables, which allow the LLM to reason locally under fixed global contexts. Evaluations on a range of optimization benchmarks show how our approach provides consistent improvements in accuracy over existing methods, while also providing a novel high-precision self-verification signal.

AI.tldr: VeriSimpl is a framework that uses simplification-based verification to ensure LLM-generated optimization formulations correctly implement intended tasks, improving accuracy over existing methods.
AI.motivation: Natural language interfaces can improve optimization modeling accessibility, but existing LLM approaches struggle to ensure that generated formulations correctly implement the intended task, even when they execute without errors.
AI.method: Uses simplification-based verification where the optimization solver generates simplified diagnostic queries about candidate formulations, allowing LLMs to tractably reason about correctness. Presents simplification strategies for problem constraints and decision variables that enable local reasoning under fixed global contexts.
AI.result: Evaluations on optimization benchmarks show consistent accuracy improvements over existing methods, while providing a novel high-precision self-verification signal.
AI.conclusion: The VeriSimpl framework successfully addresses the key challenge of ensuring LLM-generated optimization formulations correctly implement intended tasks through solver-assisted verification, representing an advancement in robust natural-language-to-optimization formalization.

title: ReliableTableQA:How Much Supervision Does Reliability Annotation Need?
summary: We introduce ReliableTableQA, a framework for training an LLM to annotate the statistical reliability of tabular QA results, not whether the query is answerable, but whether the computed answer is statistically meaningful. In real enterprise analytics, a syntactically correct SQL query can return a value that is based on too small a sample, has an excessively wide confidence interval, or is too confounded to support action. Existing systems answer confidently in all such cases, a failure we quantify as the Unreliable Confident Answer Rate (UCAR). We contribute (1) a ten-category reliability taxonomy (R1-R10) covering hazards such as small-sample aggregates, multiple-comparison inflation, and distribution-tail mismatch; (2) a program-first data pipeline that generates 50,000 reliability-labeled training examples from a context-free grammar over public retail schemas, with schema-stratified SFT/GRPO splits; and (3) a controlled study of how much supervision calibrated reliability annotation actually requires. We find that a small, schema-stratified SFT set is remarkably sufficient: 200 examples raise reliability-flag F1 from 0.61 to 0.98 and parse rate from 0.52 to 1.00, drive UCAR to zero, and yield a model that generalizes to an unseen retail domain (Rel-F1 0.997 on held-out H&M). Against this strong SFT baseline, GRPO, commonly assumed to be essential, helps only when SFT is under-trained (+0.06-0.16 exact-flag-set match at 100 examples, in- and out-of-distribution) and provides no measurable benefit once SFT is adequate, a null result we confirm across a hard compound-flag slice, a strict exact-match metric, and out-of-distribution evaluation. Our findings reframe reliability annotation as a data-efficiency problem and delineate precisely when reinforcement fine-tuning does and does not pay off.

AI.tldr: ReliableTableQA: A framework for training LLMs to detect statistical reliability issues in tabular QA results, showing that minimal supervised fine-tuning (200 examples) achieves near-perfect performance while reinforcement learning provides marginal benefits only with inadequate training data.
AI.motivation: In enterprise analytics, SQL queries can return statistically unreliable results (small samples, wide confidence intervals, confounding issues), but existing systems confidently present these as valid answers. The paper aims to quantify and address this "Unreliable Confident Answer Rate (UCAR)" problem by teaching LLMs to identify when query results lack statistical meaningfulness.
AI.method: The authors developed: (1) A ten-category reliability taxonomy covering statistical hazards; (2) A program-first data pipeline generating 50,000 reliability-labeled examples from a context-free grammar over public retail schemas; (3) Controlled studies comparing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and GRPO reinforcement learning, with schema-stratified splits and out-of-distribution testing on unseen domains like H&M.
AI.result: Remarkably small SFT data (200 examples) achieves: reliability-flag F1 from 0.61 to 0.98, parse rate from 0.52 to 1.00, drives UCAR to zero, and generalizes to unseen retail domains (Rel-F1 0.997). GRPO provides only marginal benefits (+0.06-0.16 exact-flag-set match) when SFT is under-trained (100 examples) but offers no measurable benefit once SFT is adequate, even on hard compound-flag slices and out-of-distribution evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Reliability annotation is a data-efficiency problem solvable with minimal supervised training. Reinforcement fine-tuning (GRPO) only helps when SFT is inadequate and provides no benefit once sufficient SFT data is available. This reframes reliability annotation requirements and clarifies when reinforcement learning techniques are actually valuable for this task.

title: SonicSampler: Unified Tile-Aware Kernels for LLM Sampling and Speculative Verification
summary: Sampling in LLM inference comprises a combinatorial set of logit processing, token selection, and verification operations for speculative decoding. However, existing implementations either accelerate only subsets of this pipeline, rely on multiple kernel launches, or assume homogeneous sampling behavior across a batch, limiting support for dynamic serving workloads and preventing efficient CUDA Graph execution. We present $\textbf{SonicSampler}$, a unified suite of tile-aware Triton kernels that vertically fuses the complete sampling pipeline into a fixed, workload-aware execution model. Our kernels support dynamic per-request sampling behaviors, including grammar-constrained decoding, repetition, frequency and presence penalties, logit bias, temperature scaling, top-$k$ / top-$p$ / min-$p$ filtering, and speculative verification - within a single batched kernel while remaining fully CUDA Graph-compatible. Central to our approach is a novel hierarchical two-stage top-$k$ algorithm that achieves up to $\textbf{10x speedup}$ over competitive baselines and exploits the low-entropy structure of LLM outputs to enable efficient selection over large vocabularies. Across heterogeneous speculative decoding workloads, SonicSampler achieves up to $\textbf{16x speedup}$ over state-of-the-art baselines while preserving flexible batched execution.

AI.tldr: SonicSampler is a unified Triton kernel framework that vertically fuses the complete LLM sampling pipeline, supporting diverse per-request sampling behaviors while enabling efficient CUDA Graph execution with up to 16x speedup over baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing implementations for LLM inference sampling are fragmented - they either accelerate only subsets of the pipeline, rely on multiple kernel launches, or assume homogeneous sampling behavior across batches, limiting support for dynamic serving workloads and preventing efficient CUDA Graph execution.
AI.method: Developed SonicSampler, a suite of tile-aware Triton kernels that vertically fuses the complete sampling pipeline into a fixed, workload-aware execution model. Introduced a novel hierarchical two-stage top-k algorithm that exploits the low-entropy structure of LLM outputs for efficient selection over large vocabularies.
AI.result: Achieves up to 10x speedup for the hierarchical two-stage top-k algorithm over competitive baselines, and up to 16x speedup across heterogeneous speculative decoding workloads while preserving flexible batched execution and full CUDA Graph compatibility.
AI.conclusion: SonicSampler provides a unified, efficient solution for LLM inference sampling that supports dynamic per-request sampling behaviors within a single batched kernel while enabling CUDA Graph execution, significantly outperforming existing state-of-the-art approaches.

title: Codec-Gauge: Learning Compression-Friendly Gauges for Transformer KV Caches
summary: Long-context Transformer inference increasingly relies on KV-cache compression or quantization. Prior rotation and transform-coding results suggest that the channel basis of each key/value vector affects how faithfully a fixed backend preserves model behavior. We introduce Codec-Gauge, a post-training cache-coordinate layer that learns small orthogonal channel transforms around existing compression and quantization backends. Its frequency-distribution objective combines a token-channel DCT spectral-centroid loss with a smooth rate proxy to concentrate KV energy in low-frequency codec-facing layouts. We evaluate actual compression and decompression using measured bytes and rolling compressed-history scoring. Across six models at $3$, $4$, and $6$ bits/value, learned gauges reduce zfp KL divergence by $44.0\%$ on average relative to raw coordinates and outperform random, Hadamard, DCT, and PCA/KLT controls. The same gauges improve quality preservation for block-uniform and KIVI-style quantization. Experiments on a 27B model and long-context task prompts reproduce the quality trend, while serial storage and timing measurements validate the implemented compressed-cache paths. These results establish cache-coordinate geometry as a practical post-training variable for improving compression fidelity without changing model weights, attention semantics, or backend coding rules.

AI.tldr: Codec-Gauge: A post-training method that learns small orthogonal channel transforms to improve KV-cache compression and quantization fidelity without modifying model weights or attention mechanisms.
AI.motivation: The motivation is that long-context Transformer inference increasingly relies on KV-cache compression/quantization, and prior work suggests that the channel basis of key/value vectors affects how faithfully compression backends preserve model behavior. The authors aim to improve compression fidelity without changing model weights, attention semantics, or backend coding rules.
AI.method: The method introduces Codec-Gauge, a post-training cache-coordinate layer that learns small orthogonal channel transforms around existing compression and quantization backends. It uses a frequency-distribution objective combining a token-channel DCT spectral-centroid loss with a smooth rate proxy to concentrate KV energy in low-frequency codec-facing layouts. The approach maintains the original compression backends but optimizes the coordinate system they operate in.
AI.result: Across six models at 3, 4, and 6 bits/value, learned gauges reduce zfp KL divergence by 44.0% on average relative to raw coordinates and outperform random, Hadamard, DCT, and PCA/KLT controls. The same gauges improve quality preservation for both block-uniform and KIVI-style quantization. Experiments on a 27B model with long-context task prompts reproduce the quality improvements, while serial storage and timing measurements validate the implemented compressed-cache paths.
AI.conclusion: The results establish cache-coordinate geometry as a practical post-training variable for improving compression fidelity without changing model weights, attention semantics, or backend coding rules, offering a promising approach to enhance KV-cache compression in long-context Transformer inference.

title: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Multi-Sensor Physical Hazard Assessment
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures. Benchmark dataset, evaluation code, and raw results publicly available at: https://github.com/Faizaniqbal52/PhysicalHazardBenchmark
summary: We present an empirical benchmark evaluating how five large language models assess multisensor physical hazard data. Testing 60 scenarios across three categories - multi-sensor joint assessment, response proportionality, and pattern disambiguation - with 1,800 API calls at temperature 0.0, we find that all tested models consistently produced no precautionary warning signal across the tested scenarios where multiple sensors are simultaneously elevated below their individual safety limits, while achieving near-perfect accuracy on single-sensor threshold violations. All five models (ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, DeepSeek, Kimi, Llama 3.1 8B) score near zero on Category A multi-sensor scenarios (Q2: 0.000-0.208; Q3: 0.000-0.592) compared to strong performance on single-sensor scenarios (Category B Q1: 0.975-1.000). Structured tabular formatting shows no consistent advantage over plain prose; ChatGPT-4o performs significantly better under prose (p = 0.001). These findings have direct implications for practitioners deploying the tested models in physical safety monitoring systems.

AI.tldr: LLMs fail to identify physical hazards from multi-sensor data when individual sensors are below safety limits, despite near-perfect performance on single-sensor threshold violations.
AI.motivation: To empirically evaluate how large language models assess multisensor physical hazard data for safety monitoring applications, identifying potential limitations in real-world deployment scenarios.
AI.method: Tested 5 LLMs (ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, DeepSeek, Kimi, Llama 3.1 8B) on 60 scenarios across three categories: multi-sensor joint assessment, response proportionality, and pattern disambiguation. Conducted 1,800 API calls at temperature 0.0.
AI.result: All models consistently failed to provide precautionary warnings when multiple sensors were simultaneously elevated below individual safety limits (Category A scores: 0.000-0.208 for Q2, 0.000-0.592 for Q3). They achieved near-perfect accuracy on single-sensor threshold violations (Category B Q1: 0.975-1.000). Tabular formatting showed no consistent advantage over plain prose, with ChatGPT-4o performing better under prose.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs have a critical limitation in multisensor hazard assessment, failing to detect patterns of risk from multiple sub-threshold signals. This has direct implications for practitioners deploying these models in physical safety monitoring systems.

title: Leveraging Biokinetic Knowledge Priors for Data-Scarce Bioprocess Modeling
comment: Accepted at ICML 2026 AI for Science Workshop
summary: While deep learning has accelerated drug discovery, its impact on biomanufacturing has been considerably more limited. The reason is data scarcity. Bioreactor experiments are high-cost, take days to weeks, and are rarely shared in public form, leaving each research work with only a handful of experiments. The domain itself, however, is rich in prior knowledge. Biokinetic ordinary differential equation (ODE) models have described microbial growth for decades, yet how to inject this knowledge into a neural network has not been studied systematically. We present the first systematic study of how to inject this ODE knowledge into a neural network, comparing a data-level prior that pre-trains a generic decoder on simulated ODE curves against an architecture-level prior that embeds the ODE inside the decoder. Both consistently outperform no-prior baselines across 11 datasets and 7 microbial species. Our central finding is that the two are substitutable. A generic decoder pre-trained on simulation matches a fully bio-structured decoder trained on real data. Simulation pre-training therefore offers a simple, data-efficient recipe for deep learning under bioprocess data scarcity.

AI.tldr: Deep learning for biomanufacturing is limited by data scarcity. This paper presents a systematic study showing that pre-training neural networks on simulated biokinetic ODE models works as well as embedding ODE knowledge directly in architecture, offering a simple solution to data limitations.
AI.motivation: Deep learning has accelerated drug discovery but had limited impact on biomanufacturing due to data scarcity. Bioreactor experiments are costly, time-consuming, and rarely shared publicly. While biokinetic ODE models have existed for decades, how to effectively inject this prior knowledge into neural networks hasn't been studied systematically.
AI.method: The study compares two approaches to injecting ODE knowledge into neural networks: 1) a data-level prior that pre-trains a generic decoder on simulated ODE curves, and 2) an architecture-level prior that embeds the ODE inside the decoder. These are tested across 11 datasets and 7 microbial species.
AI.result: Both approaches consistently outperform no-prior baselines. The central finding is that the two methods are substitutable - a generic decoder pre-trained on simulation matches the performance of a fully bio-structured decoder trained on real data.
AI.conclusion: Simulation pre-training offers a simple, data-efficient recipe for deep learning under bioprocess data scarcity. This approach leverages existing domain knowledge without requiring complex architectural changes, making it accessible for real-world biomanufacturing applications.

title: Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation
comment: Technical report for the paper "Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation" accepted KDD2026
summary:
{\em Text-Attributed Graphs} (TAGs) have emerged as an expressive data model for integrating graph topology with rich textual semantics. Existing representation learning methods over TAGs suffer from severe scalability bottlenecks, particularly together with {\em Large Language Models} (LLMs). While data distillation offers a promising data-centric solution, existing methods fail to capture the complex interplay between graph and text modalities, struggle with the label scarcity inherent in semi-supervised settings, and lack the ability to produce the human-readable textual attributes required for downstream LLM-based tasks.
  To address these challenges, we propose \algo{}, a unified semi-supervised framework guided by the {\em Wasserstein Distance} (WSD). Grounded in our empirical findings on real TAGs, \algo{} introduces a graph-text collaborative encoding module that utilizes dual-pathway encoders (graph-aware and -free) within a collaborative self-training scheme to harvest reliable pseudo-labels and fuse complementary graph-text features. Furthermore, we develop a theoretically grounded WSD-based graph sketching algorithm and a cost-effective LLM text synthesis module, which leverages cluster-based keyword extraction to generate coherent, human-readable summaries for condensed nodes. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that \algo{} achieves a state-of-the-art performance-compression trade-off in terms of both GNN- and LLM-based downstream tasks, enabling effective and efficient TAG learning or analytics.

AI.tldr: ALGO is a semi-supervised framework for Text-Attributed Graphs that uses Wasserstein Distance for data distillation, enabling efficient representation learning with both graph and text modalities while generating human-readable attributes for LLM tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing TAG representation learning methods face scalability issues with LLMs, struggle with modality interplay, suffer from label scarcity in semi-supervised settings, and cannot produce human-readable text attributes needed for downstream LLM tasks.
AI.method: ALGO introduces: 1) Graph-text collaborative encoding module with dual-pathway encoders (graph-aware and graph-free) in a collaborative self-training scheme, 2) Theoretically grounded WSD-based graph sketching algorithm, 3) Cost-effective LLM text synthesis module using cluster-based keyword extraction to generate coherent node summaries.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show ALGO achieves state-of-the-art performance-compression trade-off for both GNN- and LLM-based downstream tasks, enabling effective and efficient TAG learning and analytics.
AI.conclusion: ALGO addresses key challenges in TAG representation learning by providing a unified semi-supervised framework that effectively handles modality interplay, label scarcity, and generates human-readable text attributes while maintaining computational efficiency.

title: From Atoms to Entropy: Optimal Noise Allocation for Diffusion Training in the Convex Regime
summary: How should a diffusion model decide which noise levels to train on, and how much? Despite the importance of this choice, current noise schedules are based largely on heuristics or empirical tuning. Here, we develop a general statistical framework for studying asymptotically optimal noise-level allocation in diffusion training. Our first main result concerns the fully coupled regime, where information can spread between different time points. Under convexity or Polyak-Lojasiewicz-type assumptions, we show that the optimized training schedule admits an atomic minimizer, concentrated on finitely many noise levels. Our second main result specializes this framework to an idealized independent-learner regime, intended to model temporal specialization in neural networks. Under an additional feature-noise decoupling condition, a random-matrix analysis leads to an information-theoretic proxy: the decoupled sampling density is proportional to the square root of the generative entropy rate, the rate at which conditional entropy grows along the forward process. We test these predictions in controlled settings where the coupled objective can be optimized directly, including Dirac mixtures, low-dimensional manifolds, and MNIST. In these settings, the optimized schedules are consistently finite-support, while the smooth entropic proxy closely tracks the atomic optimum in neural-network models and breaks down mainly in the fully coupled parametric case, as the theory suggests. We then evaluate the entropic schedule in larger-scale experiments, where full schedule optimization is currently intractable. The results indicate that square-root entropy scheduling can substantially improve training efficiency on discrete domains and remains competitive with standard EDM-style heuristics on continuous images.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a theoretical framework for optimal noise scheduling in diffusion model training, proving that optimized schedules concentrate on finitely many noise levels, and introduces an entropic proxy that improves training efficiency.
AI.motivation: Current noise schedules in diffusion models are based on heuristics or empirical tuning without theoretical foundations, motivating a principled statistical framework for determining optimal noise-level allocation during training.
AI.method: Develops a statistical framework for studying asymptotically optimal noise-level allocation with two regimes: 1) fully coupled regime where information spreads between time points, 2) independent-learner regime modeling temporal specialization in neural networks, using convexity/Polyak-Lojasiewicz assumptions and random-matrix analysis.
AI.result: Optimized training schedules admit atomic minimizers concentrated on finitely many noise levels; in independent-learner regime, optimal decoupled sampling density is proportional to square root of generative entropy rate; empirical validation shows finite-support schedules and entropic proxy effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Square-root entropy scheduling provides a theoretically grounded alternative to heuristic noise schedules, improving training efficiency especially on discrete domains while remaining competitive on continuous image tasks.

title: Beyond Liars' Bench: The Impact of Lie Typology, Depth, and Sparsity on Deception Detection in LLMs
comment: Presented at the AI Transparency Conference 2026, forthcoming in the AI Transparency Journal
summary: Training probes to detect deceptive outputs from large language models is still an open problem. Recent work has demonstrated that detection probes fail especially in out-of-domain scenarios -- training on one type of lie does not transfer well to deception scenarios involving other types of lies. In this work, we conduct a systematic study on how various factors impact detection performance: representation depth, probe expressivity, sparse feature representations, and the lie typology of the training data. To this end, we augment standard benchmark training data with a supplementary dataset containing diverse types of deception, including fabrication, omission, and exaggeration examples. Analyzing these factors across seven probe types, our experimental results show that the optimal representation depth is highly dataset-dependent, more expressive probes provide only selective gains over linear baselines, and sparse autoencoder features perform similarly to dense hidden states. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the choice of training data and lie typology substantially changes detectability, highlighting that deception detection is a highly representation-dependent problem.

AI.tldr: Training probes to detect LLM deception fails in out-of-domain scenarios; optimal detection depends on representation depth, probe design, and lie typology in training data.
AI.motivation: Current probes for detecting deceptive outputs from LLMs struggle with generalization - they fail in out-of-domain scenarios where training on one type of lie doesn't transfer well to other deception types.
AI.method: Systematic study examining factors: representation depth, probe expressivity, sparse feature representations, and lie typology. Augmented standard benchmark with supplementary dataset containing diverse deception types (fabrication, omission, exaggeration). Analyzed across seven probe types.
AI.result: Optimal representation depth is dataset-dependent; expressive probes provide only selective gains over linear baselines; sparse autoencoder features perform similarly to dense hidden states. Training data choice and lie typology substantially impact detectability.
AI.conclusion: Deception detection is highly representation-dependent problem, where the specific characteristics of training data and lie types fundamentally change what detection strategies work best.

title: HypNO: A Graph-Based Neural Operator with Physics-Informed Message Passing for Hyperbolic Conservation Laws
summary: We introduce HypNO, a graph-based neural operator for scalar hyperbolic conservation laws. HypNO operates directly on a space-time graph of finite-volume cells and uses adjacency-factored, physics-informed message passing to respect upwinding and entropy admissibility near shocks. We benchmark the architecture on the Lighthill-Whitham-Richards (LWR) and Aw-Rascle-Zhang (ARZ) traffic-flow models, a stress test for operator-learning methods because of their simultaneous global transport and shock formation. HypNO predicts solution snapshots accurately across a range of initial conditions while capturing the shocks and discontinuities of the solution.

AI.tldr: HypNO is a graph-based neural operator that accurately solves hyperbolic conservation laws like traffic flow models by combining physics-informed message passing with space-time graph representations.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to develop a neural operator that can handle scalar hyperbolic conservation laws, particularly traffic-flow models (LWR and ARZ), which present challenges due to their simultaneous global transport and shock formation characteristics that test operator-learning methods.
AI.method: HypNO uses a graph-based neural operator approach that operates directly on a space-time graph of finite-volume cells. It employs adjacency-factored, physics-informed message passing to respect upwinding and entropy admissibility near shocks.
AI.result: HypNO predicts solution snapshots accurately across a range of initial conditions while successfully capturing the shocks and discontinuities of the solution. It demonstrates effective performance on benchmark problems for the Lighthill-Whitham-Richards (LWR) and Aw-Rascle-Zhang (ARZ) traffic-flow models.
AI.conclusion: HypNO represents a promising graph-based neural operator architecture for hyperbolic conservation laws that can handle the challenging combination of global transport and shock formation, making it suitable for complex physics-informed machine learning applications in fluid dynamics and related fields.

title: Enabling Scalable Topology Inference in Distribution Systems via Constrained Multi-Source Inference
summary: Accurate distribution system topology is essential for outage localization, voltage analytics, and operation of distribution grids, yet maintaining reliable connectivity records remains challenging in practice due to heterogeneous and imperfect utility data. Existing topology identification methods often rely primarily on electrical similarity or spatial records alone, which become unreliable in dense feeders and under inconsistent metadata conditions. This paper formulates distribution topology identification as a constrained inference problem that refines a utility-provided base topology using heterogeneous evidence while enforcing spatial feasibility and physical operational constraints. Instead of reconstructing connectivity from scratch, the proposed framework detects inconsistent assignments, performs localized reconnection within constrained neighborhoods to ensure scalability, and iteratively enforces physical feasibility to produce operationally consistent topology estimates. In addition, a falsification-driven reliability metric evaluates how strongly each inferred connection is supported relative to alternative feasible assignments, enabling utilities to prioritize verification efforts while preserving system-wide observability. The framework is validated using operational data from three feeders comprising more than $8{,}000$ AMI meters in collaboration with a large U.S. utility. Results demonstrate over $95\%$ topology reconstruction accuracy while significantly reducing computational effort compared with global inference approaches. The study further shows that correlation-based methods alone produce ambiguous assignments in dense urban feeders, whereas combining electrical measurements with spatial and operational constraints enables robust and scalable topology recovery under realistic deployment conditions.

AI.tldr: A constrained inference framework that refines utility-provided distribution system topology using heterogeneous data while enforcing spatial/physical constraints, achieving 95%+ accuracy on 8,000+ meter feeders.
AI.motivation: Maintaining accurate distribution system topology is challenging due to imperfect utility data. Existing methods relying solely on electrical similarity or spatial records become unreliable in dense feeders with inconsistent metadata, leading to ambiguous topology assignments.
AI.method: Formulates topology identification as a constrained inference problem that refines utility base topology. Instead of reconstructing from scratch, it detects inconsistent assignments, performs localized reconnection within constrained neighborhoods for scalability, and iteratively enforces physical feasibility. Includes a falsification-driven reliability metric to evaluate connection confidence.
AI.result: Validated on operational data from three feeders with over 8,000 AMI meters, achieving over 95% topology reconstruction accuracy while significantly reducing computational effort compared to global inference approaches. Shows correlation-based methods alone produce ambiguous assignments in dense urban feeders.
AI.conclusion: Combining electrical measurements with spatial and operational constraints enables robust and scalable topology recovery under realistic deployment conditions. The framework produces operationally consistent topology estimates and provides reliability metrics to prioritize utility verification efforts.

title: Improving Access to Essential Medicines via Decision-Aware Machine Learning
summary: A critical challenge in healthcare systems in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) is the efficient and equitable allocation of scarce resources, particularly essential medicines. This problem is complicated by limited high-quality data, which restricts the applicability of traditional data-driven techniques. We propose a novel decision-aware machine learning framework for essential medicines allocation, which additionally leverages multi-task learning to ensure sample efficiency and catalytic priors to ensure equitable allocation. In collaboration with the Sierra Leone national government, we performed a staggered, nationwide deployment of our system as a decision support tool. Our econometric evaluation finds an estimated 19% increase in consumption of allocated products in treated districts, demonstrating its efficacy at improving access to essential medicines. Our tool was subsequently scaled nationwide, covering an estimated 2 million women and children under five. Our work demonstrates how machine learning methods can improve efficiency at very low cost in resource-constrained global health settings.

AI.tldr: A novel decision-aware machine learning framework for essential medicines allocation in LMICs that combines multi-task learning for sample efficiency and catalytic priors for equitable distribution, deployed nationwide in Sierra Leone with a 19% increase in medicine consumption.
AI.motivation: The critical challenge of efficient and equitable allocation of scarce essential medicines in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), compounded by limited high-quality data that restricts traditional data-driven techniques.
AI.method: A decision-aware machine learning framework that leverages multi-task learning to ensure sample efficiency and catalytic priors to ensure equitable allocation. The system was deployed as a staggered, nationwide decision support tool in collaboration with the Sierra Leone national government.
AI.result: Econometric evaluation showed an estimated 19% increase in consumption of allocated products in treated districts, demonstrating efficacy at improving access to essential medicines. The tool was subsequently scaled nationwide, covering an estimated 2 million women and children under five.
AI.conclusion: Machine learning methods can significantly improve efficiency at very low cost in resource-constrained global health settings, as demonstrated by the successful nationwide deployment and scaling of the essential medicines allocation system in Sierra Leone.

title: Routing Without Training: Controllable-Ratio LLM Offloading via Reliability Gating
summary: Local-cloud collaboration is a practical way to deploy large language models under resource constraints, but existing methods often rely on trained routers or collaboration-aware finetuning that tie routing behavior to a particular operating regime. In this work, we show that such training may be unnecessary: the local model's own inference-time agreement across sampled responses already provides a strong signal for deciding when to trust local execution and when to offload to a stronger cloud model. We propose CARGO, a training-free routing framework that estimates this agreement through prompt-varied sampling, applies Bayesian early stopping for sample-efficient uncertainty control, and supports arbitrary target collaboration ratios through lightweight deployment-time calibration. Across diverse reasoning and question-answering tasks, multiple local LLM families and scales, and both pretrained and finetuned local models, CARGO consistently outperforms other training-free baselines and in several settings surpasses supervised learned routers. These results suggest that effective and adaptable local-cloud collaboration can emerge directly from the local model's intrinsic response behavior, without requiring an additional trained router.

AI.tldr: CARGO is a training-free routing framework for local-cloud LLM collaboration that uses the local model's inference-time agreement across sampled responses to decide when to offload to the cloud, without requiring router training.
AI.motivation: Existing local-cloud collaboration methods require trained routers or collaboration-aware finetuning, which ties routing behavior to specific operating regimes and requires additional training overhead.
AI.method: CARGO estimates local model agreement through prompt-varied sampling, applies Bayesian early stopping for sample-efficient uncertainty control, and supports arbitrary target collaboration ratios through lightweight deployment-time calibration.
AI.result: CARGO consistently outperforms other training-free baselines across diverse reasoning and QA tasks, multiple local LLM families and scales, and both pretrained and finetuned models. It even surpasses supervised learned routers in several settings.
AI.conclusion: Effective local-cloud collaboration can emerge directly from the local model's intrinsic response behavior without requiring additional trained routers, enabling adaptable and efficient deployment under resource constraints.

title: When RLVR Shrinks the Reasoning Boundary: Diagnosing Pass@k Inversion
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can improve one-sample accuracy while making a model worse under repeated sampling. We study this pass@k inversion: after training, the policy may solve fewer distinct problems than its base model at large $k$. The failure concentrates on boundary prompts, where the base model contains rare correct trajectories that are recoverable by sampling but too sparse to reliably appear in finite RLVR rollout groups. We argue that a two-mode account explains this as an absence-of-evidence failure: rare correct trajectories may disappear before RLVR samples and reinforces them often enough. The main contribution is this diagnostic and mechanistic framing. Per-Problem Base Anchoring (PBA) is a deliberately simple proof-of-concept: sharpen prompts with sufficient frozen-base correct evidence, and anchor risky prompts to the base distribution. Across three training seeds on Omni-MATH-Test, with MATH500 as a secondary high-coverage validation benchmark, PBA improves both \PassK{1} and high-budget coverage over matched GRPO. A 3000-prompt regime-controlled diagnostic study is consistent across seeds with the expected signature: ordinary GRPO loses base-solvable boundary prompts, while PBA preserves rare verifier-positive trajectories. We use mathematical verifiers as a controlled testbed for verifier-guided optimization; the same pass@k inversion risk applies to ECCV-relevant vision-language agents when repeated visual, spatial, or chart-reasoning attempts are checked by external tools or verifiers. Reasoning post-training should decide not only how strongly to optimize, but which prompts are safe to optimize.

AI.tldr: RLVR training can paradoxically reduce problem-solving coverage at high sampling budgets (pass@k inversion). Rare correct trajectories from base models may disappear during RL training, harming high-k performance.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) can improve one-sample accuracy but degrade performance under repeated sampling (pass@k inversion). The authors aim to understand and address this paradoxical failure where policies solve fewer distinct problems than base models at large k.
AI.method: Propose Per-Problem Base Anchoring (PBA) - a simple approach that: 1) sharpens prompts with sufficient frozen-base correct evidence, and 2) anchors risky prompts to the base distribution. Evaluate on Omni-MATH-Test with MATH500 as validation, comparing against matched GRPO. Conduct diagnostic study with 3000-prompt regime.
AI.result: PBA improves both Pass@1 and high-budget coverage over GRPO across three training seeds. Diagnostic study shows GRPO loses base-solvable boundary prompts while PBA preserves rare verifier-positive trajectories. Consistent with two-mode absence-of-evidence failure mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Pass@k inversion risk exists in RLVR, requiring decisions about which prompts are safe to optimize. PBA demonstrates a practical solution by preserving rare correct trajectories. Findings apply to vision-language agents with external verifiers in reasoning tasks.

title: PersonaTrail: Benchmarking Personalized Web Agents through Browsing Trails
summary: Recent advances in large language models have enabled web agents to autonomously execute complex tasks. In practice, users frequently provide underspecified instructions, requiring agents to infer the missing context from their raw browsing histories. Existing benchmarks fail to capture this form of personalization, as they either restrict tasks to fully explicit prompts or abstract web interaction history into simplified forms. To bridge this gap, we introduce PersonaTrail, a benchmark for personalized web agents operating in a managed open web environment. By leveraging realistic browsing trajectories as user history, PersonaTrail evaluates an agent's ability to infer user preferences and recall information from past browsing sessions. We further propose Preference-Aware Contextual Memory (PACMem), a framework that decomposes raw browsing histories into two types of structured memory: factual memories that summarize individual sessions and preference memories that distill recurring behavioral patterns. At inference time, the agent retrieves the most relevant entries from these memories to guide personalized navigation. Extensive experiments show that PACMem consistently outperforms existing memory-based baselines on both tasks.

AI.tldr: PersonaTrail is a new benchmark for personalized web agents that uses realistic browsing histories, and PACMem is a framework that structures browsing histories into factual and preference memories to improve personalized task performance.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks fail to capture realistic personalization in web agents because they either use fully explicit prompts or simplify web interaction history, missing the challenge of inferring missing context from raw browsing histories that users naturally provide.
AI.method: 1. Introduce PersonaTrail benchmark with realistic browsing trajectories as user history. 2. Propose PACMem framework that decomposes raw browsing histories into two structured memory types: factual memories (summarize individual sessions) and preference memories (distill recurring behavioral patterns). 3. At inference, agents retrieve relevant memory entries to guide personalized navigation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that PACMem consistently outperforms existing memory-based baselines on both tasks of inferring user preferences and recalling information from past browsing sessions.
AI.conclusion: The PersonaTrail benchmark and PACMem framework effectively address the gap in evaluating personalized web agents by using realistic browsing histories and structured memory decomposition, enabling better inference of user preferences from underspecified instructions.

title: Conflict Resolution under Degraded Surveillance in Air Corridors Using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: Safe Advanced Air Mobility operations require aircraft to maintain separation when surveillance information is noisy, delayed, incomplete, or temporarily unavailable. This study develops a Deep Q-Network-based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning framework for decentralized conflict resolution among heterogeneous small unmanned aerial vehicles and electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft operating within a structured three-dimensional corridor. Separate policies are trained for the two aircraft categories using local observations and a 14-action space that includes maintaining course, turning, vertical maneuvering, landing, and speed control. The simulation incorporates aircraft-specific dynamics, energy use, corridor constraints, observation noise, communication delay, information dropout, wind disturbance, actuator uncertainty, and model uncertainty. The trained policies are evaluated across 90 combinations of traffic density and minimum separation thresholds. Loss-of-separation frequency and duration generally increase with traffic density and separation requirements, although most events are resolved within 1s. Under safe conditions, agents maintain their motion approximately 79% of the time. During conflicts, turning accounts for 33% of actions, followed by maintaining motion at 29%, speed control at 25%, and vertical maneuvers at 13%. Six Pareto-optimal configurations reveal trade-offs between safety and corridor capacity. The framework supports the simulation-based evaluation of safer AAM conflict-resolution strategies under degraded surveillance conditions.

AI.tldr: A Deep Q-Network Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning framework for decentralized conflict resolution among heterogeneous UAVs and eVTOLs in structured 3D corridors under degraded surveillance conditions.
AI.motivation: Advanced Air Mobility operations require safe separation assurance when surveillance information is degraded (noisy, delayed, incomplete, or temporarily unavailable). There's a need for robust conflict resolution strategies for heterogeneous aircraft operating in structured corridors.
AI.method: Developed a Deep Q-Network-based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning framework with separate policies for two aircraft categories (UAVs and eVTOLs). Uses local observations with 14-action space (maintaining course, turning, vertical maneuvering, landing, speed control). Simulation incorporates comprehensive factors: aircraft-specific dynamics, energy use, corridor constraints, observation noise, communication delay, information dropout, wind disturbance, actuator uncertainty, and model uncertainty.
AI.result: Policies evaluated across 90 combinations of traffic density and minimum separation thresholds. Loss-of-separation frequency and duration increase with traffic density and separation requirements, but most events resolved within 1s. Under safe conditions, agents maintain motion ~79% of time. During conflicts: turning (33%), maintaining motion (29%), speed control (25%), vertical maneuvers (13%). Identified six Pareto-optimal configurations showing safety-capacity trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables simulation-based evaluation of safer AAM conflict-resolution strategies under degraded surveillance conditions, supporting the development of robust systems for future air mobility operations where perfect surveillance cannot be guaranteed.

title: Tractable Hierarchical Control of Autoregressive Language Models
summary: Constraining the generation of autoregressive large language models (LLMs) is an important component of integrating language models into formal systems. In the generation of code and data for tasks like program synthesis, ensuring that language models produce syntactically valid output is a prerequisite for processing such output. These languages (such as SQL or JSON) are often designed as $LR(k)$ context-free grammars. By distilling the LLM to a tractable probabilistic model, its autoregressive generation can be steered and masked to incorporate the probability of satisfying logical constraints, ensuring high quality output that is guaranteed to be valid. This paper demonstrates that the satisfaction of any $LR(k)$ grammar of finite duration can be calculated in polynomial time, an improvement over the exponential time of applying previous methods to such grammars. This result enables efficient constraint and steering of LLM generation towards output that better satisfies formal syntactic constraints.

AI.tldr: LLM generation can be efficiently steered to satisfy LR(k) grammar constraints using polynomial-time algorithms, ensuring syntactically valid output for formal languages like SQL/JSON.
AI.motivation: When integrating LLMs into formal systems for tasks like program synthesis, ensuring syntactically valid output (e.g., SQL, JSON) is essential. Current constraint satisfaction methods are exponential for LR(k) grammars, limiting practical application.
AI.method: The paper distills LLMs to tractable probabilistic models and develops polynomial-time algorithms to calculate satisfaction of LR(k) grammar constraints. This enables steering and masking during autoregressive generation to incorporate constraint satisfaction probabilities.
AI.result: The key result shows that satisfaction of any LR(k) grammar of finite duration can be calculated in polynomial time, a significant improvement over previous exponential methods. This enables efficient constraint satisfaction during LLM generation.
AI.conclusion: The polynomial-time constraint satisfaction method enables practical steering of LLM generation to produce syntactically valid output for formal languages, improving integration of LLMs into systems requiring guaranteed validity like program synthesis tools.

title: SOAP, Muon, and Beyond: Pushing LLM Pretraining Scales
summary: Higher-order optimizers such as Muon and SOAP offer faster convergence than AdamW, but their computational cost and numerical stability challenges have limited adoption at scale. In this work, we adapt and enhance preconditioned gradient methods to overcome the practical challenges of large-scale LLM pretraining. We first identify instabilities in SOAP at large batch sizes and propose algorithmic modifications including per-step QR orthogonalization and improved preconditioning strategies that eliminate loss spikes and enable stable training in these regimes. We then present a unified empirical study of SOAP, Muon, and AdamW using update-RMS matching to ensure fair learning rate transfer across optimizers. As part of this analysis, we empirically evaluate the orthogonalization quality of Muon. Our experiments on multi-billion-parameter models trained on trillions of tokens reveal that SOAP and Muon consistently outperform AdamW at the scales we tested. Notably, at batch sizes of up to 100M tokens for next-token prediction, these optimizers maintain training stability and quality while AdamW degrades. To enable efficient training at large scale, we introduce a layer-wise distributed optimizer compatible with Megatron-LM. Our implementation balances memory and hides communication while avoiding approximations to the optimizer computations, thus retaining their convergence benefits. Additionally, we identify and build specific system-level improvements to further accelerate our layer-wise implementation. To support the research community, we release a codebase that contains emerging algorithms for optimization: https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Emerging-Optimizers

AI.tldr: Higher-order optimizers (SOAP and Muon) outperform AdamW for large-scale LLM pretraining with improved stability at large batch sizes through algorithmic enhancements and efficient layer-wise distributed implementation.
AI.motivation: Higher-order optimizers like Muon and SOAP offer faster convergence than AdamW but face practical challenges in computational cost and numerical stability at scale, limiting their adoption for large-scale LLM pretraining.
