AI.result: On HumanEval, multi-full achieves +3.1 pp improvement. Strongest result: with DeepSeekCoder V2 Lite, accuracy jumps from 57.5% (oneshot) to 80.0% (multi-full), a +22.5 pp improvement supporting scaling hypothesis. Multi-agent decomposition shows value grows with base-model capability.
AI.conclusion: The primary contribution is methodological: a single codebase enabling controlled measurement of different approaches (one-shot, execution-retry, per-agent ablation). Multi-agent decomposition's value scales with base-model capability, providing a framework for systematic code synthesis validation.

title: Exact ReLU realization of affine one-dimensional refinement iterates via residual memory and offset frames
summary:
We study vector-valued affine refinement operators of the form [
(Wγ)(t)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb{Z}} A_jγ(Mt-j)+B(t), ]
with finitely supported matrix mask and compactly supported continuous piecewise linear input and forcing data. Building on the homogeneous realization theorem for (B\equiv 0), we prove that, for (M\ge 3), every finite affine iterate (W^nγ) admits an exact fixed-width ReLU realization whose depth is (O(n)).
  The main new ingredient is a residual memory controller. It replaces the noninvertible residual dynamics by an injective skew-product and permits exact backward replay of the residual states required by a Horner-type evaluation of the affine forcing sum. Offset frames align the forcing atoms away from residual seams, allowing complementary loop readouts to recover their values exactly. The remaining branch-selection ambiguity occurs only where the accumulated affine state has already vanished.
  For (M\ge 3), the result applies to arbitrary compactly supported continuous piecewise linear forcing terms. For (M=2), the same construction applies to ordinary-frame seam-separated forcing. We also prove a stage-dependent extension for forcing terms in a fixed finite-dimensional continuous piecewise linear span and record the resulting linear-depth upgrade for open-curve, finite-state, and Hilbert- and Morton-type recursive constructions.

AI.tldr: Exact fixed-width ReLU realizations exist for affine refinement operators with O(n) depth, using residual memory controllers and offset frames for exact forcing term recovery.
AI.motivation: To establish exact fixed-width ReLU network realizations for affine refinement operators (which include both homogeneous and forcing terms), building on previous work that handled only homogeneous cases.
AI.method: Introduce a residual memory controller that replaces noninvertible residual dynamics with an injective skew-product, enabling exact backward replay of residual states via Horner-type evaluation. Use offset frames to align forcing atoms away from residual seams, allowing complementary loop readouts for exact value recovery.
AI.result: For M≥3, every finite affine iterate Wⁿγ admits an exact fixed-width ReLU realization with O(n) depth. For M=2, the construction applies to ordinary-frame seam-separated forcing. Also provides extensions for various forcing term classes and linear-depth upgrades for recursive constructions.
AI.conclusion: The residual memory controller approach successfully enables exact ReLU realizations of affine refinement operators with linear depth, overcoming limitations of previous homogeneous-only results and handling both continuous piecewise linear input and forcing data.

title: FlowEdit: Information-Theoretic Control of LLM Reasoning Flows for Ill-posed Problems Involving Conflicts
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) perform strongly on well-specified reasoning tasks with a feasible answer. However, problems encountered in the open world can become ill-posed due to inconsistent conditions, conflicting statements, or mutually incompatible requirements, admitting no valid responses. We argue that reasoning of such ill-posed problems involving conflicts require novel LLM capabilities to make hidden conflicts explicit, maintain competing hypotheses via multiple reasoning branches, and generate alternative responses in a single pass, all of which are challenging due to the limitation of the next-token prediction mechanism in LLMs. To this end, we propose FlowEdit, a novel framework that leverages information-theoretic principles to quantify and regulate internal reasoning flows of LLMs, for generating a full set of alternative responses under valid hypotheses. FlowEdit can be viewed as enforcing a branch-aware reasoning process using two dual information-theoretic objectives on the model's internal reasoning representations: maximizing the information flow from each selected hypothesis to the branch outcome, while minimizing the overlap and conditional dependence across sibling branches, to provide a diverse, informative set of responses with broad coverage. We show that this is achieved through tractable variational bounds under boundary embeddings being ε-sufficient, optimizing the underlying conditional mutual information in LLM reasoning process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FlowEdit outperforms leading proprietary models, improving exact-set-match accuracy by 68%, while boosting overall response informativeness by 24%. We further show that flow regulation surfaces in the token stream as a redistribution of next-token entropy that concentrates inside each branch, amplifies at flow boundaries, and scales with the number of flows the problem requires.

AI.tldr: FlowEdit is a framework that uses information-theoretic principles to help LLMs handle ill-posed problems by generating multiple alternative responses through branch-aware reasoning.
AI.motivation: Current LLMs struggle with ill-posed problems that have inconsistent conditions, conflicting statements, or incompatible requirements, as they can't handle hidden conflicts or maintain competing hypotheses due to limitations of next-token prediction.
AI.method: FlowEdit leverages information-theoretic principles to quantify and regulate internal reasoning flows in LLMs. It uses two dual objectives: maximizing information flow from each hypothesis to branch outcomes, while minimizing overlap across sibling branches. This is achieved through tractable variational bounds under boundary embeddings being ε-sufficient.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show FlowEdit outperforms leading proprietary models, improving exact-set-match accuracy by 68% and boosting overall response informativeness by 24%. It redistributes next-token entropy to concentrate within branches and amplifies at flow boundaries.
AI.conclusion: FlowEdit successfully enables LLMs to handle ill-posed problems by generating diverse, informative alternative responses through branch-aware reasoning, overcoming limitations of next-token prediction and demonstrating measurable improvements in performance.

title: Detecting Neural Network Failures through Spectral Analysis of Internal Activations
summary:
Neural network misclassifications exhibit characteristic spectral instability in internal activations that is invisible at the output layer. This phenomenon is identified and formalized as Spectral Drift -- the frequency-domain distance between consecutive layer activations -- with empirical validation showing that failures exhibit significantly higher drift than correct predictions (1.9% increase, p<0.001). This spectral signature emerges during internal processing but becomes masked in final outputs, explaining why confidence-based detection methods struggle.
  This work introduces Self-Detecting Neural Networks (SDNN), a framework that monitors spectral dynamics across network depth using Short-Time Fourier Transform, wavelet decomposition, and statistical moments to capture multi-scale spectral features. A lightweight detector network (5% parameter overhead) learns to identify failure-indicative patterns via curriculum learning on progressively challenging distributions: natural misclassifications, distribution shifts, and adversarial perturbations.
  Experiments on CIFAR-10 demonstrate that SDNN achieves 79.0 +/- 25.3% AUROC across three seeds, substantially outperforming confidence-based baselines including MaxSoftmax (50.5%) and Energy Score (52.9%) by approximately 25-30 percentage points. Ablation studies reveal that wavelet decomposition and statistical features make consistent contributions, while STFT's role remains unclear. This work establishes spectral analysis of internal activations as a promising direction for neural network reliability, revealing diagnostic information inaccessible to output-based approaches.

AI.tldr: Neural network failures exhibit spectral instability in internal activations (Spectral Drift) that's invisible at outputs. The paper introduces Self-Detecting Neural Networks (SDNN) that monitor this spectral signature to detect misclassifications, outperforming confidence-based methods by ~25-30% AUROC.
AI.motivation: Current neural network failure detection relies on output-based methods like confidence scores, which often struggle because failure-indicative spectral patterns in internal activations become masked in final outputs. There's a need for methods that can detect failures by analyzing internal spectral dynamics rather than just output distributions.
AI.method: Proposes Self-Detecting Neural Networks (SDNN) framework that: 1) Identifies and formalizes Spectral Drift (frequency-domain distance between consecutive layer activations) as a failure signature, 2) Uses Short-Time Fourier Transform, wavelet decomposition, and statistical moments to capture multi-scale spectral features across network depth, 3) Trains a lightweight detector network (5% parameter overhead) via curriculum learning on progressively challenging distributions (natural misclassifications, distribution shifts, adversarial perturbations).
AI.result: On CIFAR-10, SDNN achieves 79.0 +/- 25.3% AUROC across three seeds, substantially outperforming confidence-based baselines: MaxSoftmax (50.5%) and Energy Score (52.9%) by approximately 25-30 percentage points. Failure cases show 1.9% higher Spectral Drift than correct predictions (p<0.001). Ablation shows wavelet decomposition and statistical features consistently contribute, while STFT's role is unclear.
AI.conclusion: Internal spectral analysis reveals diagnostic information inaccessible to output-based approaches, establishing spectral dynamics as a promising direction for neural network reliability. The work demonstrates that failure detection can be significantly improved by monitoring spectral signatures in internal activations rather than relying solely on output confidence.

title: STeMP: Spatio-Temporal Modelling Protocol
summary:
Spatio-temporal machine-learning modelling is an important tool in environmental research. However, machine-learning models are highly sensitive to both the characteristics of the training data, such as its distribution, and methodological choices, including the cross-validation strategy. Each decision has impact and implications on the model itself as well as the estimation of the model quality and applicability for certain purposes. Taking into account the large role of machine-learning based maps of the environment in science and their transfer into practice, transparent reporting of spatio-temporal models, ideally using standardized model protocols, is essential to enable trust, transparency and comparability. However, such protocols are currently lacking for spatio-temporal modelling.
  We propose STeMP (Spatio-Temporal Modelling Protocol) to fill this gap by serving two purposes: standardized reporting to understand the model functioning as well as providing guidance during the modelling process by pointing at critical decisions and parameters. The protocol is structured in three sections: Overview, Model and Prediction. The Overview section contains metadata, while the Model and Prediction sections go into detail, describing predictors, evaluation and software, and further relevant elements of the modelling workflow.
  The protocol definition is hosted on GitHub and accompanied by an R-package (https://github.com/LOEK-RS/STeMP). The R-package contains a web application that can be used to fill the protocol either manually or in a semi-automated way from provided modelling objects. Warnings are returned from the protocol when common pitfalls are encountered, which may help authors as a guide through the modelling process but also support reviewers in the assessment of modelling studies. Via GitHub, incorporation of contributions and feedback from the community is encouraged.

AI.tldr: STeMP protocol provides standardized reporting and guidance for spatio-temporal machine-learning models to ensure transparency, reproducibility, and comparability in environmental research.
AI.motivation: Current lack of standardized protocols for spatio-temporal machine-learning models leads to issues with trust, transparency, and comparability, especially given the sensitivity of models to training data characteristics and methodological choices.
AI.method: Developed STeMP protocol structured in three sections (Overview, Model, Prediction) with metadata and detailed workflow elements, accompanied by an R-package with web application for filling protocol manually or semi-automatically, and hosted on GitHub for community contributions.
AI.result: Created STeMP protocol that serves dual purposes: standardized reporting to understand model functioning, and guidance during modelling by highlighting critical decisions and parameters, with warnings for common pitfalls.
AI.conclusion: STeMP fills a critical gap in spatio-temporal modelling by providing a standardized protocol that enables transparent reporting, improves reproducibility, and facilitates better assessment of machine-learning models in environmental research.

title: Inducing Comparability of Factorised Probability Distributions
summary: To allow for principled comparison between two probabilistic graphical models defined over non-identical variable sets, they have to be lifted to a common measurable space. To this end, we propose an extension scheme for any two given models and establish the formal foundation: Unmatched components are completed using conditionally uniform (Laplace) extensions such that the resulting joint distributions differ from the original ones only by multiplicative constants and coincide under projection. This preserves the probabilistic semantics while enabling the application of well-defined distributional discrepancy measures. We establish the invariance of the induced joint under projection and use the extensions to provide a minimal structural extension of two factor graphs to the smalles common measurable space as well as to a common graphical structure by a deterministic algorithm. In addition, we discuss structural and measure-theoretic properties and identify promising criteria for comparison methodologies.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an extension scheme to compare probabilistic graphical models defined over different variable sets by lifting them to a common measurable space using conditionally uniform (Laplace) extensions, enabling principled comparison while preserving probabilistic semantics.
AI.motivation: When comparing two probabilistic graphical models defined over non-identical variable sets, they cannot be directly compared because they exist in different measurable spaces. There's a need for a principled approach to extend models to a common space while preserving their probabilistic semantics.
AI.method: The authors propose using conditionally uniform (Laplace) extensions to complete unmatched components between two models. This creates extensions where resulting joint distributions differ from originals only by multiplicative constants and coincide under projection. They develop a deterministic algorithm to extend factor graphs to the smallest common measurable space and common graphical structure.
AI.result: The approach establishes formal foundations for model comparison by preserving probabilistic semantics while enabling application of well-defined distributional discrepancy measures. The method provides a minimal structural extension algorithm and maintains invariance of induced joint distributions under projection.
AI.conclusion: The proposed extension scheme provides a principled framework for comparing probabilistic graphical models over different variable sets, with promising criteria for comparison methodologies while preserving structural and measure-theoretic properties.

title: When Does Recurrence Become an Algorithm? Convergence Selection in Weight-Tied Looped Transformers
summary: When does a weight-tied looped transformer -- one block applied T times -- implement an actual algorithm? We answer with four findings from controlled populations on group word problems. (1) The budget law: free training installs a linear computation frontier, a mechanism that solves v positions per loop, whose speed is priced by the training contract: v ~ n_train/T_train (exponent 0.98 +/- 0.04, R^2=0.99), exactly unity under T=n training. SGD selects a frontier matching the minimum the contract demands; granting more test-time loops than ever trained rescues late positions at fixed input length, yielding a principled halting rule T* = ceil(n / v-hat). (2) Architecture prior, not expressivity, picks the algorithm: standard-depth transformers learn parallel scans on this family; weight tying flips the selection to the serial frontier, even when positional addressing for a log-depth scan is supplied. At matched depth and parameters, untied models extrapolate worst and fail to learn A5 at all. (3) The walls are not where circuit complexity says: NC1-completeness costs nothing (A5 generalizes fully), while group order does (S5's 120x120 operator deadlocks joint learning) -- and an operator-first curriculum dissolves the wall in every seed. (4) Mechanisms are portable, not mandatable: warm-starting across budget contracts transfers the algorithm in every seed, re-pricing its speed, while imposing seriality through the input schedule fails where free training succeeds. These results are invisible to standard instruments, which provably saturate at the fixed points trained loops converge to. We introduce a head instrument, the convergence-time scaling tau(n,i), validate it causally via damage cones whose slope reproduces v, and show in-distribution head measurements predict out-of-distribution fate where tail metrics do not. Results replicate on the public easy-to-hard benchmark.

AI.tldr: Weight-tied looped transformers learn algorithmic behaviors with a computational frontier speed determined by training budget (v ~ n_train/T_train). Architecture prior (weight tying) selects serial algorithms over parallel ones, and warm-starting transfers mechanisms across budgets while re-pricing their speed.
AI.motivation: To understand when weight-tied looped transformers implement actual algorithms, rather than just pattern matching, by studying their behavior on group word problems where algorithmic computation is required.
AI.method: Controlled experiments on group word problems using weight-tied looped transformers (single block applied T times). Introduced convergence-time scaling τ(n,i) as a head instrument, validated via damage cones, and studied how training budget (n_train/T_train) determines computational frontier speed.
AI.result: Four key findings: (1) Budget law establishes linear computation frontier (v ~ n_train/T_train); (2) Architecture prior (weight tying) selects serial algorithms over parallel ones; (3) Algorithmic walls don't align with circuit complexity but with group order; (4) Mechanisms transfer across budgets via warm-starting while re-pricing speed.
AI.conclusion: Weight-tied transformers learn genuine algorithms whose computational speed is priced by training budget. Standard metrics miss these phenomena, requiring specialized instruments like convergence-time scaling. Architecture choice (weight tying) fundamentally shapes algorithmic selection beyond mere expressivity.

title: LeanFlow: A Case Study in Workflow-Driven Lean Autoformalization
comment: 14 pages, 3 figures, ICML 2026: AI for Math Workshop
summary: We present and evaluate LeanFlow, an LLM agent system specialized for translating mathematical papers into buildable Lean projects. Recent verifier-in-the-loop systems show that large formal artifacts can be produced, but it remains unclear which runtime mechanisms affect completion, auditability, or efficiency in document-to-project formalization. We study this question through case studies on two previously unformalized mathematical papers in number theory and measure theory, using model, proof-workflow, and toolset ablations with Kimi2.6 and GPT5.5; we report task outcome, API calls, input tokens, and output tokens. With Kimi2.6, the full workflow completes both document-level projects within the 2000-call budget, while no-queue variants reach the budget limit; with GPT5.5, all document-level variants complete, and the full workflow has the lowest or tied-lowest input-token cost on both sources. As complementary calibration, LeanFlow reaches 75.7% BEq+ on the PFR slice of RLM25 and solves all five ICML 2026 AI for Math TCS challenge projects in our GPT5.5 runs.

AI.tldr: LeanFlow is an LLM agent system that successfully translates mathematical papers into buildable Lean projects, completing document-level formalization tasks within budget constraints and achieving competitive performance on benchmark challenges.
AI.motivation: While recent verifier-in-the-loop systems show that large formal artifacts can be produced, it remains unclear which runtime mechanisms affect completion, auditability, or efficiency in document-to-project formalization. The authors aim to study this question.
AI.method: The authors present LeanFlow, an LLM agent system specialized for translating mathematical papers into buildable Lean projects. They evaluate it through case studies on two previously unformalized mathematical papers in number theory and measure theory, using model, proof-workflow, and toolset ablations with Kimi2.6 and GPT5.5. They report task outcome, API calls, input tokens, and output tokens.
AI.result: With Kimi2.6, the full workflow completes both document-level projects within the 2000-call budget, while no-queue variants reach the budget limit. With GPT5.5, all document-level variants complete, and the full workflow has the lowest or tied-lowest input-token cost on both sources. As complementary calibration, LeanFlow reaches 75.7% BEq+ on the PFR slice of RLM25 and solves all five ICML 2026 AI for Math TCS challenge projects in their GPT5.5 runs.
AI.conclusion: LeanFlow demonstrates effective formalization capabilities for mathematical papers, showing that proper workflow design and toolset integration enable successful document-to-project translation within practical computational budgets, while providing insights into how different runtime mechanisms affect formalization efficiency.

title: Are Single-Token Sparse Autoencoder Features Causally Necessary? Layer-Depth and SAE-Family Effects
summary: Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features are used to interpret and steer large language models, yet whether a feature's causal role is stable across SAE families remains untested. Single-token features that activate on one vocabulary item provide the diagnostic case where ground truth permits direct comparison. We analyze 3.9M features across six models and three SAE families using zero-ablation at full layer depth. Single-token features cluster 4.7x tighter in decoder space and concentrate in early layers (Layer 0 in GPT2-Small; L0-L4 in Gemma). Ablating them yields Benjamini-Hochberg-significant logit reductions in 178 of 208 full-layer conditions, with depth controlling whether damage cascades downstream or shapes the output directly. Cross-family causal differences exceed within-family scale effects: on the same base model, GemmaScope and BatchTopK features remain causally anchored, while LlamaScope features are locally redundant. The target token's rank recovers to within 2x baseline 96-98% of the time after the same ablation, and a controlled activation-function comparison reverses sign within the same model, leaving training recipe as the residual candidate. Cross-family interpretability claims are therefore sensitive to training methodology, not just activation function or scale.

AI.tldr: SAE features' causal stability across different sparse autoencoder families is tested using single-token features as diagnostic cases, revealing cross-family causal differences exceed scale effects and interpretability claims depend on training methodology.
AI.motivation: There's a lack of understanding about whether SAE (sparse autoencoder) features maintain consistent causal roles across different SAE families, despite their widespread use for interpreting and steering large language models. This is important for reliable interpretability and feature-based interventions.
AI.method: Analyzed 3.9M features across six models and three SAE families, focusing on single-token features (activating on one vocabulary item) as a diagnostic case. Used zero-ablation at full layer depth, examined feature clustering in decoder space, studied cascade effects across layers, and conducted cross-family comparisons including controlled activation-function comparisons.
AI.result: Single-token features cluster 4.7x tighter in decoder space and concentrate in early layers. Ablation causes significant logit reductions in 178/208 conditions. Cross-family causal differences exceed within-family scale effects: GemmaScope and BatchTopK features remain causally anchored while LlamaScope features show local redundancy. Target token rank recovers within 2x baseline 96-98% of the time, and activation-function comparisons can reverse sign within same model.
AI.conclusion: Cross-family interpretability claims are sensitive to training methodology rather than just activation function or scale. Training recipe emerges as the residual candidate explaining causal differences, highlighting the importance of SAE training methodology for reliable feature interpretation across different approaches.

title: Optimizing Hypergraph-Based RAG: Toward Better Fact Extraction and Chunk Retrieval
summary: GraphRAG enables deeper reasoning by structuring knowledge as graphs but struggles with n-ary facts. HyperGraphRAG uses hypergraphs for richer semantics, improving accuracy, yet relies on error-prone LLM extraction and inefficient standard chunk retrieval. We address this by employing self-consistency prompting to improve the extraction, and Personalized PageRank algorithm over hypergraph to enhance chunk retrieval.

AI.tldr: HyperGraphRAG improves on GraphRAG by using hypergraphs for better n-ary fact handling, with two key enhancements: self-consistency prompting for extraction and Personalized PageRank for retrieval.
AI.motivation: GraphRAG struggles with n-ary facts, and while HyperGraphRAG addresses this with hypergraphs for richer semantics, it still suffers from error-prone LLM extraction and inefficient standard chunk retrieval methods.
AI.method: The paper proposes two main improvements: (1) using self-consistency prompting to enhance the accuracy of LLM-based extraction, and (2) employing Personalized PageRank algorithm over hypergraphs to improve chunk retrieval efficiency.
AI.result: The enhanced HyperGraphRAG system achieves improved extraction accuracy through self-consistency prompting and more efficient chunk retrieval through hypergraph-based Personalized PageRank, overcoming limitations of the original approaches.
AI.conclusion: By combining self-consistency prompting for better extraction and Personalized PageRank over hypergraphs for superior retrieval, the enhanced HyperGraphRAG system provides a more robust solution for handling n-ary facts and complex knowledge structures.

title: One Round Is All You Need: Analytic Federated Learning for Task-Heterogeneous Multi-Label Medical Image Classification
comment: The 14th IEEE International Conference on Healthcare Informatics
summary: Federated learning (FL) enables multiple clinical institutions to collaboratively train a shared disease classifier without centralizing patient data. In practice, however, each institution annotates only the pathologies within its area of expertise, so the federation operates under task heterogeneity: each client holds labels for a strict subset of the target disease categories while the remaining classes are entirely unobserved at that site. Existing gradient-based FL methods fail under this setting because they require hundreds of communication rounds to converge and because missing class labels introduce systematic false-negative bias that the model cannot correct without a principled mechanism. We propose an analytic federated learning framework for multi-label medical image classification under task heterogeneity. The proposed method replaces iterative gradient optimization with three closed-form operations: a balanced label projection that neutralizes class-imbalance bias by normalizing positive and negative contributions to equal total mass; a per-class absolute aggregation law that independently assembles the optimal ridge-regression classifier for each disease category from the sufficient statistics uploaded by its annotating clients; and an optional analytic pseudo-label refinement round that propagates missing-class knowledge from a confidence-filtered teacher classifier to non-annotating clients. The entire procedure requires at most two communication rounds, irrespective of the degree of task heterogeneity or the number of participating clients. Experiments on ChestXray14 under four progressively severe missing-class configurations demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art federated multi-label method FedMLP by up to 18.44 BACC points and 13.24 AUC points, while reducing the communication.

AI.tldr: Analytic federated learning framework for multi-label medical image classification that handles task heterogeneity (missing class labels at different institutions) with closed-form operations requiring only 1-2 communication rounds.
AI.motivation: Federated learning in clinical settings faces task heterogeneity where each institution only annotates pathologies within its expertise, holding labels for strict subsets of target disease categories. Existing gradient-based FL methods fail due to slow convergence (hundreds of rounds) and systematic false-negative bias from missing class labels.
AI.method: Three closed-form operations: 1) balanced label projection that neutralizes class-imbalance bias by normalizing positive/negative contributions; 2) per-class absolute aggregation law that independently assembles optimal ridge-regression classifiers for each disease from sufficient statistics; 3) optional analytic pseudo-label refinement round propagating missing-class knowledge via confidence-filtered teacher classifier to non-annotating clients.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art federated multi-label method FedMLP by up to 18.44 BACC points and 13.24 AUC points on ChestXray14 dataset under four progressively severe missing-class configurations, while significantly reducing communication overhead to at most 2 rounds.
AI.conclusion: Proposed analytic framework successfully addresses task heterogeneity in federated multi-label medical image classification through closed-form solutions that eliminate iterative gradient optimization, enabling efficient knowledge sharing with minimal communication rounds while correcting systematic biases from missing class labels.

title: MiniCache: Reusable Program Caching with Small Model Interfaces for Efficient LLM Inference
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for program-aided reasoning, agentic decision making, and structured task execution, but these applications often incur high inference cost. We present MiniCache, a reusable program caching framework that transforms Program-of-Thought (PoT) programs into parameterized cache objects, enabling reusable computation across structurally similar requests. MiniCache reuses the same small model for semantic variable extraction on cache-hit requests and speculative drafting during target-LLM generation, reducing expensive target-LLM invocations while preserving task quality. Experiments on shopping-style request datasets, WebShop, Formula, and CodeTAT-QA demonstrate that MiniCache improves the trade-off between inference latency, cache reuse, and accuracy, achieving up to 3.1x lower latency and 2.8x higher throughput under parallel serving. These results show that small models are most effective not as replacements for large models, but as lightweight interface models that enable reliable and efficient reusable program caching.

AI.tldr: MiniCache is a program caching framework that reduces LLM inference costs by reusing parameterized computation across similar requests, using small models for semantic extraction and speculative drafting instead of replacing large models.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for program-aided reasoning and agentic decision making, but these applications incur high inference costs. There's a need to reduce expensive target-LLM invocations while preserving task quality.
AI.method: MiniCache transforms Program-of-Thought programs into parameterized cache objects for reusable computation. It uses small models for semantic variable extraction on cache-hit requests and speculative drafting during target-LLM generation, enabling computation reuse across structurally similar requests.
AI.result: Experiments on shopping-style request datasets (WebShop, Formula, CodeTAT-QA) show MiniCache achieves up to 3.1x lower latency and 2.8x higher throughput under parallel serving, improving the trade-off between inference latency, cache reuse, and accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Small models are most effective not as replacements for large models, but as lightweight interface models that enable reliable and efficient reusable program caching, demonstrating practical optimization for LLM-based program execution.

title: Scaling Interpretable Transformers with Parity Bottleneck Layers
summary: Language models are thought to exhibit the phenomenon of superposition, representing many more features than dimensions in their residual streams. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are designed to recover such features post-hoc, but training models that are interpretable by construction has remained impractical, as a per-layer over-complete bottleneck is prohibitively expensive in both memory and compute. To overcome this issue, we introduce the ParityTransformer, a GPT-2-scale architecture whose intermediate representations are efficient and wide / sparse by design. At each layer, a Deep Parity Bottleneck (DPB) replaces a learned over-complete basis with a parameter-free algebraic dictionary, providing a deterministic incoherence guarantee and eliminating the memory requirements that have prevented per-layer interpretable bottlenecks at scale. A DPB is a hierarchically structured sparse bottleneck which efficiently enforces sparsity using a multi-level mixture-of-experts approach: a hardware-aware implementation that closes the cost gap between activation sparse and dense training to a manageable interpretability tax. Empirically, ParityTransformers perform at least as well as post-hoc SAEs on sparse probing tasks, while out-performing on measures of feature absorption, steering effectiveness, and fine-grained causal interventions. Because subsequent computation acts only on features that survive the sparse bottleneck, the ParityTransformer's features are native to the model's forwards pass by construction, addressing the question of whether SAEs probe features the model actually uses during computation. We see this as a step toward training models whose internal representations are interpretable by design rather than recovered post hoc.

AI.tldr: The ParityTransformer is a GPT-2-scale architecture with built-in interpretability through a Deep Parity Bottleneck that replaces learned over-complete bases with parameter-free algebraic dictionaries, enabling efficient sparse feature representation by design rather than post-hoc recovery.
AI.motivation: Current approaches to interpretability rely on post-hoc sparse autoencoders (SAEs) that are computationally expensive and memory-intensive when applied per-layer at scale. There's a need for models that are interpretable by construction rather than requiring feature recovery after training.
AI.method: The ParityTransformer architecture uses a Deep Parity Bottleneck (DPB) at each layer that replaces learned over-complete bases with parameter-free algebraic dictionaries. The DPB provides deterministic incoherence guarantees and uses a hierarchically structured sparse bottleneck with multi-level mixture-of-experts approach for efficient hardware-aware implementation.
AI.result: ParityTransformers perform at least as well as post-hoc SAEs on sparse probing tasks while outperforming them on feature absorption, steering effectiveness, and fine-grained causal interventions. The features are native to the model's forward pass by construction, addressing whether SAEs probe features the model actually uses.
AI.conclusion: The ParityTransformer represents a significant step toward training models whose internal representations are interpretable by design rather than recovered post-hoc, overcoming the practical barriers that have prevented per-layer interpretable bottlenecks at scale.

title: Telco-GAIA: Bilingual Benchmark for Agents in Telecom Domain
summary: We introduce Telco-GAIA, a bilingual, multi-modal benchmark for evaluating tool-using agents on the data of a real-world telecommunications operator. Telco-GAIA comprises 100 human-verified question-answering tasks, in English and Arabic, that each demand multi-hop reasoning (4.2 hops on average) over three heterogeneous sources: a static website snapshot (HTML, images, and linked PDFs), a synthetic relational SQL database, and external web archives, spanning text, image, and tabular modalities. The benchmark is delivered as a sandboxed Docker environment and scored by normalized exact string matching, making evaluation objective, deterministic, and reproducible over time without any LLM-as-a-Judge. Evaluating a purpose-built reference agent across twelve commercial and open LLMs, we find Telco-GAIA challenging: even the strongest model solves only 71% of tasks; under a moderate cost budget, this falls to about 40%, and the visually grounded categories remain the weakest, where the average backend scores below 30%, leaving substantial headroom in document and image understanding. Telco-GAIA offers a rigorous, reproducible testbed for enterprise agents and a template for constructing closed-domain benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Telco-GAIA is a bilingual (English/Arabic) multi-modal benchmark for evaluating tool-using agents on real-world telecom data, featuring 100 QA tasks requiring multi-hop reasoning across website snapshots, SQL databases, and web archives, delivered as a sandboxed Docker environment.
AI.motivation: There is a need for rigorous, reproducible evaluation of tool-using agents in enterprise settings, particularly for real-world telecommunications data that involves complex multi-modal reasoning across different data sources and modalities.
AI.method: Created a benchmark with 100 human-verified QA tasks requiring multi-hop reasoning (4.2 hops avg) across three heterogeneous sources: static website snapshots (HTML, images, PDFs), synthetic relational SQL database, and external web archives. Implemented as a sandboxed Docker environment with scoring via normalized exact string matching.
AI.result: Even the strongest LLM solves only 71% of tasks; under moderate cost budget this falls to ~40%. Visually grounded categories are weakest with average backend scores below 30%, showing substantial room for improvement in document and image understanding.
AI.conclusion: Telco-GAIA provides a rigorous, reproducible testbed for enterprise agents and serves as a template for constructing closed-domain benchmarks, demonstrating significant challenges remain in multi-modal reasoning for real-world enterprise applications.

title: SalesLoop: Reinforcement Learning from Performance Feedback for Sales Lead Ranking
summary:
Lead ranking in Customer Relationship Management (CRM) systems faces a persistent challenge: models achieving high offline accuracy often underperform in production. We identify three fundamental gaps responsible for this disconnect: offline-online metric mismatch, pointwise-listwise objective misalignment, and temporal distribution drift. To address these gaps, we propose SalesLoop, a reinforcement learning framework that establishes a closed feedback loop between model predictions and real-world business outcomes. Our approach introduces (1) a performance-aware reward that encodes conversion outcomes weighted by ranking position and conversion velocity, and (2) Discriminative GRPO, a listwise optimization objective that adapts Group Relative Policy Optimization to discriminative ranking models.
  SalesLoop improves NDCG@K by +7.9\% and P@K by +15.8\% over the strongest static baseline. A 160-day production A/B test at a New Energy Vehicle manufacturer, spanning 16.5M leads and 280 sales specialists across two provincial markets, validates statistically significant cumulative lift of +4.7\% ($p=0.047$) and +8.7\% ($p=0.002$). In production, the ranking backbone achieves Top-10\% recall of 44.1\% and surfaces high-intent leads at $2.3\times$ the conversion rate of specialist baselines.

AI.tldr: SalesLoop is a reinforcement learning framework for CRM lead ranking that addresses offline-online performance gaps through a closed feedback loop with position/velocity-weighted rewards and listwise optimization, achieving significant production improvements over baselines.
AI.motivation: There's a persistent challenge in CRM lead ranking where models with high offline accuracy often underperform in production. Three fundamental gaps are identified: offline-online metric mismatch, pointwise-listwise objective misalignment, and temporal distribution drift.
AI.method: SalesLoop is a reinforcement learning framework with: (1) a performance-aware reward that encodes conversion outcomes weighted by ranking position and conversion velocity, and (2) Discriminative GRPO, a listwise optimization objective that adapts Group Relative Policy Optimization to discriminative ranking models.
AI.result: SalesLoop improves NDCG@K by +7.9% and P@K by +15.8% over strongest static baseline. Production A/B test at a New Energy Vehicle manufacturer (16.5M leads, 280 specialists) showed statistically significant cumulative lift of +4.7% (p=0.047) and +8.7% (p=0.002). In production, achieves 44.1% Top-10% recall and surfaces high-intent leads at 2.3× conversion rate of specialist baselines.
AI.conclusion: SalesLoop successfully addresses the offline-online performance gap in CRM lead ranking through a reinforcement learning framework that creates a closed feedback loop between model predictions and real-world business outcomes, demonstrating significant improvements in both offline metrics and production performance.

title: SiGMA: Sign-Guided Merging and Adaptation for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
summary: Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT) is crucial for adapting Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to evolving a sequence of downstream tasks. Prior methods mostly utilize Mixture of Experts or expansion merge approach, primarily focusing on catastrophic forgetting, yet they still suffer from negative interference during inference, where newly learned updates overwrite useful prior knowledge and degrade overall performance. To address this, we propose SiGMA (Sign Guided Merging and Adaptation), a simple yet effective framework that mitigates negative interference with two components: sign guided adaptive tuning during training and sign guided merging at inference. Sign guided adaptive tuning reduces collisions with past knowledge and learns the current task with minimal drift, mitigating severe forgetting. Sign guided merging further improves consolidation by selectively scaling salient parameters to preserve and amplify useful task specific knowledge. Experiments on UCIT and DCL benchmarks show that SiGMA significantly reduces negative interference and outperforms state of the art MCIT methods. Our code is available at SiGMA.

AI.tldr: SiGMA is a new framework for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning that reduces negative interference between tasks by using sign-guided adaptive tuning during training and sign-guided merging during inference.
AI.motivation: Previous methods for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT) focus on catastrophic forgetting but still suffer from negative interference during inference, where newly learned updates overwrite useful prior knowledge and degrade overall performance.
AI.method: SiGMA uses two components: 1) Sign guided adaptive tuning during training - reduces collisions with past knowledge and learns current tasks with minimal drift; 2) Sign guided merging at inference - selectively scales salient parameters to preserve and amplify useful task-specific knowledge.
AI.result: Experiments on UCIT and DCL benchmarks show that SiGMA significantly reduces negative interference and outperforms state-of-the-art MCIT methods.
AI.conclusion: SiGMA provides a simple yet effective framework for mitigating negative interference in Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning, addressing limitations of previous approaches that focused primarily on catastrophic forgetting but still suffered from interference issues.

title: Adaptive Multi-Horizon Reinforcement Learning
summary: Effective decision-making in complex and changing environments requires balancing short-term and long-term consequences. In reinforcement learning (RL), this trade-off is typically controlled through a fixed discount factor, which imposes a single exponentially discounted temporal horizon. However, biological agents exhibit flexible and adaptive temporal discounting, suggesting that effective planning requires multiple timescales. Here, we propose a multi-horizon approach that adaptively selects and combines temporal horizons, enabling robust adaptation to changes in reward structure without manual discount-factor tuning. This flexibility makes the method particularly suitable for continual learning scenarios involving task switches and varying environmental configurations. Empirically, we demonstrate that our approach identifies effective discount factors across a range of MiniGrid environments, including continual settings composed of three sequentially changing tasks. These results suggest that adaptive temporal discounting can improve parameter efficiency and enhance adaptability in both artificial and biologically inspired learning systems.

AI.tldr: Proposes multi-horizon RL approach with adaptive temporal discounting that selects and combines temporal horizons automatically, enabling robust adaptation to changing reward structures without manual tuning.
AI.motivation: Current RL uses fixed discount factors imposing single temporal horizons, but biological agents exhibit flexible adaptive temporal discounting for effective planning across multiple timescales.
AI.method: Multi-horizon approach that adaptively selects and combines temporal horizons, eliminating need for manual discount-factor tuning and enabling adaptation to changing reward structures.
AI.result: Method identifies effective discount factors across MiniGrid environments and continual settings with three sequentially changing tasks, demonstrating improved adaptability and parameter efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive temporal discounting improves parameter efficiency and enhances adaptability in both artificial and biologically inspired learning systems, particularly suitable for continual learning scenarios.

title: Reliability-Aware LLM Alignment from Inconsistent Human Feedback
summary: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is critical for aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human preferences. However, its efficacy is often compromised by the inherent inconsistency and subjectivity of human annotations. Existing preference optimization frameworks, such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), typically treat ambiguous pairs with high annotator disagreement identically to those with unanimous consensus, forcing models to overfit to inconsistent supervision signals and leading to suboptimal alignment. In this work, we propose Reliability-Guided Preference Optimization (RGPO), a robust framework designed to mitigate the impact of inconsistent human feedback. RGPO estimates annotator reliability and infers latent ground truth labels from noisy human feedback to identify robust preferences. Furthermore, we introduce a reliability-aware consistency optimization that dynamically modulates the training objective based on the consensus level of annotations, ensuring the model prioritizes high-consensus supervision signals. Extensive experiments on LLM alignment benchmarks demonstrate that RGPO effectively reduces inconsistency and noise in training data and achieves superior performance compared to widely adopted RLHF baselines. Our code and configurations are available at https://github.com/GenieHuang/RGPO.

AI.tldr: RGPO (Reliability-Guided Preference Optimization) is a novel framework that addresses inconsistency in human feedback for LLM alignment by estimating annotator reliability and dynamically adjusting training objectives based on consensus levels.
AI.motivation: RLHF is crucial for aligning LLMs with human preferences, but its effectiveness is undermined by inconsistent and subjective human annotations. Current methods like DPO treat ambiguous preference pairs the same as clear consensus pairs, forcing models to overfit to inconsistent signals and resulting in suboptimal alignment performance.
AI.method: RGPO introduces two key innovations: 1) Estimating annotator reliability and inferring latent ground truth labels from noisy human feedback to identify robust preferences, and 2) A reliability-aware consistency optimization that dynamically modulates the training objective based on annotation consensus levels, prioritizing high-consensus supervision signals.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on LLM alignment benchmarks show that RGPO effectively reduces inconsistency and noise in training data and achieves superior performance compared to widely adopted RLHF baselines.
AI.conclusion: RGPO provides a robust framework for addressing the critical challenge of inconsistent human feedback in LLM alignment, enabling more reliable preference optimization by intelligently weighting training signals based on annotation consensus and reliability.

title: End-to-End Learning of Safe Optimal Feedback Control in High Dimensions with Control Barrier Function Layers
summary: We consider the problem of learning high-dimensional semi-global feedback controllers under hard safety constraints enforced by control barrier functions (CBFs). Incorporating CBFs into end-to-end policy training requires embedding a quadratic-program-based safety filter as an optimization layer, but computational and differentiation bottlenecks have largely restricted prior approaches to low-dimensional systems, typically with at most 16 state dimensions. We address this limitation by combining operator splitting with the recently developed Jacobian-Free Backpropagation (JFB) method to enable scalable end-to-end training while preserving hard safety guarantees through the CBF safety filter. We justify this training methodology theoretically using nonsmooth analysis techniques and demonstrate its effectiveness on high-dimensional multi-agent nonlinear control problems with state and control dimensions up to 1200 and 400, respectively.

AI.tldr: Scalable end-to-end training of high-dimensional safety-critical controllers using operator splitting and Jacobian-Free Backpropagation to handle CBF safety filters efficiently.
AI.motivation: Prior approaches for learning safety-constrained controllers using control barrier functions (CBFs) have been limited to low-dimensional systems (≤16 state dimensions) due to computational and differentiation bottlenecks when embedding CBF safety filters as optimization layers in end-to-end training.
AI.method: Combines operator splitting with Jacobian-Free Backpropagation (JFB) to enable scalable end-to-end training while maintaining hard safety guarantees through CBF safety filters. Uses nonsmooth analysis techniques to theoretically justify the training methodology.
AI.result: Successfully demonstrates the approach on high-dimensional multi-agent nonlinear control problems with state dimensions up to 1200 and control dimensions up to 400, overcoming previous scalability limitations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed operator splitting + JFB method enables scalable end-to-end training of safety-critical controllers for high-dimensional systems while preserving hard safety guarantees, overcoming previous computational barriers.

title: CANN Bench: Benchmarking Agent Generated Kernels against Real NPU and Algorithmic Limits
summary: AI agents are now capable of writing, compiling, and iteratively optimizing low-level operator kernels on different hardware platforms. Existing benchmarks, however, focus almost exclusively on CUDA and Triton, leaving hardware ecosystems with less-exposed programming models without a common evaluation baseline. We present CANN Bench, an open benchmark for AI-generated operator code on Huawei's Ascend NPU. The current release covers 53 operators and 1060 test cases organized into four difficulty tiers -- from simple elementwise primitives to MoE dispatch and FlashAttention kernels -- spanning FP16, BF16, FP32, and INT8 precision formats. Evaluation adopts a \textbf{three-dimensional weighted composite score} that treats compilation, functional correctness, and performance as independent axes, providing a principled reward signal for kernel-generation agents. Performance is graded against an out-of-the-box PyTorch-on-Ascend baseline and an analytical per-case Hardware-Anchored Performance (HAP) limit on real NPU hardware, ensuring scores reflect genuine optimization headroom rather than measurement artifacts. The evaluation harness is designed to resist reward hacking from the ground up. CANN Bench is versioned within the official CANN repository and is designed for long-term community co-construction, providing the Ascend ecosystem with a quantitative, reproducible, and sustainably maintained yardstick for AI operator-authoring capability.

AI.tldr: CANN Bench is an open benchmark for AI-generated operator code on Huawei's Ascend NPU, addressing the lack of evaluation baselines for hardware ecosystems beyond CUDA/Triton with 53 operators across 1060 test cases and a three-dimensional scoring system.
AI.motivation: Existing AI kernel generation benchmarks focus almost exclusively on CUDA and Triton, leaving hardware ecosystems with less-exposed programming models (like Huawei's Ascend NPU) without a common evaluation baseline, creating a gap in the ecosystem.
AI.method: The benchmark covers 53 operators and 1060 test cases organized into four difficulty tiers (from simple elementwise to complex MoE/FlashAttention kernels) spanning multiple precision formats. It uses a three-dimensional weighted composite score treating compilation, functional correctness, and performance as independent axes, with performance graded against both PyTorch-on-Ascend baseline and Hardware-Anchored Performance limits on real NPU hardware.
AI.result: CANN Bench provides the Ascend ecosystem with a quantitative, reproducible benchmark for AI operator-authoring capability. It's versioned within the official CANN repository and designed for long-term community co-construction, with evaluation harness designed to resist reward hacking.
AI.conclusion: The paper introduces CANN Bench as a much-needed benchmark for AI-generated operator code on Huawei's Ascend NPU, offering a principled, multi-dimensional evaluation framework that addresses the current ecosystem gap and provides a sustainable, community-maintained yardstick for measuring AI kernel-authoring capabilities on this platform.

title: Explanation-Based Runtime Verification for Trustworthy ML-driven Optical Networks
comment: 6 Pages, 2 Figures. Accepted and presented at the 30th International Conference on Optical Network Design and Modelling (ONDM 2026), Munich, Germany, 12-15 May 2026
summary: Machine learning (ML) models are increasingly integrated into optical network automation frameworks to support tasks such as failure management, performance monitoring and resource allocation. In these environments, ML-driven predictions may be directly coupled with control-plane actions where incorrect decisions can immediately impact service quality, resource efficiency, and network stability. As automation levels increase, ensuring the reliability of individual decisions at deployment time becomes a critical requirement. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques have emerged to improve transparency by highlighting the factors influencing ML predictions. In addition to identifying influential features, they provide insights into the underlying reasoning process of the model, revealing how different input variables contribute to the final outcome and how feature interactions shape the decision boundary. In this work, we introduce explanation-based runtime verification, an approach that exploits model explanations to assess the soundness of individual ML decisions before they are executed in the network control loop. The proposed approach evaluates explanation coherence and physics grounding consistency at runtime, enabling the system to defer or reject decisions flagged as uncertain. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a representative use case of lightpath quality of transmission classification. Experimental results show that explanation-based verification can intercept a significant fraction of erroneous decisions while preserving high automation rate.

AI.tldr: Explanation-based runtime verification uses ML model explanations to assess decision reliability in optical network automation before execution, intercepting erroneous decisions while maintaining high automation.
AI.motivation: As ML models are increasingly integrated into optical network automation for critical tasks like failure management and resource allocation, incorrect decisions can immediately impact service quality and network stability. With rising automation levels, ensuring the reliability of individual ML decisions at deployment time becomes critical, requiring methods to verify decision soundness before execution.
AI.method: The authors introduce explanation-based runtime verification, which exploits model explanations from XAI techniques to assess ML decision soundness before execution in the network control loop. The approach evaluates explanation coherence and physics grounding consistency at runtime, allowing the system to defer or reject decisions flagged as uncertain.
AI.result: Experimental results on a representative use case of lightpath quality of transmission classification demonstrate that explanation-based verification can intercept a significant fraction of erroneous decisions while preserving high automation rate.
AI.conclusion: Explanation-based runtime verification provides an effective approach for ensuring ML decision reliability in optical network automation by leveraging model explanations to identify and intercept uncertain decisions before they impact network operations, balancing automation with reliability requirements.

title: Representation Robustness Under Executable Reasoning Constraints in Large Language Models for Mathematical Problem Solving
comment: presented at the 28th International Conference on Human-Computer Interaction (2026), Montreal, Canada
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated on mathematical problem solving, yet prior work often treats representationally equivalent formulations as interchangeable and conflates reasoning errors with interface failures. This paper investigates representation robustness in LLM-based mathematical problem solving by systematically varying surface representations of the same underlying problems, including story problems, word-equations, symbolic equations, and isomorphic paraphrases. Using a curated dataset of mathematically equivalent problems, we evaluate five contemporary LLMs under a direct answer generation condition. We find substantial representational sensitivity: models frequently change correctness across equivalent formulations, with nontrivial flip rates across story, symbolic, and word-equation variants. We also observe systematic regressions under isomorphic reformulations, showing that even subtle paraphrase-level changes can degrade performance despite preserved mathematical structure. We then evaluate a code-augmented condition in which models externalize reasoning as executable Python code that is run locally for validation. This interface reveals strong latent reasoning capability in some models that perform poorly under direct prompting, but it does not uniformly improve robustness. Instead, failures shift across interaction layers, from opaque reasoning errors to protocol violations and execution failures. Even when executable reasoning succeeds, representation sensitivity often persists. Overall, our results show that reasoning scaffolds do not eliminate representational brittleness, but expose new tradeoffs among correctness, reliability, latency, and cost. We argue that representation should be treated as a first-class interface design variable in LLM evaluation and deployment, especially for AI-assisted problem-solving systems.

AI.tldr: LLM performance on math problems is highly sensitive to surface representations of equivalent problems, and even code-augmented reasoning doesn't eliminate this brittleness.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluations treat mathematically equivalent formulations as interchangeable and conflate reasoning errors with interface failures, failing to account for representation sensitivity in problem solving.
AI.method: Created a curated dataset of mathematically equivalent problems with varying surface representations (story problems, word-equations, symbolic equations, isomorphic paraphrases). Evaluated 5 contemporary LLMs under direct answer generation, and also tested code-augmented reasoning where models externalize thinking as executable Python code.
AI.result: Found substantial representational sensitivity - models frequently change correctness across equivalent formulations. Code-augmented reasoning reveals latent reasoning capabilities but doesn't uniformly improve robustness - failures shift to protocol violations and execution errors. Representation sensitivity persists even when executable reasoning succeeds.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning scaffolds don't eliminate representational brittleness but create tradeoffs among correctness, reliability, latency, and cost. Representation should be treated as a first-class interface design variable in LLM evaluation and deployment for AI-assisted problem-solving systems.

title: Attribution Markets: A Fisher-Market Formulation for Fractional Credit Assignment Between Planned Tasks and Performed Actions
comment: 35 pages, 3 figures. Companion technical report with extended treatment of dynamic/forward-looking markets and reinforcement-learning extensions available separately
summary: Personal and organizational planning systems maintain two records that drift apart: what was planned (a task's effort budget) and what was done (a logged action's duration and description). Existing systems bridge them with an exclusive, all-or-nothing link that strands genuinely related but unlinked effort and reports false stalls on active goals. We formulate the bridge as a quasi-linear Fisher market: planned tasks are budget-constrained buyers, performed actions are divisible goods, and a fused text/structural/temporal signal sets each buyer's valuation. Two market instruments - a seller reserve price and a buyer cash option - yield conservation, a hard budget cap, and a provable junk filter as theorems. We extend the market with a concave completion utility discounting progress as a task nears its plan; standard convergence theory for the market's algorithm does not transfer here, resolved by a satiation-threshold fixed point with existence (Brouwer) and local uniqueness under an explicit diagonal-dominance condition, validated empirically on random and adversarial instances. A de-circularized, multi-seed benchmark - observed affinity corrupted independently of the scored ground truth - surfaces a genuine weak spot: the market's sharp, zero-entropy equilibrium is more sensitive to affinity noise than entropy-regularized optimal transport's permanently smoothed one. We resolve this with a one-parameter entropy-regularized generalization unifying the two, plus a noise-adaptive rule for its regularization strength. We report full reproducibility parameters, discuss limitations candidly, and relate the result to multi-touch attribution, optimal transport, and online Fisher-market algorithms.

AI.tldr: A Fisher market-based system bridges planning budgets and logged actions using text/structural/temporal signals, with entropy regularization to handle noise sensitivity.
AI.motivation: Existing planning systems maintain separate records for planned tasks and actual work logs, using exclusive links that misrepresent related effort and create false stalls on active goals.
AI.method: Formulate planning-action reconciliation as a quasi-linear Fisher market where tasks are budget-constrained buyers, actions are divisible goods. Extend with completion utility discounting and entropy regularization to handle affinity noise sensitivity.
AI.result: Market instruments yield conservation, hard budget caps, and provable junk filtering. Convergence issues resolved via satiation-threshold fixed point. Entropy regularization unifies market equilibrium with optimal transport for noise robustness.
AI.conclusion: The approach effectively bridges planning and execution records, overcoming limitations of exclusive linking, with applications to multi-touch attribution and connections to optimal transport and online Fisher-market algorithms.

title: Attention Degradation, Function Token Anchoring, and the Limits of Attention-Based Intervention in Large Language Models
summary: Mean cross-positional attention degradation is widely reported in transformer interpretability, yet whether it causally limits contextual retrieval remains untested. We present six coordinated experiments across GPT-2, LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, OPT-1.3B, and distilgpt2. We first characterise short-term (5-100 token) attention degradation, finding a universal exponential-then-plateau pattern whose rate is inversely correlated with depth, with distinct layer-wise entropy signatures per architecture. Function token anchoring proves architecture-dependent: OPT-1.3B (absolute positional encoding) shows distance-dependent preposition specificity, GPT-2 shows uniform non-specific dependence, and LLaMA (RoPE) shows reversal at long distances. Strategic comma insertion at clause boundaries causally reduces prediction degradation in the 40-80 token range, with the benefit tied to syntactic boundary alignment rather than token density. We then test the mechanism causally: Relay-Aware Attention (RAA), which biases attention logits toward function token positions, verifiably increases attention mass by 16-24% yet yields null effects on GPT-2 and LLaMA-1B, preliminary harm on LLaMA-3B, and a mixed effect on OPT-1.3B that nets to approximately zero. Multi-fact retrieval probes further show that degradation rate does not predict retrieval accuracy across models. We conclude that mean attention degradation is largely descriptive rather than prescriptive: function tokens contribute through what their hidden states compute, not through the attention they receive -- with implications for interpretability methodology and attention-score-based inference optimisations such as KV-cache eviction.

AI.tldr: Mean attention degradation doesn't causally limit contextual retrieval; function tokens contribute through hidden state computations rather than attention scores.
AI.motivation: Address the untested assumption that mean cross-positional attention degradation causally limits contextual retrieval in transformers, despite being widely reported in interpretability research.
AI.method: Six coordinated experiments across GPT-2, LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, OPT-1.3B, and distilgpt2; characterizations of short-term attention degradation patterns; testing with strategic comma insertion; causal testing with Relay-Aware Attention (RAA); multi-fact retrieval probes.
AI.result: Found universal exponential-then-plateau degradation pattern with architecture-specific signatures; comma insertion reduces degradation when aligned with syntactic boundaries; RAA increases attention mass but yields null/mixed effects on model performance; degradation rate doesn't predict retrieval accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Mean attention degradation is largely descriptive rather than prescriptive - function tokens contribute through what their hidden states compute, not through the attention they receive, challenging current interpretability methods and attention-based optimizations.

title: CEDAR: Causal Edge Discovery for Autoregressive Processes
summary: We propose CEDAR (Causal Edge Discovery for Autoregressive Processes), a constraint-based method for lagged causal edge discovery in sparse autoregressive time series. CEDAR screens candidate cross-variable lags using AR(1)-residualized, U-centered distance correlation, then applies two targeted conditional-independence tests per significant cross-variable lag candidate and accepts at most one lag per ordered pair. A stable MCI pruning step removes indirect edges, and optional deterministic C-nodes adjust for specified trend-like nonstationarity. In sparse regimes where few lags survive screening, CEDAR requires $O(d^2)$ CI tests after screening while retaining edge-level interpretability. CEDAR is most effective when data are scarce and variables exhibit lag-1 self-dynamics; methods with richer conditioning sets become preferable as $T$ grows or when higher-order autoregressive or simultaneous multi-lag effects are common.

AI.tldr: CEDAR is a constraint-based method for discovering lagged causal edges in sparse autoregressive time series using distance correlation screening and targeted conditional independence tests.
AI.motivation: There's a need for efficient causal discovery methods for time series data, particularly in sparse regimes where data is scarce and variables exhibit simple self-dynamics. Existing methods often have high computational complexity or lose edge-level interpretability.
AI.method: CEDAR screens candidate cross-variable lags using AR(1)-residualized, U-centered distance correlation. For significant candidates, it applies two targeted conditional-independence tests per candidate while accepting at most one lag per ordered pair. It includes stable MCI pruning to remove indirect edges and optional deterministic C-nodes to adjust for trend-like nonstationarity.
AI.result: In sparse regimes where few lags survive screening, CEDAR requires only O(d²) conditional independence tests after screening while maintaining edge-level interpretability, making it efficient for scarce data.
AI.conclusion: CEDAR is most effective when data are scarce and variables exhibit lag-1 self-dynamics. Methods with richer conditioning sets become preferable as sample size grows or when higher-order autoregressive or simultaneous multi-lag effects are common.

title: Autonomous disproofs of the sum-product conjecture over $\mathbb R$ with GPT-5.5 Pro
summary: OpenAI's recent disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture marked a milestone for AI in mathematics. It also inspired another breakthrough: a human disproof of the Erdős--Szemerédi sum-product conjecture over $\mathbb R$. In this paper, we present a simple agent built on GPT-5.5 Pro. Using a problem-agnostic, three-stage prompting pipeline -- proof-plan proposal, proof construction, and review -- the agent autonomously generated correct proofs that the sum-product conjecture is false over $\mathbb R$ in 7 of 8 independent trials; in the remaining trial, it identified an unresolved gap in its argument. The seven proofs are diverse: some are close to existing unit-based constructions, while others avoid units by using $L^p$-type regions of algebraic integers. The system used an average of 132.4k reasoning tokens per trial. We release the code, intermediate outputs, and generated proofs, providing a reproducible, data-contamination-free case study in autonomous proof generation.

AI.tldr: A GPT-5.5 Pro-based autonomous agent successfully disproved the Erdős-Szemerédi sum-product conjecture over real numbers in 7 out of 8 independent trials using a three-stage prompting pipeline, generating diverse proofs including unit-based and algebraic integer approaches.
AI.motivation: Inspired by OpenAI's recent disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture, which demonstrated AI capabilities in mathematics, the researchers aimed to build upon this breakthrough by developing an autonomous agent that could tackle another major conjecture - the Erdős-Szemerédi sum-product conjecture.
AI.method: Built a simple agent on GPT-5.5 Pro using a problem-agnostic three-stage prompting pipeline: 1) proof-plan proposal, 2) proof construction, and 3) review. The system autonomously generated and evaluated proofs across 8 independent trials.
AI.result: The agent generated correct proofs disproving the sum-product conjecture over ℝ in 7 of 8 trials (87.5% success rate). Proofs were diverse: some used unit-based constructions similar to existing approaches, while others employed novel approaches using L^p-type regions of algebraic integers. The remaining trial identified an unresolved gap in the argument.
AI.conclusion: This work demonstrates successful autonomous proof generation in mathematics using large language models, provides reproducible case study free from data contamination, and shows that diverse proof strategies can emerge from AI systems. The authors release code and outputs for verification.

title: Perspective Latents as an Architectural Condition for Causal Emergence in Active Inference Agents
summary: A recent line of work measures causal emergence in reinforcement learning agents through Integrated Information Decomposition, reporting that $Φ_r$ grows with training and tracks reward improvement. For active inference, this raises the question of how reward-free predictive organization relates to such information-theoretic signatures. I test this within an active inference agent whose architecture separates a fast perception latent $z$ from a slow global latent $g$, where $g$ is driven by prediction error and structurally decoupled from policy gradients. In a reward-free environmental regime-switching protocol, $Φ_r$ concentrates in $g$; its aggregate magnitude is largely architectural and decreases with training. The substantive effect of learning becomes legible only at the atom-compositional level: decoupling flips sign from negative to positive and becomes regime-invariant under environmental change, while downward causation carries the regime-dependent adjustment. These results identify $g$ as the architectural locus of $Φ_r$-relevant temporal organization in an active inference agent, and argue against reading scalar $Φ_r$ as a direct index of learned integration.

AI.tldr: Active inference agent shows reward-free predictive organization manifests in slow global latent (g) as Φr signatures, but scalar Φr doesn't directly track learned integration - compositional analysis reveals true learning effects.
AI.motivation: Recent work shows Φr (causal emergence) grows with training and tracks reward in RL agents, raising question: how does reward-free predictive organization in active inference agents relate to such information-theoretic signatures?
AI.method: Tested active inference agent with architecture separating fast perception latent (z) from slow global latent (g), where g is driven by prediction error and structurally decoupled from policy gradients. Used reward-free environmental regime-switching protocol.
AI.result: Φr concentrates in g; aggregate magnitude is largely architectural and decreases with training. Learning effects become visible only at atom-compositional level: decoupling flips sign (negative→positive) and becomes regime-invariant, while downward causation carries regime-dependent adjustment.
AI.conclusion: g is the architectural locus of Φr-relevant temporal organization in active inference agents, and scalar Φr should not be read as a direct index of learned integration - compositional analysis is necessary to identify true learning effects.

title: ConfidenceBench: Evaluating Confidence Calibration in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in settings where fluent but incorrect answers can be costly. In these settings, accuracy alone is insufficient: models must also know when they are likely to be wrong. We present ConfidenceBench, a calibration benchmark that evaluates verbalized confidence estimates in 15 frontier LLMs using the Brier score, a proper scoring rule that incentivises truthful probability reporting. Confidence is elicited via prompting, requiring no access to model logits and making the framework applicable to both closed-source and open-source systems. The benchmark comprises 200 private multiple-choice questions across four categories: spatial reasoning, high-precision mathematics, word lookup, and unknowable questions. Across three independent runs, Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview achieve the lowest Brier scores, both reported as 0.103. Both substantially outperform the calibrated-random baseline of 0.1875, while Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite scores 0.367, indicating severe miscalibration. Accuracy and calibration diverge substantially across model families: the most accurate model is not the best-calibrated, and several models perform worse than the calibrated-random Brier baseline despite reasonable accuracy. These results show that verbalized confidence calibration is a distinct and practically important axis of LLM reliability, complementary to standard accuracy-based evaluation.

AI.tldr: ConfidenceBench is a calibration benchmark that evaluates how well frontier LLMs can provide truthful verbalized confidence estimates for their answers using the Brier score. Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview perform best, showing calibration is distinct from accuracy.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used in high-stakes settings where incorrect answers can be costly. Accuracy alone is insufficient - models need to know when they are likely to be wrong, requiring proper confidence calibration that's complementary to accuracy-based evaluation.
