Drawing on Margaret Boden's foundational framework, both her three properties of creativity (novelty, surprise, and value) and her three types of creative processes (combinatorial, exploratory, and transformational), the paper argues that AI systems are structurally incapable of creativity in its strongest sense. While they exhibit genuine capability in the domain of combinatorial creativity, they are significantly bounded in exploratory creativity, and fundamentally incapable of transformational creativity. The paper further argues that the most important limitation of current AI systems is not the absence of novelty per se, but the absence of any mechanism for serendipity, accident, or the unexpected, all of which play a central role in the phenomenology of creativity, and the absence of any subject position from which to recognize and welcome such chance events. The paper concludes by proposing a model of human, AI creative collaboration that is both realistic and generative, illustrated by several concrete experiments. The paper is itself a demonstration of the thesis it advances: it was composed through a deliberate human AI collaborative process, which is described in the methodological note that opens it.

AI.tldr: AI systems are structurally incapable of true creativity in its strongest sense, showing limited capabilities in exploratory creativity and fundamentally incapable of transformational creativity, with absence of serendipity mechanisms being the key limitation.
AI.motivation: To examine whether AI systems can be truly creative, using a dual perspective from engineering/machine learning and artistic/philosophical backgrounds, addressing the fundamental question of machine creativity.
AI.method: Uses Margaret Boden's framework of creativity (novelty, surprise, value) and creative processes (combinatorial, exploratory, transformational). The paper itself demonstrates human-AI collaboration as it was composed through such a process described in a methodological note.
AI.result: AI systems show genuine capability in combinatorial creativity, are significantly bounded in exploratory creativity, and fundamentally incapable of transformational creativity. Key limitation is absence of mechanisms for serendipity, accident, or unexpected events, and lack of subjective position to recognize such events.
AI.conclusion: Proposes a realistic and generative model of human-AI creative collaboration, illustrated with concrete experiments. The paper serves as both theoretical analysis and practical demonstration of its thesis through its own collaborative creation process.

title: Position Bias is Hidden Behind Ceiling Effects: A Permutation Diagnostic for LLM Benchmarks
comment: 25 pages, 4 figures, 2 appendices. Code, data, and preregistration verification at https://github.com/TambaClan/inspect_permute. Companion paper: arXiv:2606.26185
summary: Position bias in multiple-choice LLM evaluation is widely cited as a confound in capability comparisons, but published measurements rely on single answer-order shuffles whose results confound the bias signal with content-level noise and sampling stochasticity. I introduce inspect_permute, an open-source extension to the inspect_ai evaluation framework that runs exhaustive answer-order permutations per question and reports the chi-squared / Cramer V signature of position bias with bootstrap confidence intervals. I apply the tool across four vendors (gpt-4o-mini, claude-haiku-4-5, gemini-2.5-flash, grok-3) on five MMLU subjects, 24,000 API calls under temperature-0 generation, with falsifier predictions pre-registered via a public SHA-256 hash before half the data was observed. Position bias turns out to be statistically detectable only within a roughly 60-95% base-accuracy Goldilocks zone. Below it, processing-load dominance swamps subject-specific signal; above it, ceiling effects compress the variance below the chi-squared test resolution. Detectable cells separate into two mechanism types: monotone A-to-D decrease (processing_load, in low-tier models) and non-monotone D-drop (content_ambiguity, in a narrow capability band). Standard MMLU places every frontier-tier model above the detection band, so absence of signal there should be read as not measurable, not unbiased. Together with the ceiling-effect characterisation in arXiv:2606.26185, this work brackets the detectable region of position-bias measurement and makes the field central question askable in a verifiable form. Package, data, preregistration under MIT.

AI.tldr: The study introduces inspect_permute, a tool for accurately measuring position bias in LLM evaluations by running exhaustive answer-order permutations, revealing that position bias is only statistically detectable within a specific accuracy range (60-95%), with different bias mechanisms emerging at different capability levels.
AI.motivation: Existing position bias measurements in multiple-choice LLM evaluations rely on single answer-order shuffles, which confound bias signals with content-level noise and sampling stochasticity, making it difficult to obtain reliable bias measurements.
AI.method: Developed inspect_permute, an open-source extension to inspect_ai that runs exhaustive answer-order permutations per question and reports chi-squared/Cramer V signature of position bias with bootstrap confidence intervals. Applied to four vendors (gpt-4o-mini, claude-haiku-4-5, gemini-2.5-flash, grok-3) on five MMLU subjects with 24,000 API calls under temperature-0 generation, using pre-registered predictions via public SHA-256 hash.
AI.result: Position bias is statistically detectable only within a 60-95% base-accuracy "Goldilocks zone." Below this zone, processing load dominance swamps subject-specific signal; above it, ceiling effects compress variance below test resolution. Two bias mechanisms were identified: monotone A-to-D decrease (processing load in low-tier models) and non-monotone D-drop (content ambiguity in narrow capability bands). Frontier-tier models typically fall above the detection band.
AI.conclusion: Standard MMLU places frontier-tier models above the position bias detection band, meaning absence of signal should be interpreted as not measurable rather than unbiased. This work, together with ceiling-effect characterization in prior research, brackets the detectable region of position-bias measurement and enables verifiable inquiry into this field-wide question.

title: Profiling Lightweight Large Language Models
summary: Lightweight large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being deployed locally on personal computers and are expected to play a growing role in resource-constrained edge and mobile environments. In such settings, energy consumption, execution time, and memory usage directly affect practical usability, yet existing evaluations of LLM efficiency largely rely on proxy descriptors such as parameter count or FLOPs, often decoupled from task precision. This paper introduces a PTME-based experimental framework for the precision-aware profiling of lightweight LLM inference, jointly measuring Precision, execution Time, peak Memory usage, and Energy consumption through direct hardware-level measurements. The methodology is applied to a representative set of lightweight LLMs executed locally under edge-class resource envelopes on a controlled desktop platform, using benchmarks spanning code generation, mathematical reasoning, and multi-task understanding. We find that static proxy descriptors approximate inference cost well but fail to predict precision. Tightening the resource envelope increases cost without affecting precision, amplifying execution time more strongly than energy and penalizing larger models the most. Moreover, no single model dominates across all PTME dimensions, and a Pareto analysis reveals non-dominated configurations that would be hidden by accuracy-only or efficiency-only assessments, providing practical guidance for selecting models under different resource envelopes. These results show that selecting lightweight LLMs by size, FLOPs, latency, or accuracy alone can select the wrong deployment candidate; PTME profiling exposes configurations that preserve useful accuracy at lower physical cost.

AI.tldr: A framework called PTME (Precision-Time-Memory-Energy) enables holistic evaluation of lightweight LLMs by measuring real hardware performance across multiple dimensions simultaneously, revealing that traditional proxy metrics fail to identify optimal models for resource-constrained deployments.
AI.motivation: Current LLM efficiency evaluations rely on proxy metrics like parameter count or FLOPs that don't capture real-world performance on edge/mobile devices, where energy, time, and memory directly impact usability. There's a need for precision-aware profiling that measures actual hardware performance.
AI.method: Developed a PTME-based experimental framework for precision-aware profiling of lightweight LLM inference, measuring Precision, execution Time, peak Memory usage, and Energy consumption through direct hardware-level measurements. Applied to representative lightweight LLMs on edge-class resource envelopes using benchmarks for code generation, mathematical reasoning, and multi-task understanding.
AI.result: Static proxy descriptors approximate inference cost but fail to predict precision; tightening resource envelopes increases cost without affecting precision; larger models penalized most by constraints; no single model dominates across all PTME dimensions; Pareto analysis reveals non-dominated configurations hidden by accuracy-only or efficiency-only assessments.
AI.conclusion: Traditional selection metrics (size, FLOPs, latency, or accuracy alone) can choose wrong deployment candidates; PTME profiling identifies configurations that preserve useful accuracy at lower physical cost, providing practical guidance for selecting models under different resource envelopes in edge/mobile environments.

title: TwistedMerge: Certified Higher-Order Diagnostics and Abstention for Model Merging
summary: Model merging combines independently trained or fine-tuned models, but pairwise alignability does not imply globally consistent alignment. We formulate merging as a finite descent problem in which checkpoints are local objects, alignment maps are transitions, and cycle products are residuals. TwistedMerge is a conservative certification pipeline that separates fixed-chart averaging, synchronization-removable gauge inconsistency, a certified central obstruction on a specified comparison complex, and nonabelian holonomy. A residual is promoted to a cohomology class only after inverse-consistency, coefficient-identification, centrality, and closure tests; otherwise the method abstains and returns an ordinary or synchronized fallback. We prove a constant-edge no-go result, frozen-complex three-way and predeclared-family error-control theorems, and a refinement test for comparison-complex sensitivity. A planted neural alignment defect is removed by cycle-consistent synchronization, showing that a nonzero cycle score alone is not a higher obstruction. Controlled central systems recover the predicted non-coboundary and projective-rank behavior, while noisy estimates move from certification to abstention without false lifts on the tested controls. A trained low-rank-adapter audit shows that naive factor averaging depends on the chosen GLr representative, whereas global factor synchronization and dense-delta SVD are stable. On natural checkpoint collections, cycle residuals do not predict merge degradation and no natural central or period-index class is certified. The results position descent theory as a falsifiable certification and abstention framework.

AI.tldr: TwistedMerge is a certification framework for model merging that identifies alignment inconsistencies as cohomology classes in a comparison complex, abstaining from merging when inconsistencies are detected.
AI.motivation: Model merging combines trained models, but pairwise alignability doesn't guarantee globally consistent alignment. Current methods may produce suboptimal merges due to hidden alignment inconsistencies that need systematic detection.
AI.method: Formulates merging as finite descent problem: checkpoints as local objects, alignment maps as transitions, cycle products as residuals. Uses TwistedMerge pipeline with fixed-chart averaging, synchronization removal, certified central obstruction detection on comparison complex, and nonabelian holonomy analysis.
AI.result: Proves theoretical results: constant-edge no-go theorem, error-control theorems. Shows cycle-consistent synchronization removes planted defects. Demonstrates trained low-rank-adapter audit reveals naive factor averaging depends on GLr choice, while global synchronization is stable. On natural checkpoints, cycle residuals don't predict merge degradation.
AI.conclusion: Descent theory provides falsifiable certification and abstention framework for model merging, offering rigorous detection of alignment inconsistencies without producing false positive certifications.

title: Enhancing Explainable Cardiac Diagnosis with Guide-Grounded Multimodal LLMs
summary: The electrocardiogram (ECG) is a cornerstone of cardiac as- sessment, yet clinical deployment of deep learning models remains con- strained by limited interpretability and the hallucination risk of large language models (LLMs). Existing CNN+Grad-CAM+multimodal LLM frameworks can generate ECG reports, but their explanations are often only weakly grounded in established diagnostic criteria, reducing trust- worthiness and reproducibility. We propose a guide-grounded multimodal framework that explicitly anchors report generation in curated clinical knowledge. A convolutional neural network (CNN) and Grad-CAM first produce class probabilities and class-specific heatmaps from 12-lead ECG images. In parallel, authoritative ECG textbooks and guideline materials are distilled offline into a structured ECG Interpretation Guide, which is injected as a fixed knowledge block for every sample. Conditioned on the ECG image, Grad-CAM overlay, CNN-derived fact pack, and the in- jected guide, a multimodal LLM generates structured diagnostic reports with guideline-consistent terminology and criteria usage. Experiments on the full PTB-XL test set demonstrate that guide grounding improves se- mantic quality and perceived consistency of generated reports while pre- serving competitive classification performance. In particular, our method increases the average BERTScore of generated impressions from 0.818 to 0.953 relative to a strong CNN+Grad-CAM+MLLM baseline, indicat- ing closer alignment with reference reports. These findings suggest that injecting a distilled interpretation guide into the multimodal prompting pipeline offers a practical pathway to reduce hallucinations and enhance the clinical plausibility of LLM-based ECG explanations, bringing ex- plainable cardiac diagnosis closer to real-world deployment.

AI.tldr: A guide-grounded multimodal framework that uses a distilled ECG interpretation guide to anchor LLM-generated ECG reports in clinical knowledge, reducing hallucinations and improving report quality while maintaining classification performance.
AI.motivation: Clinical deployment of deep learning models for ECG interpretation is limited by poor interpretability and hallucination risks of LLMs. Existing frameworks generate reports with explanations weakly grounded in diagnostic criteria, reducing trustworthiness and reproducibility.
AI.method: CNN+Grad-CAM produces class probabilities and heatmaps from 12-lead ECG images. Authoritative ECG textbooks/guidelines are distilled into a structured ECG Interpretation Guide, injected as fixed knowledge. A multimodal LLM, conditioned on ECG image, Grad-CAM overlay, CNN-derived facts, and the injected guide, generates structured diagnostic reports.
AI.result: On PTB-XL test set, guide grounding improves semantic quality and perceived consistency of generated reports while preserving competitive classification performance. BERTScore of generated impressions increased from 0.818 to 0.953 compared to baseline.
AI.conclusion: Injecting a distilled interpretation guide into multimodal prompting reduces hallucinations and enhances clinical plausibility of LLM-based ECG explanations, bringing explainable cardiac diagnosis closer to real-world deployment.

title: Information-Theoretically Secure Aggregation for Lightweight Federated Learning: Resilient to Dropouts and Adversaries
summary: On-device federated learning (FL) enables privacy-preserving and personalized model training on resource-constrained devices such as smartphones and IoT nodes. To reduce communication cost, sign-based methods (e.g., signSGD) transmit one-bit gradients. However, exposing gradient signs makes them vulnerable to inference attacks, while existing secure aggregation schemes are often incompatible with such methods or incur significant computational and communication overhead. We propose a lightweight and information-theoretically secure aggregation framework tailored for sign-based FL. The framework securely computes the majority vote (MV) polynomial through single-round secure multiplication, ensuring end-to-end information-theoretic security under the honest-majority assumption while revealing only the final aggregated sign to the server. To enhance efficiency and scalability, we introduce two key techniques. First, inverse-form exponent reduction halves the effective MV polynomial degree, reducing both communication and computation costs. Second, we propose single-round secure multiplication, achieving linear offline complexity and storage with only a single online communication. Together, these techniques reduce online communication by up to 99.5% and latency by up to 85.7% compared to conventional approaches. Also, by leveraging inherent MDS-code-based decoding, the framework achieves robustness against both dropouts and adversarial behaviors, yielding accuracy gains of up to 20.65% and 10.74%, respectively. Overall, the proposed framework establishes a practical foundation for large-scale, low-latency, and information-theoretically secure aggregation in sign-based FL.

AI.tldr: Lightweight information-theoretically secure aggregation framework for sign-based federated learning that enables efficient secure majority voting of gradient signs with strong privacy guarantees and robustness against dropouts/adversaries.
AI.motivation: Sign-based methods in federated learning (like signSGD) transmit one-bit gradients to reduce communication but expose gradient signs to inference attacks. Existing secure aggregation schemes are incompatible with sign-based methods or incur high computational/communication overhead.
AI.method: Proposes a lightweight secure aggregation framework for sign-based FL that: 1) Securely computes majority vote polynomial through single-round secure multiplication, 2) Uses inverse-form exponent reduction to halve effective MV polynomial degree, 3) Implements single-round secure multiplication with linear offline complexity, and 4) Leverages MDS-code-based decoding for robustness.
AI.result: Achieves 99.5% reduction in online communication and 85.7% reduction in latency compared to conventional approaches. Provides accuracy gains up to 20.65% against dropouts and 10.74% against adversarial behaviors. Ensures end-to-end information-theoretic security revealing only aggregated sign to server.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework establishes a practical foundation for large-scale, low-latency, and information-theoretically secure aggregation in sign-based federated learning, addressing the tension between communication efficiency and privacy preservation.

title: Efficient and Interpretable Body-Based Emotion Recognition with Lightweight Temporal Convolutional Networks
comment: Accepted at the 14th International Conference on Affective Computing and Intelligent Interaction (ACII 2026)
summary: Body-based emotion recognition is important for real-time affective systems, but graph-based skeleton models can be computationally expensive. This paper studies whether lightweight temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) can provide an efficient and interpretable alternative for body-based emotion classification. We evaluate a family of TCN models on DIEM-A and compare them with a graph-based time-series graph (G-TSG) baseline using accuracy, macro-F1, parameter count, and inference latency. Although G-TSG achieves the highest mean performance, TCN-Base remains within $1.58$ accuracy points and $1.25$ macro-F1 points while using $79.18\%$ fewer parameters and reducing classifier latency by approximately $12.5\times$. We also analyze body-region contributions using region-specific TCN models, zero-based occlusion, and G-TSG gradient saliency. The results show that upper-body motion provides the strongest standalone regional cue, that the usefulness of body regions varies across emotions, and that different interpretability methods capture distinct aspects of model behavior. These findings suggest that lightweight TCNs can support efficient body-based emotion recognition while also providing practical insight into how motion cues contribute to classification.

AI.tldr: Lightweight temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) offer efficient and interpretable alternatives to graph-based models for body-based emotion recognition, achieving competitive performance with significantly reduced computational cost while providing insights into regional motion contributions.
AI.motivation: Graph-based skeleton models for body-based emotion recognition are computationally expensive, creating a need for more efficient alternatives that can still provide interpretability into how body motion contributes to emotion classification.
AI.method: Evaluated a family of TCN models on DIEM-A dataset compared to graph-based time-series graph (G-TSG) baseline, using accuracy, macro-F1, parameter count, and inference latency metrics. Also analyzed body-region contributions using region-specific TCN models, zero-based occlusion, and G-TSG gradient saliency methods.
AI.result: G-TSG achieved highest mean performance, but TCN-Base remained within 1.58 accuracy points and 1.25 macro-F1 points while using 79.18% fewer parameters and reducing classifier latency by approximately 12.5×. Upper-body motion provides strongest standalone regional cue, body region usefulness varies across emotions, and different interpretability methods capture distinct model behavior aspects.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight TCNs can support efficient body-based emotion recognition while providing practical insight into how motion cues contribute to classification, making them a viable alternative to computationally expensive graph-based models.

title: HierarchicalDAEW: Domain-Aware Edge-Weighted Graph Convolution with Evidential Uncertainty for Multi-Section Spatial Gene Expression Prediction from H&E Histology
summary: Spatial transcriptomics assays remain costly and technically demanding, restricting transcriptome-wide profiling to specialist settings and preventing routine clinical deployment. Predicting spatially resolved gene expression from H&E histology could close this gap, yet current methods largely ignore the underlying tissue architecture and rarely quantify how their predictions can be trusted. We introduce HierarchicalDAEW, a dual-graph architecture that addresses both gaps. On the spot graph, a Domain-Aware Edge-Weighted convolutional operator learns separate projections for inter-domain, intra-domain, and boundary edges derived from Leiden clustering, allowing the model to treat tissue heterogeneity as an explicit structural signal rather than an implicit one. A second gene-level graph then fuses protein-protein interaction priors from STRING-DB with tissue-specific co-expression through learned attention gating, propagating predictions from a landmark gene set to a broader gene panel. Reliability is handled through evidential uncertainty estimation, which produces far better calibrated confidence intervals than Monte Carlo dropout under identical conditions. Across six human Visium sections spanning breast, colorectal, prostate, and cerebellar tissue, and against thirteen published baselines, HierarchicalDAEW achieves the strongest correlation with ground-truth expression, with gains that hold up under multi-seed reproducibility checks and negative controls that rule out positional shortcuts. Ablations further confirm that both the domain-aware edge typing and the hierarchical depth are necessary to this improvement, and calibrated uncertainty estimates identify low-confidence predictions for pathologist review before clinical action.

AI.tldr: HierarchicalDAEW is a dual-graph neural network that predicts spatially resolved gene expression from H&E histology images by learning from tissue architecture and providing calibrated uncertainty estimates, outperforming 13 baselines across multiple tissue types.
AI.motivation: Spatial transcriptomics is expensive and technically demanding, limiting its clinical use. Predicting gene expression from routine H&E histology could make spatial transcriptomics more accessible, but current methods ignore tissue architecture and lack reliability quantification.
AI.method: HierarchicalDAEW uses a dual-graph architecture: (1) Spot graph with Domain-Aware Edge-Weighted convolutional operator that learns separate projections for inter-domain, intra-domain, and boundary edges from Leiden clustering, explicitly modeling tissue heterogeneity; (2) Gene-level graph that fuses protein-protein interaction priors (STRING-DB) with tissue-specific co-expression through learned attention gating, propagating predictions from landmark genes to broader panels; (3) Evidential uncertainty estimation for reliability quantification.
AI.result: On six human Visium sections spanning breast, colorectal, prostate, and cerebellar tissue, HierarchicalDAEW achieved the strongest correlation with ground-truth expression compared to 13 published baselines. Gains held up under multi-seed reproducibility checks and negative controls. Ablations confirmed both domain-aware edge typing and hierarchical depth are necessary for improvement. Calibrated uncertainty estimates effectively identified low-confidence predictions.
AI.conclusion: HierarchicalDAEW successfully addresses limitations of current methods by explicitly modeling tissue architecture and providing reliable uncertainty estimates, making spatial transcriptomics prediction from routine H&E histology more robust and potentially clinically deployable.

title: Auditing Provenance Sensitivity in LLM Agent Action Selection
summary: LLM agents choose tools and arguments from context that mixes user requests, tool outputs, retrieved records, memory, and untrusted text. Evidence can be relevant without being authorized to determine a decision, so a correct action need not be grounded only in permitted evidence. We introduce a target-specific authorization audit that labels context factors separately for each tool and argument target. Its primary test holds the task, proposition, position, and policy fixed while changing only the proposition's source authority. We then test behavior when valid evidence is weakened and use context-subset interactions as a secondary localization diagnostic. Across 450 controlled next-action tasks and multiple open-weight LLM families, trusted and untrusted variants produce different actions in 5.4 percent of competing cases versus 1.7 percent of supporting cases. Under controlled degradation, unauthorized competition is retained in a full-correct, mixed-error, clean-correct pattern in 2.4 percent of comparisons, with a 95 percent confidence interval from 2.1 to 3.0 percent. These are controlled stress-set rates, not deployment prevalence. The models respond to textual source-authority cues, but this does not prevent untrusted evidence from influencing their actions.

AI.tldr: LLMs struggle to filter out unauthorized evidence when making tool-use decisions, with untrusted sources influencing actions despite source-authority cues.
AI.motivation: LLM agents making decisions based on mixed-context information (user requests, tool outputs, retrieved records, memory, untrusted text) face the problem that relevant evidence might not be authorized to determine decisions. Current systems don't adequately distinguish between relevant and authorized evidence.
AI.method: Introduces a target-specific authorization audit that labels context factors separately for each tool and argument target. Uses primary test holding task, proposition, position, and policy fixed while changing only the proposition's source authority. Tests behavior when valid evidence is weakened, and uses context-subset interactions as a secondary localization diagnostic.
AI.result: Across 450 controlled next-action tasks and multiple LLM families, trusted and untrusted variants produce different actions in 5.4% of competing cases vs 1.7% of supporting cases. Under controlled degradation, unauthorized competition is retained in a full-correct, mixed-error, clean-correct pattern in 2.4% of comparisons (95% CI: 2.1-3.0%). Models respond to textual source-authority cues but this doesn't prevent untrusted evidence from influencing actions.
AI.conclusion: LLMs are influenced by unauthorized evidence when making tool-use decisions despite source-authority cues, revealing a vulnerability in evidence authorization that needs addressing for reliable agent systems. The study provides controlled stress-set rates showing this phenomenon exists across multiple model families.

title: Multi-turn RL with Structural and Performance Aware Rewards for CUDA Kernel Generation
summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a powerful technique to enhance the reasoning capacity of LLMs for optimized code generation. However, existing RLVR approaches primarily rely on outcome-based signals such as correctness and speedup, overlooking performance-critical structural properties of programs that are essential for generating optimized code. In this work, we propose CudaPerf, a reflective RL framework that incorporates both verifiable execution rewards and structural code-aware rewards derived from parallelization features (e.g., memory coalescing, occupancy, Arithmatic Intensity, and synchronization patterns). CudaPerf operates in two stages: (1) an offline pairwise ranking module that learns to distinguish strong and weak program candidates via contrastive comparisons, and (2) an online RL training phase that jointly optimizes for correctness, performance, and structural efficiency through a unified reward signal. To further enhance learning, CudaPerf utilizes iterative refinement using execution feedback enabling progressive improvement of generated candidates. We also introduce a dataset comprising 2.9k C to CUDA and 1k PyTorch to CUDA programs, each paired with diverse input configurations and multiple CUDA implementations encompassing diverse optimization strategies. CudaPerf is evaluated across multiple benchmarks comprising both C to CUDA and PyTorch to CUDA transformations. Empirical findings suggest that CudaPerf significantly outperforms strong baselines, including Qwen-3-32B (for C to CUDA) and CUDA Agent (for PyTorch to CUDA) by achieving up to 5X & 3.32X improvements in speedup, and 17% & 7% improvements in correctness, respectively.

AI.tldr: CudaPerf is a reinforcement learning framework for CUDA code generation that combines verifiable execution rewards with structural code-aware rewards, achieving significant improvements over baseline methods in both correctness and performance.
AI.motivation: Existing RLVR approaches focus only on outcome-based signals like correctness and speedup, but overlook important structural properties of programs that are critical for generating optimized code. There's a need to incorporate parallelization features and structural efficiency into the reward mechanism for better CUDA code generation.
AI.method: CudaPerf uses a two-stage reflective RL framework: (1) offline pairwise ranking module that learns to distinguish strong vs. weak program candidates via contrastive comparisons, and (2) online RL training phase that jointly optimizes correctness, performance, and structural efficiency through unified rewards. It also employs iterative refinement using execution feedback for progressive improvement.
AI.result: CudaPerf significantly outperforms baselines including Qwen-3-32B (for C to CUDA) and CUDA Agent (for PyTorch to CUDA), achieving up to 5X & 3.32X improvements in speedup, and 17% & 7% improvements in correctness, respectively. A new dataset of 2.9k C to CUDA and 1k PyTorch to CUDA programs with diverse implementations was created.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating structural code-aware rewards along with verifiable execution rewards in RL frameworks for code generation leads to significantly better optimization outcomes, demonstrating the importance of considering parallelization features like memory coalescing, occupancy, arithmetic intensity, and synchronization patterns for generating high-performance CUDA code.

title: Auditing Evidence Use in Medical LLM Diagnosis
summary: Medical LLMs are often evaluated by whether they select the correct diagnosis, but diagnostic accuracy alone does not show whether the model used the case evidence appropriately. We present a behavioral audit of evidence use in medical diagnosis. For each case, we decompose patient information into evidence units, score candidate diagnoses under controlled evidence subsets, and mine low-order interactions in diagnostic margins. Because medical evidence is diagnosis-relative, the audit separates interaction discovery from failure assignment: large or negative interactions can reflect plausible differential diagnosis, while suspicious interactions require robustness checks and clinical review. We evaluate five open-weight LLMs on DDXPlus, CupCase, and MedCase. Across datasets, faithful support and differential conflict or cancellation account for most interaction strength, showing that many evidence interactions are clinically plausible rather than failures. In a DDXPlus-focused blinded five-reviewer 130-item enriched review sample, invalid or shortcut-like cases concentrate in negated or absent findings and clinically local evidence. These results show that accuracy can hide candidate evidence-use failures and motivate role-aware audits for medical LLM evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a behavioral audit method to evaluate how medical LLMs use evidence in diagnosis, showing that diagnostic accuracy alone can mask evidence-use failures and proposing role-aware audits for better evaluation.
AI.motivation: Medical LLMs are typically evaluated based on diagnostic accuracy, but this doesn't reveal whether models use case evidence appropriately. There's a need to audit how LLMs process and combine evidence units in medical diagnosis to identify potential failures in evidence use that accuracy metrics might hide.
AI.method: The authors develop a behavioral audit of evidence use by: 1) decomposing patient information into evidence units, 2) scoring candidate diagnoses under controlled evidence subsets, and 3) mining low-order interactions in diagnostic margins. The method separates interaction discovery from failure assignment since medical evidence is diagnosis-relative, allowing differentiation between clinically plausible differential diagnosis interactions and suspicious patterns requiring further review.
AI.result: Evaluation of five open-weight LLMs on DDXPlus, CupCase, and MedCase datasets showed that faithful support and differential conflict/cancellation account for most interaction strength, indicating many evidence interactions are clinically plausible. In a blinded review of 130 enriched items from DDXPlus, invalid or shortcut-like cases were concentrated in negated/absent findings and clinically local evidence. The audit revealed cases where accuracy would hide evidence-use failures.
AI.conclusion: Diagnostic accuracy alone can conceal candidate evidence-use failures in medical LLMs. The proposed behavioral audit method provides a more nuanced evaluation of evidence processing, with role-aware audits being necessary for comprehensive medical LLM evaluation to ensure clinically appropriate reasoning beyond mere accuracy metrics.

title: Three-Pronged Spectral Control for Federated Parameter Efficient Fine Tuning
summary: Federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) enables communication-efficient adaptation of large pretrained models on decentralized edge data, but it remains fragile under non-IID client heterogeneity. In low-rank adaptation (LoRA), different clients may learn locally useful but spectrally misaligned update subspaces, causing high-variance aggregation and poor global transfer. We propose TRISHUL, a spectral-control framework for robust federated PEFT. TRISHUL follows the FL no-raw-data-sharing setting but does not itself provide formal privacy guarantees. TRISHUL uses shared frozen multi-head low-rank bases to obtain algebraically exact aggregation of compact core updates, applies nuclear norm proximal shrinkage to suppress client-specific high-rank spectral components before upload, and allocates adaptation heads non-uniformly across layers using a concave water filling budget rule derived from pretrained layer capacity. Because shrinkage is performed only on small core matrices, TRISHUL adds negligible computation and no extra per-round communication over the underlying multi-head PEFT protocol. Across vision and language benchmarks, including CIFAR-100, SVHN, 20 Newsgroups, MRQA, and GLUE with LLaMA3.2-1B, TRISHUL improves convergence, stability, and final performance over federated LoRA baselines, with greater gains under stronger heterogeneity.

AI.tldr: TRISHUL is a spectral-control framework for federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) that improves robustness under non-IID client heterogeneity through shared frozen low-rank bases, nuclear norm shrinkage, and strategic head allocation.
AI.motivation: Federated PEFT (especially LoRA) is fragile under non-IID client heterogeneity, where different clients learn locally useful but spectrally misaligned update subspaces, leading to high-variance aggregation and poor global transfer performance.
AI.method: 1) Uses shared frozen multi-head low-rank bases for algebraically exact aggregation of compact core updates; 2) Applies nuclear norm proximal shrinkage to suppress client-specific high-rank spectral components before upload; 3) Allocates adaptation heads non-uniformly across layers using a concave water filling budget rule based on pretrained layer capacity.
AI.result: Across vision (CIFAR-100, SVHN) and language (20 Newsgroups, MRQA, GLUE) benchmarks with LLaMA3.2-1B, TRISHUL improves convergence, stability, and final performance over federated LoRA baselines, with greater gains under stronger heterogeneity.
AI.conclusion: TRISHUL provides a computationally efficient spectral-control framework for robust federated PEFT that addresses spectral misalignment in non-IID settings without adding significant computation or communication overhead, while maintaining the FL privacy setting.

title: Code Monitor Red Teaming for Public-Test-Passing Code
summary: Visible tests are a common gate for LLM-generated code, but passing them does not certify specification correctness. We study a deployment-like monitoring problem: after code has passed public tests, can a weaker LLM verifier identify the residual hidden bugs? We introduce Code Monitor Red Teaming, a monitor-red-teaming protocol that fixes a public-check information boundary while varying generator pressure, verifier scaffolding, and weak-to-strong capability. We instantiate it as CodeMonitorBench, spanning function-level, data-science, and workflow code. Across 71,000 generated candidates, 43,677 pass public tests and 23,081 of those fail hidden tests. Weak verifiers improve with scaffolding and model family, but still miss most hidden bugs at 5% false-positive rate. As a robustness stress test, adversarial public-test-overfit pressure lowers verifier AUROC and raises low-FPR miss rates in most cells. A GLM-5.1 verifier recovers part of the gap under the same evidence boundary; an inferability audit shows that remaining misses mix verifier failures with M1 evidence limits.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CodeMonitorBench, a benchmark for evaluating how well weaker LLMs can detect hidden bugs in code that already passes visible tests, using a monitor-red-teaming protocol that varies generator pressure, verifier scaffolding, and weak-to-strong capabilities.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-generated code is typically evaluated using visible tests, but passing these tests doesn't guarantee specification correctness. The paper addresses the deployment-like monitoring problem of whether weaker LLM verifiers can identify residual hidden bugs after code has already passed public tests.
AI.method: The authors introduce Code Monitor Red Teaming, a protocol that maintains a fixed public-check information boundary while varying three key factors: generator pressure (including adversarial public-test-overfit scenarios), verifier scaffolding, and weak-to-strong capability differences. They instantiate this as CodeMonitorBench across function-level, data-science, and workflow code domains, generating 71,000 code candidates and analyzing verifier performance.
AI.result: Out of 43,677 candidates passing public tests, 23,081 fail hidden tests (53% bug rate). Weak verifiers improve with better scaffolding and model family selection, but still miss most hidden bugs at 5% false-positive rate. Adversarial public-test-overfit pressure lowers verifier AUROC and increases low-FPR miss rates. A GLM-5.1 verifier partially recovers performance gaps, and an audit shows remaining failures mix verifier limitations with evidence boundary constraints.
AI.conclusion: The study reveals significant challenges in weak LLM-based code monitoring, showing that current verifiers miss most hidden bugs even with improvements. The findings highlight fundamental limitations of post-public-test monitoring and suggest that both verifier capability improvements and better evidence availability are needed for effective deployment monitoring.

title: Best-of-Evidence: Best-of-N Selection under Partial Verification
summary: BoN improves model outputs by sampling several candidates and selecting one with a proxy score, but it assumes that complete candidates can be evaluated reliably. Many vision-language tasks instead provide only partial verification: a finding, span, value, region, or relation may be checkable even when no dependable whole-response verifier exists. Moreover, the same claim may recur across candidates with opposing stances, allowing one observation to support part of the pool and contradict another. We introduce Best-of-Evidence (BoE), an inference-time selection framework that keeps the BoN candidate pool fixed, represents reusable claims with a signed candidate--factor graph, and allocates a limited budget to evidence actions that can change the final choice. BoE formalizes selection under partial verification and provides a practical score-based controller, with the zero-budget case recovering the underlying BoN decision. Theoretically, we show that residual evidence capacity limits any evidence-driven improvement and that shared factor queries can achieve an O(log K) versus Θ(K) query separation in a factor-code model. Common-ledger experiments on four medical VQA settings show that BoE can improve fixed-pool selection and rescue some BoN failures when evidence is reliable, contrastive, and decision-relevant, while also revealing the channel-quality and candidate-generation limits that prevent universal gains.

AI.tldr: BoE (Best-of-Evidence) is a framework that extends Best-of-N sampling by allowing partial verification of claims in vision-language tasks through evidence collection, improving selection when complete candidate evaluation is unreliable.
AI.motivation: Best-of-N (BoN) assumes complete candidate evaluation is reliable, but many vision-language tasks only allow partial verification (checking specific claims, spans, regions, etc.). Additionally, the same claim can appear in different candidates with opposing stances, allowing evidence to support some candidates while contradicting others.
AI.method: BoE keeps the BoN candidate pool fixed but represents reusable claims as a signed candidate-factor graph. It allocates a limited budget to evidence collection actions that can influence the final selection, providing a score-based controller that formalizes selection under partial verification.
AI.result: Theoretically, BoE shows residual evidence capacity limits evidence-driven improvement and achieves O(log K) vs Θ(K) query separation in factor-code models. Experiments on four medical VQA settings show BoE improves fixed-pool selection and can rescue some BoN failures when evidence is reliable, contrastive, and decision-relevant.
AI.conclusion: BoE provides a practical framework for inference-time selection under partial verification constraints, extending BoN's capabilities for vision-language tasks where only specific claims can be verified, while also identifying limitations related to channel quality and candidate generation.

title: Is Deep Research Reliable? Misleading Knowledge Induces False Conclusions
summary: Deep Research agents extend LLM-based assistants into long-horizon workflows involving planning, retrieval, evidence synthesis, and report generation, yet their reliability in open information environments remains underexplored. A key concern is whether apparently credible but factually misleading knowledge encountered in such environments can propagate through these workflows and be adopted as false conclusions in final reports. To study this failure mode, we introduce MisKnow-Agent, a framework for constructing and validating misleading knowledge for Deep Research tasks. MisKnow-Agent generates misleading instances with controllable authority levels and styles, yielding 5,933 quality-controlled instances built on DeepResearch Benchmark tasks. Extensive experiments across open-source and closed-source Deep Research agents show that even limited exposure to misleading knowledge can induce false-conclusion adoption in final reports, revealing a broad reliability vulnerability in current Deep Research agents. Although search-enabled verifier models consistently identify the retained instances as misleading during focused corpus validation, the same instances can still be adopted during long-horizon research, revealing a disconnect between focused verification and workflow-level evidence use. Finally, we evaluate pre- and post-research defenses, both individually and in combination, finding that all three configurations mitigate but do not fully prevent false-conclusion adoption. Our findings suggest that reliable Deep Research requires evidence verification and correction capabilities at both the model and framework levels, beyond improvements in planning, retrieval, evidence integration, or report-generation abilities.

AI.tldr: A framework called MisKnow-Agent reveals that Deep Research agents are vulnerable to adopting misleading knowledge in final reports, even with limited exposure, highlighting a reliability gap between focused verification and workflow-level evidence use.
AI.motivation: Deep Research agents extend LLM capabilities to long-horizon workflows, but their reliability in open information environments with misleading knowledge is underexplored. Key concern: whether factually misleading but seemingly credible knowledge can propagate through research workflows and appear as false conclusions in final reports.
AI.method: Introduced MisKnow-Agent framework to construct and validate misleading knowledge for Deep Research tasks. Generated 5,933 quality-controlled misleading instances with controllable authority levels and styles, built on DeepResearch Benchmark tasks. Conducted extensive experiments across open-source and closed-source Deep Research agents, evaluated pre- and post-research defenses.
AI.result: Even limited exposure to misleading knowledge can induce false-conclusion adoption in final reports, revealing broad reliability vulnerability. Search-enabled verifier models consistently identify misleading instances during focused validation, but same instances can still be adopted during long-horizon research. All tested defense configurations (pre- and post-research, individual and combined) mitigate but don't fully prevent false-conclusion adoption.
AI.conclusion: Reliable Deep Research requires evidence verification and correction capabilities at both model and framework levels, beyond improvements in planning, retrieval, evidence integration, or report-generation abilities. There's a disconnect between focused verification and workflow-level evidence use that needs to be addressed.

title: The Weight of Silence: A Causal Case for Weights Over the Scratchpad in Latent Chess Reasoning
comment: 28 pages, 5 figures, preprint also available at Zenodo: https://zenodo.org/records/21454434
summary: Latent, or silent, reasoning lets language models carry out intermediate computation in continuous vector space instead of words, and is widely assumed to function as an internal scratchpad the model actively consults during inference. Whether that assumption survives reinforcement learning has not been tested directly: existing causal analyses of latent reasoning are confined to math and logic tasks, and compare a model's reliance on its thoughts within a single checkpoint, never before and after an RL stage. We train a chess-playing model through a staged latent-reasoning curriculum followed by reinforcement learning, and find legality climbs monotonically to 61% (from a 48% pre-RL baseline) while checkmate confabulation is eliminated entirely. To locate this gain, we run a six-condition causal intervention suite on the same model before and after RL: substituting or adding matched noise to the latent thought vectors leaves performance unchanged, ablating them causes only mild degradation, and only exact-zero vectors cause collapse. This robustness gap is itself the finding: under exact-zero corruption, legality collapses to 1% pre-RL versus 9% post-RL, a gap that survives correction for testing across the full battery; milder conditions trend similarly without independently reaching significance. RL appears to add robustness to disruption, not reliance on thought content. These results push back against the field's default assumption that latent thoughts function as an actively consulted inference-time scratchpad, and instead indicate latent reasoning's principal effect here is shaping the model's parameters during training. We also demonstrate a working RL gain in chess, a domain outside the math and logic settings where multiple groups report the same latent-reasoning-plus-RL recipe failing to improve accuracy over SFT.

AI.tldr: RL doesn't make models rely more on latent reasoning as a scratchpad during inference; instead it makes them more robust to disruption of those thoughts, while latent reasoning mainly shapes parameters during training.
AI.motivation: To test whether the common assumption that latent reasoning functions as an internal scratchpad that models actively consult during inference holds true after reinforcement learning, particularly in non-math/logic domains like chess where previous research has shown mixed results.
AI.method: Trained a chess-playing model through staged latent-reasoning curriculum followed by RL, then conducted a six-condition causal intervention suite comparing the same model before and after RL with interventions including substituting/adding matched noise to latent thought vectors, ablating them, and using exact-zero vectors.
AI.result: Legality improved from 48% to 61% pre-RL to post-RL, with checkmate confabulation eliminated. Crucially, latent thought interventions showed minimal performance impact except for exact-zero vectors, where legality collapsed to 1% pre-RL vs 9% post-RL, indicating RL added robustness to disruption rather than increasing reliance on thought content.
AI.conclusion: Latent reasoning doesn't primarily function as an actively consulted inference-time scratchpad; instead its main effect is shaping model parameters during training. RL adds robustness to disruption rather than increasing dependence on latent thoughts, challenging the field's default assumptions.

title: Source-Prior-Driven Selective Adaptation for Efficient Diffusion Model Finetuning
summary: Fine-tuning large diffusion models for new domains or styles involves a trade-off: improving target-specific generation often degrades the pretrained model's broad generative capability. Existing full and parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods typically handle this trade-off only implicitly. In this work, we propose a novel source-prior-driven selective adaptation method to efficiently fine-tune diffusion models, achieving a favorable trade-off. Our method relies on two key observations: (1) the loss of general generative capability is highly inconsistent across pretrained parameters, and (2) parameters that have a relatively small impact on the model's general generative capability remain structurally inconsistent across layers and parameter types. Motivated by these observations, we first learn a static mask to explicitly identify parameters better suited for downstream adaptation, and then construct structured update strategies for the selected subset. Experiments show that our method achieves a better adaptation-retention trade-off than existing strong baselines.

AI.tldr: Selective parameter adaptation for diffusion models that preserves general capabilities while adapting to new domains/styles
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning diffusion models often improves target-specific generation but degrades the pretrained model's broad generative capability. Existing methods handle this trade-off only implicitly.
AI.method: Proposes source-prior-driven selective adaptation: (1) learns a static mask to identify parameters better suited for downstream adaptation, (2) constructs structured update strategies for the selected subset based on observations about parameter impact on general capability.
AI.result: Experiments show the method achieves a better adaptation-retention trade-off than existing strong baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed selective adaptation method efficiently fine-tunes diffusion models while maintaining a favorable balance between adaptation to new domains/styles and retention of general generative capabilities.

title: ADABORD: a novel AdaBoost approach for ordinal classification
comment: 42 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Submitted to CS top tier journal
summary: Ordinal Classification (OC) deals with classification tasks where the classes follow a natural order. Despite the progress in OC, many existing approaches fail to fully leverage the ordinal information, treating the problem as nominal classification and thereby losing performance potential. In this work, ADABORD, an AdaBoost framework specifically designed for ordinal classification problems, is introduced. The ordinal nature of the classes is incorporated into two key components of the well-known AdaBoost algorithm: 1) the base estimator, where decision trees with the ordinal Gini splitting criterion are proposed; 2) the error function used to update sample weights at each stage and the weights of the classifier in the final ensemble model, given by the absolute ranked probability score, a measure that accounts for both the ordering and the distance between classes. ADABORD is extensively compared against seven state-of-the-art methods on the TOC-UCO repository, the largest benchmark collection for OC to date. The experimental results, supported by statistical analysis, show that ADABORD significantly outperforms competing methods, particularly on datasets with five or more classes, where the ordinal structure becomes more pronounced. Source code, along with all experimental protocols, is publicly available to ensure reproducibility and facilitate future research in OC.

AI.tldr: ADABORD is a new AdaBoost framework for ordinal classification that incorporates ordinal information into both the base decision tree estimators and the error weighting function, achieving superior performance on ordinal datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing ordinal classification approaches often fail to fully leverage the natural order between classes, treating the problem as nominal classification and losing performance potential. There's a need for methods that properly incorporate ordinal structure.
AI.method: ADABORD adapts the AdaBoost algorithm for ordinal classification by: 1) using decision trees with an ordinal Gini splitting criterion as base estimators, and 2) employing an absolute ranked probability score as the error function for updating sample weights and classifier weights in the ensemble.
AI.result: ADABORD significantly outperforms seven state-of-the-art methods on the TOC-UCO repository (the largest OC benchmark), particularly on datasets with five or more classes where ordinal structure is more pronounced. Statistical analysis supports these findings.
AI.conclusion: ADABORD successfully incorporates ordinal information into both base estimators and weighting mechanisms of the AdaBoost framework, providing a superior approach for ordinal classification tasks. The method is made publicly available to support reproducibility and future research.

title: Traceable Scholarship: Page Anchors and Ariadne's Thread for Humanistic Inquiry in the Age of Generative AI
comment: 33 pages, 8 tables. This paper proposes a normative and infrastructural framework for traceable, AI-assisted humanistic research and presents an auditable Kant case study
summary: Generative AI lets large language models produce scholarly-looking text within seconds, yet fluency does not equal valid explanation. The deepest risk is not factual error alone but the appearance that an explanation is already established without clear sources, page numbers, editions, or evidence. We liken the page anchor to Ariadne's thread: within the labyrinth of generative fluency, it is the thread that leads the scholar back to the source. This paper proposes Traceable Scholarship as the minimum normative condition for AI-assisted humanistic research, situating it across the three revolutions of knowledge infrastructure: print, digital, and generative AI. We introduce page anchors, dual page numbers, citation-first generation, NO_EVIDENCE, human verification, four-level compliance, and Scope Contract, and present AIH-Infra as a three-layer reference implementation: Contexture (document structuring), Open WebUI AIH-Infra (traceable knowledge base), and AIH-Infra MCP Server (agent gateway). A case study on a 29-volume Kant Akademie-Ausgabe knowledge base illustrates how traceability supports retrieval correction, evidence grading, and judgment downgrading. Traceability is not a software feature; it is the condition under which humanistic research can remain public and refutable in the age of generative AI.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes "Traceable Scholarship" as a necessary normative framework for AI-assisted humanities research, emphasizing the importance of maintaining source traceability (like page anchors) in generative AI systems to ensure research remains public, verifiable, and refutable.
AI.motivation: While generative AI can produce scholarly-looking text quickly, fluency doesn't guarantee valid explanations. The core risk is that AI-generated content appears to present established explanations without proper source attribution (page numbers, editions, evidence). This threatens the fundamental principles of humanistic research that require traceability back to original sources.
AI.method: The paper introduces Traceable Scholarship as a normative framework with specific mechanisms: page anchors, dual page numbers, citation-first generation, NO_EVIDENCE tagging, human verification, four-level compliance, and Scope Contract. It presents AIH-Infra as a three-layer reference implementation (Contexture for document structuring, Open WebUI AIH-Infra for traceable knowledge base, and AIH-Infra MCP Server for agent gateway). A case study on Kant Akademie-Ausgabe knowledge base demonstrates the approach.
AI.result: The proposed framework enables retrieval correction, evidence grading, and judgment downgrading. The case study illustrates how traceability mechanisms work in practice to maintain scholarly rigor in AI-assisted research. The system ensures AI-generated content can be traced back to specific sources and evidence levels.
AI.conclusion: Traceability is not merely a software feature but the essential condition for humanistic research to remain public and refutable in the generative AI era. The paper argues that without such traceability frameworks, AI-assisted scholarship risks losing the ability to verify claims and engage in proper scholarly discourse.

title: Weight-norm Criticality: A Mechanism for Loss Spikes Induced by the Normalization and Weight Decay
summary: Most explanations of training instability focus on \emph{learning-rate criticality}, typically characterized by the Edge of Stability, beyond which optimization becomes unstable. We argue that, in practical deep neural network training, there is an additional and often overlooked \emph{weight-norm criticality}. This criticality is induced by the interaction between normalization (which introduces scale-invariant components) and weight decay (which persistently shrinks parameter norms). As the weight decay coefficient increases, the norms of scale-invariant weights are progressively driven toward zero. Meanwhile, the sharpness of the loss landscape increases rapidly, destabilizing the optimization dynamics and resulting in abrupt loss spikes. This perspective provides a rationale for why weight penalties can improve generalization yet cannot be made arbitrarily strong: excessive decay drives scale-invariant weight norms past a critical boundary and destabilizes training. Our work provides a new mechanistic understanding of loss spikes through the lens of \emph{weight-norm criticality}. Moreover, \emph{weight-norm criticality} yields testable predictions that we validate empirically in networks with scale-invariant components, providing empirical support for the proposed mechanism.

AI.tldr: Weight-norm criticality explains training instability in deep networks due to interaction between normalization and weight decay, where excessive weight decay drives scale-invariant weights to zero, increasing sharpness and causing loss spikes.
AI.motivation: Existing explanations of training instability focus mainly on learning-rate criticality (Edge of Stability), but this paper argues there's an overlooked weight-norm criticality that occurs in practical deep neural network training when normalization and weight decay interact.
AI.method: The paper analyzes the interaction between normalization layers (which create scale-invariant components) and weight decay regularization. It develops the concept of weight-norm criticality where as weight decay coefficient increases, scale-invariant weight norms approach zero, increasing loss landscape sharpness and destabilizing optimization.
AI.result: The analysis provides a mechanistic understanding of loss spikes through weight-norm criticality, explaining why weight penalties improve generalization but cannot be made arbitrarily strong. Empirical validation in networks with scale-invariant components supports the proposed mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Weight-norm criticality offers a new perspective on training instability, complementing learning-rate criticality, and provides testable predictions about how excessive weight decay destabilizes training by driving scale-invariant weight norms past a critical boundary.

title: OPOD: On-Policy Omni Distillation
summary: Omni-modal models can handle text, images, and audio in one system, but improving all of these abilities together remains difficult. Training a single model on pooled multimodal data often fails to match models specialized for individual modalities. On-policy distillation (OPD) offers a way to combine such specialists: the student generates a response, and a teacher evaluates that same response, so the student learns directly from behaviors it actually produces. Yet using several teachers can introduce competing guidance and improve one modality at the expense of another. We present On-Policy Omni Distillation (OPOD), which routes each student response to the matching text, image, or audio teacher. OPOD keeps teacher guidance only on tokens where the teacher assigns a higher probability than the student, adjusts the influence of each modality teacher independently during training, and asks the routed teacher to assess both the final answer and whether the reasoning supports the correct answer. Across twelve benchmarks and three backbone sizes, OPOD achieves the best average score at every scale, reaching 70.8, 51.7, and 46.2 and exceeding the strongest comparator by 2.1, 1.8, and 1.7 points. On the 30B model, it outperforms both the base model and a counterpart post-trained jointly on pooled multimodal data on all twelve benchmarks, and ranks first or second on eleven even when the individual specialists are included. The specialists are discarded after training, leaving one deployable omni-modal model. These results show that coordinating modality-specific teachers is an effective way to improve a shared model while maintaining cross-modal balance.

AI.tldr: OPOD is an on-policy distillation method that uses modality-specific teachers to improve omni-modal models while maintaining balanced performance across text, image, and audio modalities.
AI.motivation: Omni-modal models struggle to match specialist models in individual modalities when trained on pooled multimodal data, and existing distillation methods can introduce competing guidance that improves one modality at the expense of others.
AI.method: OPOD routes each student response to the matching text, image, or audio teacher, keeps guidance only where teachers have higher probability than students, adjusts modality influence independently, and has teachers assess both final answers and reasoning support.
AI.result: OPOD achieves best average scores across 12 benchmarks at three backbone sizes (70.8, 51.7, 46.2 points), outperforming strongest comparators by 2.1, 1.8, and 1.7 points. On 30B model, outperforms base model and pooled-training counterpart on all benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Coordinating modality-specific teachers through OPOD is effective for improving shared omni-modal models while maintaining cross-modal balance, producing a single deployable model without needing specialists after training.

title: Regularized Optimization on Grassmann Manifold: Theory, Algorithm and Applications
summary: Spectral methods are among the most widely used techniques for community detection, clustering, and graph learning. Their performance, however, critically depends on the accurate estimation of the underlying spectral subspace and can deteriorate substantially in the presence of noise, outliers, or model perturbations. To address this limitation, we propose a Regularized Projection Matrix Approximation (RPMA) framework for robust estimation of rank-$K$ projection matrices. RPMA extends classical spectral projection by incorporating a regularization term, producing projection estimates that are more robust, sparse, and interpretable. We formulate the proposed model as an optimization problem on the manifold of rank-$K$ projection matrices and exploit its geometric equivalence to the Grassmann manifold. Based on this manifold characterization, we derive the first- and second-order optimality conditions, establish the local stability of the regularized leading eigenspace, and characterize the stability of the critical-point landscape under sufficiently small regularization. To efficiently solve the resulting nonconvex optimization problem, we develop a Riemannian gradient projection algorithm with backtracking line search, together with a more efficient Cayley--Sherman--Morrison--Woodbury (Cayley--SMW) gradient method that avoids repeated eigendecompositions. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that RPMA substantially improves the recovery accuracy of projection matrices and consistently outperforms conventional spectral projection methods for community detection and clustering under noisy environments.

AI.tldr: RPMA is a robust spectral projection method that regularizes projection matrix estimation for improved community detection and clustering in noisy environments.
AI.motivation: Traditional spectral methods are sensitive to noise, outliers, and model perturbations, which degrade their performance in community detection and graph learning tasks.
AI.method: Developed RPMA framework that extends classical spectral projection with a regularization term, formulating optimization on rank-K projection manifolds (equivalent to Grassmann manifold), and derived Riemannian gradient algorithms with Cayley-SMW updates.
AI.result: RPMA substantially improves projection matrix recovery accuracy and consistently outperforms conventional spectral methods in both synthetic and real-world datasets under noisy conditions.
AI.conclusion: The RPMA framework provides a robust, sparse, and interpretable alternative to traditional spectral projection methods, with strong theoretical guarantees and efficient computational methods for practical applications.

title: Representing Entity Importance in AI Knowledge Systems: A Dual-Signal Framework of Audience Evaluation and Structural Authority
summary:
AI knowledge systems require representations of entity importance for retrieval, recommendation, evidence selection, and knowledge-intensive reasoning. Yet importance is often reduced to a single score derived from either human response or graph structure. Such compression may discard distinctions that matter when an AI system must choose among entities for different tasks. This study introduces an interpretable dual-signal representation in which each entity is characterized by an audience-evaluation dimension and a structural-authority dimension.
  The framework is evaluated using movie entities as an empirical validation domain. IMDb non-commercial datasets provide a rating-based audience ranking, Wikidata supports entity alignment, and English Wikipedia hyperlinks form the knowledge network on which PageRank estimates structural authority. Experiments on 482 entities and 13,690 directed relationships reveal a statistically significant but weak association between the two dimensions (Spearman rho = 0.2275, p < 0.001). Their overlap is only 10% in the top 10 and 34% in the top 100, while entity-level divergence occurs in both directions.
  The results show that audience evaluation and structural authority are non-redundant signals and should not automatically be collapsed into a single scalar notion of importance. The contribution is not a new ranking algorithm or learned embedding, but a minimal knowledge-representation framework and an empirical test of its dimensional necessity. The findings support task-aware AI knowledge systems that preserve distinct importance signals before applying context-specific selection or aggregation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a dual-signal representation for entity importance (audience-evaluation + structural-authority) and empirically shows these dimensions are non-redundant, supporting task-aware AI knowledge systems rather than single-score importance metrics.
AI.motivation: Current AI knowledge systems often reduce entity importance to a single score derived from human responses or graph structure, potentially discarding distinctions that matter when AI systems must choose among entities for different tasks.
AI.method: Proposes an interpretable dual-signal representation with audience-evaluation dimension (from IMDb ratings) and structural-authority dimension (from Wikipedia PageRank). Evaluated on 482 movie entities and 13,690 directed relationships using entity alignment from Wikidata, English Wikipedia hyperlinks, and statistical correlation analysis.
AI.result: Found statistically significant but weak association between dimensions (Spearman rho = 0.2275, p < 0.001). Overlap is only 10% in top 10 and 34% in top 100 entities, with entity-level divergence occurring in both directions, showing the dimensions are largely independent.
AI.conclusion: Audience evaluation and structural authority are non-redundant signals and should not be collapsed into a single scalar importance measure. The framework supports task-aware AI knowledge systems that preserve distinct importance signals before context-specific selection or aggregation.

title: Counterfactual Explainability Framework With CycleGAN And Counterfactual-Classifier Alignnment Score for Retinal Disease Classification
summary: Automated detection of vision impairing retina-based ocular conditions from fundus images is important for early screening, timely referral and reducing dependency on specialist-only assessment, for which neural network-based deep learning (DL) models have been widely utilized. However, explainability of the DL frameworks remains a major bottleneck for clinical adoption, particularly when model decisions are not linked to retinal regions that are clinically meaningful. To address this issue, this study presents CounterFundus, a novel CycleGAN-driven counterfactual explainability framework, integrating EfficientNet-B5-based retinal disease detection with visually interpretable disease-to-normal fundus image translation. For each pathological image, the counterfactual yielded by the CycleGAN generator represents an estimated healthy counterpart and the resultant difference map is utilized to localize disease-associated retinal changes. Unlike conventional post-hoc saliency methods, CounterFundus provides counterfactual explanations through visually plausible disease-to-normal retinal translation. Thereafter, to quantify the spatial agreement between counterfactual difference maps and classifier saliency, the Counterfactual-Classifier Alignment Score (CCAS) is introduced, embedding Spearman correlation, binary IoU and pointing accuracy into a single assessment protocol. To this end, EigenCAM-aligned evaluation demonstrates that the generated counterfactual explanations remain spatially consistent with classifier-relevant retinal evidence across all CCAS dimensions. Along with that, ablation studies further confirm that CCAS-filtered counterfactual augmentation improves the downstream classification performance in fundus images, establishing CounterFundus as a clinically-grounded, explainable artificially intelligence (XAI) framework for retinal disease detection.

AI.tldr: CounterFundus is a novel CycleGAN-based counterfactual explainability framework for retinal disease detection that generates healthy-looking fundus images from pathological ones, providing visually interpretable explanations by highlighting disease-associated retinal changes.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models for automated retinal disease detection lack explainability and clinical adoption due to their black-box nature. Current methods don't link model decisions to clinically meaningful retinal regions, making them difficult for clinicians to trust and use in practice.
AI.method: The framework integrates EfficientNet-B5 for disease detection with a CycleGAN architecture for disease-to-normal fundus image translation. For each pathological image, it generates a counterfactual healthy counterpart, then creates difference maps to localize disease changes. Introduces Counterfactual-Classifier Alignment Score (CCAS) to measure spatial agreement between counterfactual explanations and classifier saliency using Spearman correlation, binary IoU, and pointing accuracy metrics.
AI.result: The generated counterfactual explanations show spatial consistency with classifier-relevant retinal evidence across all CCAS dimensions. Ablation studies confirm that CCAS-filtered counterfactual augmentation improves downstream classification performance in fundus images.
AI.conclusion: CounterFundus establishes a clinically-grounded explainable AI framework for retinal disease detection that provides visually plausible explanations through disease-to-normal translation, addressing the explainability bottleneck and improving both interpretability and classification performance.

title: SciExplore: Evaluating Autonomous Agents from Scientific Navigation to Information Integration
summary: Scientific research involves complex information-seeking and reasoning workflows across heterogeneous sources. However, existing benchmarks primarily emphasize general-domain retrieval or static scientific question answering, and therefore fail to assess key capabilities required in realistic scientific research workflows. We introduce SciExplore, a benchmark designed to evaluate scientific information-seeking and reasoning capabilities of LLMs and agents. SciExplore comprises four task types covering 103 expert-curated tasks across more than ten scientific disciplines: scientific database navigation, ambiguous literature retrieval, missing reference completion, and cross-source structured knowledge synthesis, which probe progressively higher-level abilities from entity-level reasoning and document-level identification to evidence-level grounding and domain-level synthesis. We evaluate over ten state-of-the-art LLMs and autonomous agents on SciExplore, revealing substantial performance gaps with performance degrading sharply as task complexity increases and extremely low accuracy on the most challenging structured synthesis tasks. These results highlight significant limitations of current models and agents in realistic scientific information-seeking scenarios.

AI.tldr: SciExplore is a new benchmark that evaluates LLMs' scientific information-seeking and reasoning capabilities through four task types across 10+ scientific disciplines, revealing significant performance gaps as task complexity increases.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks focus on general-domain retrieval or static scientific QA, but fail to assess key capabilities needed for realistic scientific research workflows, which involve complex information-seeking and reasoning across heterogeneous sources.
AI.method: The authors introduce SciExplore benchmark with four task types: scientific database navigation, ambiguous literature retrieval, missing reference completion, and cross-source structured knowledge synthesis. They evaluate over 10 state-of-the-art LLMs and autonomous agents on 103 expert-curated tasks across more than ten scientific disciplines.
AI.result: Substantial performance gaps are revealed, with performance degrading sharply as task complexity increases. Models show extremely low accuracy on the most challenging structured synthesis tasks, highlighting significant limitations in realistic scientific information-seeking scenarios.
