AI.conclusion: Current LLMs and autonomous agents have significant limitations in handling realistic scientific information-seeking workflows, particularly for complex tasks requiring evidence-level grounding and domain-level synthesis. The benchmark exposes critical gaps in scientific research capabilities that need to be addressed.

title: From Evaluation to Optimisation: Hierarchy-Aware Training Signals for CWE Prediction in Python
summary: The original ALPHA benchmark introduced a taxonomy-aware penalty for evaluating CWE-level vulnerability prediction in Python and proposed that the penalty could theoretically also serve as a training signal. This paper provides that validation. We compare three delivery mechanisms: supervised fine-tuning, a dual-head classification loss, and reinforcement learning with a dense reward derived from the normalised penalty. We find that supervised approaches consistently regress below the zero-shot baseline under distribution shift, while GRPO succeeds. Our best policy reduces the cumulative ALPHA penalty of Qwen2.5-Coder-7B on Security Hardening and Adversarial Testing (SVEN) dataset by 27.9% under greedy decoding, and by 25.5% under sampled decoding(p = 0.005, Welch's t-test), reaching statistical parity with its 4.5x larger zero-shot teacher. We conclude that the value of a hierarchical penalty as a training signal depends largely on the directness of its delivery.

AI.tldr: Validates that the ALPHA benchmark's hierarchical penalty can effectively serve as a training signal when delivered via reinforcement learning, enabling smaller models to achieve performance parity with much larger zero-shot models.
AI.motivation: The ALPHA benchmark proposed that its taxonomy-aware penalty for evaluating CWE-level vulnerability prediction could theoretically serve as a training signal, but this had not been validated. This paper aims to provide that validation by testing different delivery mechanisms for this penalty as a training signal.
AI.method: Compared three delivery mechanisms for the normalized penalty: 1) supervised fine-tuning, 2) dual-head classification loss, and 3) reinforcement learning with dense reward derived from the normalized penalty (GRPO - Group Relative Policy Optimization). Evaluated on Security Hardening and Adversarial Testing (SVEN) dataset using Qwen2.5-Coder-7B model.
AI.result: Supervised approaches regressed below zero-shot baseline under distribution shift, while GRPO succeeded. The best policy reduced cumulative ALPHA penalty by 27.9% under greedy decoding and 25.5% under sampled decoding (p=0.005), achieving statistical parity with a 4.5x larger zero-shot teacher model.
AI.conclusion: The value of a hierarchical penalty as a training signal depends largely on the directness of its delivery. Reinforcement learning with dense rewards (GRPO) is effective for leveraging this penalty, allowing smaller models to match or exceed the performance of much larger zero-shot models on vulnerability prediction tasks.

title: Clustered Edge Intelligence: Beyond Just Convergence of Edge Computing and AI
comment: This is not survey or position paper. 28 Pages, 10 figures, 4 Tables, 108 references, Under review, submitted to Information Fusion
summary: We are moving from an information age to the age of intelligence. A decade, or possibly less than that, data will not be the gold anymore rather the derived intelligence out of the data and the information we posses from the edge of the network. Existing Edge Intelligence research focuses mainly on two directions: using AI for edge resource management and deploying lightweight AI models on edge devices. However, existing edge computing research lacks an intelligence-centric framework in which derived intelligence is treated as a first-class, independently manageable entity that can be described, discovered, observed, shared, reused, and dynamically clustered across heterogeneous edge devices and applications. To address these research gaps, we introduced Clustered Edge Intelligence, a visionary intelligence-centric approach. The aim of CEI is to make intelligence a shareable and reusable first-class entity that can be independently represented, discovered, observed, exchanged, and managed across the distributed edge-cloud continuum. We present a three layer CEI architecture and examine enabling technologies and research dimensions, including intelligence inventories, semantic knowledge representation, communication, discoverability, observability, lifecycle automation, clustering mechanisms, marketplaces, interoperability, and standardization.

AI.tldr: Clustered Edge Intelligence (CEI) is a new intelligence-centric framework that treats derived intelligence as a first-class, independently manageable entity that can be shared, reused, and dynamically clustered across heterogeneous edge devices and applications.
AI.motivation: We are moving from information age to intelligence age where derived intelligence (not just data) becomes the valuable asset. Existing Edge Intelligence research lacks an intelligence-centric framework where intelligence is treated as a first-class, independently manageable entity that can be described, discovered, observed, shared, reused, and dynamically clustered across heterogeneous edge devices and applications.
AI.method: Introduced Clustered Edge Intelligence (CEI) - a visionary intelligence-centric approach with a three-layer CEI architecture. It focuses on enabling technologies and research dimensions including intelligence inventories, semantic knowledge representation, communication, discoverability, observability, lifecycle automation, clustering mechanisms, marketplaces, interoperability, and standardization.
AI.result: Proposed CEI framework makes intelligence a shareable and reusable first-class entity that can be independently represented, discovered, observed, exchanged, and managed across the distributed edge-cloud continuum.
AI.conclusion: CEI addresses the research gap in edge computing by providing an intelligence-centric framework that treats derived intelligence as a first-class entity, enabling more effective intelligence sharing, reuse, and management across edge-cloud environments.

title: Spectral Transformation for Layer-wise Global Rank Discovery in Federated LoRA for Vision Transformers
comment: Accepted at ECML-PKDD 2026 (Research Track). This is the submitted version, prior to peer review. Code: https://github.com/DASS-Lab-Group/SpecTraL
summary: Fine-tuning Vision Transformers (ViTs) with low-rank adapters (LoRA) promises better communication efficiency under federated setup, yet existing aggregation strategies face fundamental limitations. Independently averaging these LoRA factors is mathematically inconsistent, introducing cross-term aggregation error. In contrast, approaches that preserve heterogeneous client ranks by concatenating local adapters on the server substantially increase download cost and often require merging global LoRA updates into pretrained weights on the clients, causing reinitialization lag and unstable convergence. Other approaches further increase server-side overhead by reconstructing dense weight updates or training auxiliary models to refine aggregation error. In this work, we propose SpecTraL, spectral transformation for layer-wise global rank discovery, that resolves these challenges within a unified design. SpecTraL stacks local LoRA modules from clients and performs orthonormal Householder Transformation of the stacked adapters directly in the low-rank latent space, eliminating dense reconstruction of the global update and any auxiliary refinement on the server. By leveraging the Spiked Covariance Model from Random Matrix Theory, SpecTraL analytically separates the global consensus signal from non-IID noise, discovering optimal layer-wise global ranks without manual hyperparameter tuning. To match local ranks in subsequent rounds, we introduce a padding-aware initialization framework that lets clients incorporate residual LoRA dimensions without re-merging them into the pre-trained base model. Experiments on federated fine-tuning of ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 over DomainNet and NICO++ demonstrate improved accuracy-communication trade-offs, reduced server computation, and elimination of hyperparameter search for rank selection. Our code is available at https://github.com/DASS-Lab-Group/SpecTraL

AI.tldr: SpecTraL is a federated learning method that uses spectral transformation and Householder Transformation to efficiently aggregate low-rank adapters (LoRA) for vision transformers, discovering optimal global ranks without manual tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing federated learning approaches for fine-tuning Vision Transformers with LoRA face limitations: averaging LoRA factors causes mathematical inconsistency and aggregation error, while concatenation methods increase communication costs and cause unstable convergence. Other methods increase server overhead through dense reconstruction or auxiliary models.
AI.method: SpecTraL stacks local LoRA modules from clients and performs orthonormal Householder Transformation directly in low-rank latent space, avoiding dense reconstruction. Using Spiked Covariance Model from Random Matrix Theory, it separates global consensus signal from non-IID noise to discover optimal layer-wise global ranks. A padding-aware initialization framework allows clients to incorporate residual LoRA dimensions without re-merging into base model.
AI.result: Experiments on federated fine-tuning of ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 over DomainNet and NICO++ show improved accuracy-communication trade-offs, reduced server computation, and elimination of hyperparameter search for rank selection.
AI.conclusion: SpecTraL provides a unified solution that addresses mathematical inconsistency, communication overhead, and server computation challenges in federated fine-tuning of Vision Transformers with LoRA, while eliminating manual rank selection through principled spectral analysis.

title: From Scalars to Time Series: Rethinking Implicit Neural Representations for Time-Varying Volumetric Data
summary: Implicit neural representations (INRs) for time-varying volumetric data are typically trained using dense sampling over spatiotemporal coordinates, where each observation corresponds to a single point in space and time. This coordinate-wise formulation requires extensive sampling during optimization, leading to high computational cost and inefficient use of temporal structure. In this work, we revisit this design choice and show that dense spatiotemporal sampling is not necessary for learning time-varying fields. Instead, we represent the data as a collection of spatially indexed time series and train INRs using sequence-level supervision over each spatial location, rather than coordinate-wise scalar samples. This reformulation eliminates the need for dense spatiotemporal sampling and instead learns each spatial location from its full temporal evolution in a structured manner. We demonstrate that this representation is compatible with a range of existing INR architectures and consistently improves reconstruction quality, while significantly reducing training cost. Furthermore, we show that this formulation can be combined with mixture-of-experts architectures, and that our MoE instantiation further improves reconstruction quality compared to both the base reformulation and existing MoE-based INR methods, providing a stronger capacity allocation under heterogeneous temporal dynamics.

AI.tldr: A novel approach for implicit neural representations of time-varying volumetric data that replaces dense spatiotemporal sampling with sequence-level supervision over spatially indexed time series, improving reconstruction quality while reducing computational cost.
AI.motivation: Traditional implicit neural representations (INRs) for time-varying volumetric data require dense sampling over spatiotemporal coordinates, which is computationally expensive and inefficient for exploiting temporal structure. This coordinate-wise formulation leads to high training costs.
AI.method: Instead of dense spatiotemporal sampling, the authors represent data as a collection of spatially indexed time series and train INRs using sequence-level supervision over each spatial location. This learns from the full temporal evolution at each point in a structured manner. The approach is compatible with existing INR architectures and can be combined with mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures for handling heterogeneous temporal dynamics.
AI.result: The proposed approach consistently improves reconstruction quality while significantly reducing training cost compared to traditional dense sampling methods. When combined with MoE architectures, it provides even better reconstruction quality than both the base reformulation and existing MoE-based INR methods, offering stronger capacity allocation under varying temporal dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Dense spatiotemporal sampling is unnecessary for learning time-varying fields with INRs. The sequence-level supervision approach offers a more efficient and effective alternative that better exploits temporal structure, reduces computational burden, and can be enhanced with mixture-of-experts architectures for handling complex temporal dynamics.

title: Nipping the Butterfly Effect in the Bud: Self-Output Fine-Tuning for Autoregressive Weather Prediction
summary: Long-horizon weather forecasting is a fundamental challenge in atmospheric science, for which autoregressive Deep Learning Weather Prediction (DLWP) has emerged as the primary paradigm. Although the autoregressive pipeline is highly scalable and flexible, its prediction errors grow rapidly over long forecasting horizons. In this work, we study this error growth phenomenon from both theoretical and empirical perspectives. Our analysis reveals that the growth is driven by a feedback loop between output errors and input distribution shifts. Specifically, the autoregressive process amplifies small initial output errors, which progressively corrupt subsequent input distributions, echoing the butterfly effect in atmospheric science and ultimately deteriorating forecasting accuracy over longer horizons. Furthermore, we show that this distributional shift originates at the earliest stage of inference, with out-of-distribution signatures detectable as early as the first autoregressive step. To mitigate this issue, we propose \textbf{Self-Output Fine-Tuning (SOFT)}, a plug-and-play strategy that leverages the model's own one-step predictions to calibrate the biased input distribution encountered at the first step. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, despite its simplicity, SOFT achieves state-of-the-art performance on long-horizon forecasting tasks and substantially reduces both prediction errors and distributional discrepancy. The success of SOFT highlights the importance of reexamining the fundamental pipeline of deep learning weather prediction, representing a critical pipeline advance for atmospheric science.

AI.tldr: Autoregressive DLWP suffers from error growth due to output error feedback loops; proposed SOFT method uses self-predictions to calibrate input distributions at first step, achieving SOTA long-horizon forecasting.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive deep learning weather prediction (DLWP) suffers from rapidly growing prediction errors over long forecasting horizons, which limits the practical utility of these models for extended weather forecasting.
AI.method: The authors analyze error growth theoretically/empirically, identify it's driven by feedback loops between output errors and input distribution shifts (butterfly effect). They propose Self-Output Fine-Tuning (SOFT) - a plug-and-play strategy that uses the model's own one-step predictions to calibrate biased input distributions encountered at the first autoregressive step.
AI.result: SOFT achieves state-of-the-art performance on long-horizon forecasting tasks, substantially reduces both prediction errors and distributional discrepancy. The method works despite its simplicity and effectively mitigates the error growth problem identified.
AI.conclusion: The success of SOFT highlights the need to reexamine fundamental DLWP pipelines, representing a critical pipeline advance for atmospheric science by addressing the core error accumulation problem in autoregressive weather forecasting.

title: Delivery, Not Storage: Cue-Anchored Working Memory as a Harness Property for Coding Agents
summary: Coding agents ship with one kind of memory: documents. Instruction files, plan artifacts, and auto-written memory directories are deliberately authored and deliberately retrieved: the agent must choose to write them and choose to read them back. Human expertise runs on a second tier that never gets written down: situationally-bound operational facts (gotchas, locations, local conventions) encoded as a side effect of the work and retrieved involuntarily when the situation cues them. We argue this second tier is the load-bearing one for long-running agents and must be a harness property, not an agent choice. We contribute: (1) a two-tier design theory grounded in the cognitive literature on memory offloading, incidental encoding, and event-based prospective memory, each mapped to an architectural requirement; (2) a cue-anchored memory model where memories carry first-class trigger conditions over a composable vocabulary (path, symbol, semantic, event, temporal), evaluated deterministically by the harness, a composition no surveyed academic or shipped system provides; (3) a controlled evaluation on a real coding task showing that voluntary memory use is near zero even with a pre-seeded store (0 memory operations in 114 turns), that deterministic injection delivered in every seeded run with zero false alarms, and that 39% of intra-session re-reads re-buy content paid for before a compaction boundary; (4) a repeated-compaction decay probe: ten facts held only in conversation vanish at the first summary and stay absent from 106 of 108 compactions, and the deprived agent greps the harness's own session files to rebuild them, while the same facts injected from a harness-owned store arrive intact through all 138 compact-resumes as the final summary carries none. Delivery, not storage, is the product: the reliable memory channel for agents is the one the agent never has to think about.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a two-tier memory system for coding agents: deliberate document memory (traditional) plus automatic situational memory triggered by cues, arguing that reliable involuntary recall is essential for long-running agents.
AI.motivation: Current coding agents only have deliberate memory systems where they must intentionally write and retrieve documents, but human expertise relies heavily on automatic situational recall of operational facts triggered by context. This gap makes current agents ineffective for long-running tasks where incidental knowledge is crucial.
AI.method: The authors developed: (1) a two-tier design theory based on cognitive science of memory offloading, (2) a cue-anchored memory model with first-class trigger conditions over composable vocabulary (path, symbol, semantic, event, temporal), and (3) experimental evaluation on real coding tasks showing traditional memory usage is near zero while their automatic system delivers memories reliably.
AI.result: Evaluation showed: voluntary memory use was near zero (0 operations in 114 turns), deterministic injection delivered memories with zero false alarms, 39% of re-reads recovered previously created content, and compaction experiments showed automatically injected memories survived while conversational facts vanished after summarization. The agent even searched harness files to rebuild lost memories.
AI.conclusion: Delivery, not storage, is key for agent memory systems. A reliable memory channel must be automatic and involuntary - something the agent never has to think about, with deterministic cue-based recall being essential for long-running coding agents. The harness should manage situational memory as a property, not an agent choice.

title: CASC: Causal Adversarial Subspace Clustering for Multivariate Spatiotemporal Data
summary: Deep subspace clustering plays a critical role in applications involving multivariate spatiotemporal data, such as sea ice monitoring, disease spread analysis, and tracking neuro-degeneration over time. Despite recent advances, existing methods primarily rely on geometric self-expressiveness, assume static subspace structures, and often fail to capture causal dependencies, local spatial interactions, and long-range temporal dynamics inherent in complex spatiotemporal systems. To address these limitations, we propose a novel Causal Adversarial Subspace Clustering (CASC) framework for discovering evolving latent regimes in high-dimensional spatiotemporal data. CASC integrates a U-Net-inspired deep adversarial clustering architecture with stacked FAConvLSTM layers to preserve spatial and temporal structure while learning robust latent representations. A graph attention transformer-based self-expressive network is introduced to jointly model local spatial relationships, global dependencies, and long-range temporal interactions. Furthermore, we propose two new learning objectives: (1) a Causal Subspace Preservation Loss that aligns self-expression coefficients with latent causal relationships, encouraging clusters to reflect underlying causal processes rather than simple feature similarity, and (2) a Dynamic Temporal Subspace Evolution Loss that captures evolving subspace structures and temporal regime transitions in nonstationary environments. Together, these components transform deep subspace clustering from a correlation-driven paradigm into a causal-temporal regime discovery framework.

AI.tldr: CASC is a deep learning framework that integrates U-Net, adversarial clustering, and attention transformers to discover evolving causal regimes in spatiotemporal data, moving beyond correlation-based approaches to capture causal dependencies and temporal dynamics.
AI.motivation: Existing deep subspace clustering methods rely on geometric self-expressiveness, assume static subspace structures, and fail to capture causal dependencies, local spatial interactions, and long-range temporal dynamics in complex spatiotemporal systems. These limitations hinder accurate analysis of multivariate spatiotemporal data in applications like sea ice monitoring, disease spread analysis, and neuro-degeneration tracking.
AI.method: Proposes Causal Adversarial Subspace Clustering (CASC) framework that integrates: (1) U-Net-inspired deep adversarial clustering architecture with stacked FAConvLSTM layers to preserve spatial/temporal structure, (2) graph attention transformer-based self-expressive network to model local/global spatial relationships and temporal interactions, (3) Causal Subspace Preservation Loss to align self-expression coefficients with latent causal relationships, and (4) Dynamic Temporal Subspace Evolution Loss to capture evolving subspace structures and temporal regime transitions.
AI.result: Transforms deep subspace clustering from a correlation-driven paradigm into a causal-temporal regime discovery framework capable of discovering evolving latent regimes in high-dimensional spatiotemporal data by capturing causal dependencies rather than simple feature similarity.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CASC framework represents a significant advancement in spatiotemporal data analysis by integrating causal discovery with temporal dynamics, enabling more meaningful regime identification in complex systems where causal relationships and temporal evolution are crucial.

title: Beyond Independent Optimization: Compression, MoE Routing, and Quantization Interactions in Multimodal Edge Intelligence
summary: Efficient multimodal inference is increasingly constrained not only by model quality or FLOP count, but also by the cost of preserving, moving, routing, caching, and quantizing multimodal representations under latency, memory, and energy constraints. This paper reviews recent advances in efficient vision-language and multimodal large language models, covering visual token compression, video token management, KV-cache optimization, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routing, low-bit quantization, edge deployment, and hardware-aware benchmarking. We argue that these techniques cannot be treated as independent optimizations. Visual token compression alters downstream feature distributions and MoE routing decisions, routing behavior affects expert utilization and quantization sensitivity, quantized router logits influence expert assignment, KV-cache policies determine retained multimodal evidence, and hardware constraints often transform computational savings into memory and communication bottlenecks. We organize the literature around these interactions and identify key design trade-offs, including accuracy versus token budget, static versus adaptive compression, sparse routing efficiency versus expert collapse, and low-bit inference versus modality-specific degradation. Finally, we introduce Temporal Routing Consistency as a diagnostic for video MoE models and highlight open research directions in routing-aware compression, cross-modal cache management, hardware-aware co-design, and unified benchmarking for multimodal edge intelligence.

AI.tldr: A review paper on efficient multimodal inference that examines the interconnected challenges of visual token compression, KV-cache optimization, MoE routing, quantization, and edge deployment, highlighting their interdependent nature and trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Multimodal inference faces practical constraints beyond just FLOPs - including costs of preserving, moving, routing, caching, and quantizing multimodal representations under latency, memory, and energy constraints. There's a need to understand how these efficiency techniques interact rather than treating them as independent optimizations.
AI.method: Comprehensive review and analysis of recent advances in efficient vision-language and multimodal large language models, organized around interactions between visual token compression, video token management, KV-cache optimization, MoE routing, low-bit quantization, edge deployment, and hardware-aware benchmarking.
AI.result: Identifies key design trade-offs including accuracy vs token budget, static vs adaptive compression, sparse routing efficiency vs expert collapse, and low-bit inference vs modality-specific degradation. Introduces Temporal Routing Consistency as a diagnostic for video MoE models.
AI.conclusion: Efficiency techniques for multimodal inference are interdependent and must be co-designed. The paper highlights open research directions in routing-aware compression, cross-modal cache management, hardware-aware co-design, and unified benchmarking for multimodal edge intelligence.

title: Training Large Language Models for Self-Explanation Faithfulness
comment: To appear at the ICLR 2026 Workshop on Representational Alignment (Re-Align), 10 pages (long paper)
summary: We propose a Reinforcement Learning (RL) method to directly optimize the faithfulness of self-explanations - the extent to which a model's generated reasoning accurately reflects its internal decision-making process. While existing work focuses on evaluating faithfulness or using inference-time prompting frameworks to improve an LLM's self-explanation's tractability, these approaches do not provide a mechanism to directly optimize a model's parameters to generate faithful self-explanations. We bridge this gap by modifying existing faithfulness metrics into an RL training objective. We investigate (1) if models can be trained to accurately detect factors that affect their decisions, and (2) whether RL can directly optimize for the disclosure of these factors thereby improving LLM self-explanations' faithfulness. We experiment with two intervention types: random-word insertions and user-bias insertions, using a per-sample reward derived from the Phi-CCT correlation metric. RL fine-tuned Llama3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B show substantial improvements on the Phi-CCT faithfulness metric, with in-distribution scores rising from near-zero to as high as 0.664, and out-of-distribution scores reaching up to 0.691 on held-out tasks such as StrategyQA. Cross-intervention generalization is weaker but more interesting: a priori we would not expect a model trained only on random word insertions to generalize to user-bias phrases, yet Llama3.1-8B shows non-zero transfer in this direction. The reverse direction and Qwen3-8B do not replicate this, indicating model-dependent and setup-dependent effects we cannot yet explain. Lastly we analyze model behavior to rule out reward gaming behaviors that often plague RL training. Ultimately, we show that models can be trained to implicitly identify influential factors and disclose them, offering a scalable path toward reducing unfaithful reasoning in LLMs.

AI.tldr: Direct RL optimization of LLM self-explanation faithfulness by converting faithfulness metrics into RL rewards, showing substantial improvements on Phi-CCT metric from near-zero to up to 0.664 in-distribution and 0.691 out-of-distribution.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches only evaluate faithfulness or use inference-time prompting to improve tractability of self-explanations, but lack mechanisms to directly optimize model parameters for generating faithful self-explanations that accurately reflect internal decision-making.
AI.method: Modify existing faithfulness metrics into RL training objective; use per-sample reward derived from Phi-CCT correlation metric; experiment with two intervention types (random-word insertions and user-bias insertions); RL fine-tune Llama3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B models.
AI.result: Substantial improvements on Phi-CCT faithfulness metric: in-distribution scores rise from near-zero to as high as 0.664; out-of-distribution scores reach up to 0.691 on held-out tasks like StrategyQA. Cross-intervention generalization is weaker but shows interesting transfer patterns. Models can be trained to implicitly identify influential factors and disclose them.
AI.conclusion: RL can directly optimize models for faithful self-explanations, offering a scalable path toward reducing unfaithful reasoning in LLMs. Models can be trained to identify and disclose influential decision factors, though cross-intervention generalization varies by model and setup.

title: GuardianAgentBench: Where Agents Fail and How to Guard Them
summary: As large language model agents increasingly operate autonomously with access to tools and external environments, ensuring their safe and reliable behavior becomes critical. We present GuardianAgentBench (GABench), a benchmark of 580 scenarios across six domains evaluated on three production-ready frameworks: LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Vectara. The benchmark incorporates rigorous multi-stage validation and five adversarial attack modes. Experiments with six state-of-the-art models reveal that even the strongest configuration achieves only 74.8% overall accuracy and expose two distinct failure regimes: stronger models under-call required tools, while weaker models mis-select and over-call tools. Performance degrades monotonically with both tool-set size and sequential turn depth, with long-horizon planning proving the steeper bottleneck. Our guardrail implementation consistently outperforms system-prompt-based defenses across all models, recovering 19.9% of failures at a false positive rate of just 0.5%. These results demonstrate that execution-time structural intervention improves safety without disrupting correct agent behavior.

AI.tldr: GuardianAgentBench (GABench) is a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating safety of autonomous LLM agents, revealing critical vulnerabilities in tool usage and demonstrating that structural guardrails outperform prompt-based defenses.
AI.motivation: As large language model agents increasingly operate autonomously with access to tools and external environments, ensuring their safe and reliable behavior becomes critical. There's a need for robust evaluation benchmarks to assess agent safety across real-world scenarios.
AI.method: Created GuardianAgentBench (GABench) with 580 scenarios across six domains, evaluated on three production frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, Vectara). Incorporated rigorous multi-stage validation and five adversarial attack modes. Tested six state-of-the-art models and implemented execution-time structural guardrails for comparison with system-prompt-based defenses.
AI.result: Even the strongest configuration achieved only 74.8% overall accuracy. Two distinct failure regimes: stronger models under-call required tools, while weaker models mis-select and over-call tools. Performance degrades with both tool-set size and sequential turn depth. Guardrail implementation consistently outperformed system-prompt-based defenses, recovering 19.9% of failures at just 0.5% false positive rate.
AI.conclusion: Execution-time structural intervention improves safety without disrupting correct agent behavior. Current autonomous LLM agents still have significant vulnerabilities in tool usage and long-horizon planning, highlighting the need for continued safety research and implementation of structural guardrails rather than relying solely on prompt-based defenses.

title: A Polynomial Architecture-Attribution Co-Design Framework for Exact Aumann-Shapley Attribution in GNNs
summary: We study feature-level and node-level explanations for graph neural networks (GNNs) through the lens of Aumann-Shapley attribution. Path-integral methods such as Integrated Gradients provide an axiomatic formulation of attribution, but their practical use in deep GNNs typically relies on finite-sample numerical approximations to the path integral, requiring a trade-off between quadrature error and computational cost. This paper proposes APEX, a model-attribution co-design framework that makes the attribution integral exactly computable under a polynomial GNN architecture. The key component is PolyGIN, a GIN-style graph network whose message-passing, normalization, and transformation operations preserve a bounded multivariate polynomial form for scalar model scores, such as pre-softmax logits. We show that, for a PolyGIN with $L$ polynomial transformation blocks, the derivative along the attribution path has degree at most $2^L-1$. Therefore, Gauss--Legendre quadrature can evaluate the Aumann--Shapley path integral exactly, up to floating-point precision, with $2^{L-1}$ deterministic evaluation points. The resulting attributions can be computed at the feature level and then aggregated into node-level scores while preserving completeness. Experiments on synthetic and real-world graph benchmarks show that PolyGIN maintains competitive predictive performance, while the complete APEX framework achieves higher attribution fidelity than the compared baselines and substantially reduces the number of evaluations required for path integration.

AI.tldr: APEX is a model-attribution co-design framework that makes attribution integrals exactly computable for GNNs using polynomial architectures, enabling efficient exact computation of Aumann-Shapley attributions with competitive predictive performance.
AI.motivation: Current path-integral attribution methods for GNNs (like Integrated Gradients) rely on finite-sample numerical approximations, requiring a trade-off between quadrature error and computational cost, which limits their practical effectiveness.
AI.method: Proposes APEX framework with PolyGIN architecture - a GIN-style graph network with polynomial message-passing, normalization, and transformation operations that preserve bounded multivariate polynomial form for model scores. Uses Gauss-Legendre quadrature to exactly compute Aumann-Shapley path integral with deterministic evaluation points.
AI.result: PolyGIN maintains competitive predictive performance on synthetic and real-world benchmarks. APEX achieves higher attribution fidelity than baselines and substantially reduces evaluation points needed for path integration (exact computation with 2^{L-1} points for L polynomial blocks).
AI.conclusion: The APEX framework successfully addresses the accuracy-computation trade-off in GNN attribution by making path integrals exactly computable through polynomial architectural design, providing both feature-level and node-level explanations with completeness preservation.

title: Workflow-Localized Mechanism Learning: Attribution-Guided Repair and Knowledge Reuse for Structured Agent Skills
summary: Agent Skills package reusable procedural knowledge as external artifacts for frozen language-model agents, yet existing optimizers do not jointly resolve where a failure occurs in a workflow, which mechanism caused it, and how relevant knowledge from third-party Skills should be reused locally. We introduce Workflow-Localized Mechanism Learning (WML). Its Node--Mechanism Attribution identifies the failed workflow node, implicated mechanisms, and smallest valid edit target, routing single-mechanism defects to L3 resources and relational defects across mechanisms to L2 composition protocols. A six-module Workflow-Guided Skill Optimization (WGSO) loop then selects provenance- and scope-aware third-party knowledge, applies bounded patches, evaluates candidates, and stores verified outcomes in optimizer-side memory. On SpreadsheetBench, WML reaches 90.33 +/- 1.53 and 74.67 +/- 3.51 Hard Accuracy with DeepSeek and Qwen3.6-Flash, respectively; without additional optimization, the learned Skills transfer to WikiTableQuestions with 84.00 +/- 2.00 and 83.00 +/- 2.00 Denotation Accuracy. On Compiler-Supported50, WML attains both the highest hard-PASS rate and the lowest cost per successful task; compiled execution sharply reduces tokens and calls relative to a direct SkillAgent while retaining most of its successful tasks. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/xiaolin9595/workflow-localized-mechanism-learning.

AI.tldr: WML (Workflow-Localized Mechanism Learning) is a framework that localizes workflow failures, identifies implicated mechanisms, and optimizes reusable knowledge from third-party Skills to improve agent performance on tasks like spreadsheet manipulation and table-based question answering.
AI.motivation: Current agent Skill optimizers cannot jointly resolve where a failure occurs in a workflow, which mechanism caused it, and how relevant knowledge from third-party Skills should be reused locally. This limitation hinders efficient debugging and knowledge transfer for frozen language-model agents.
AI.method: WML uses Node–Mechanism Attribution to identify failed workflow nodes, implicated mechanisms, and smallest valid edit targets. It routes single-mechanism defects to L3 resources and relational defects across mechanisms to L2 composition protocols. A six-module Workflow-Guided Skill Optimization loop selects provenance- and scope-aware third-party knowledge, applies bounded patches, evaluates candidates, and stores verified outcomes.
AI.result: On SpreadsheetBench, WML achieves 90.33 +/- 1.53 and 74.67 +/- 3.51 Hard Accuracy with DeepSeek and Qwen3.6-Flash respectively. Without additional optimization, learned Skills transfer to WikiTableQuestions with 84.00 +/- 2.00 and 83.00 +/- 2.00 Denotation Accuracy. On Compiler-Supported50, WML attains highest hard-PASS rate and lowest cost per successful task, with compiled execution sharply reducing tokens and calls while retaining most successful tasks.
AI.conclusion: WML provides an effective approach for workflow-localized failure analysis and knowledge reuse, enabling improved agent performance through targeted optimization of reusable procedural knowledge. The framework demonstrates strong performance on spreadsheet and table-based tasks while enabling efficient compiled execution.

title: Smooth Neural Point Processes via B-Splines
summary: Temporal point processes (TPPs) provide a general and flexible framework for modeling sequences of events in continuous time. Neural networks have been successfully employed to model TPPs in a highly expressive and data-driven way. Neural TPPs are typically trained via Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) by minimizing the negative log-likelihood (NLL), which depends on both the conditional intensity function (CIF) and its integral over time, the compensator. Recent neural TPP approaches enable exact evaluation of the NLL without numerical integration. However, these methods typically model the compensator rather than the CIF directly, impose constraints on the neural network architecture, and are computationally expensive during training, as event contributions to the NLL are evaluated sequentially rather than in parallel. In this work, we propose a novel neural TPP model that directly parametrizes the CIF as a non-negative combination of B-spline basis functions, whose coefficients are predicted by a neural network. This formulation enables exact evaluation of the NLL, preserves full flexibility in the neural architecture, allows efficient parallelization during training, and naturally supports CIF smoothness regularization through the integrated squared second derivative. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show improved computational efficiency and predictive accuracy compared to the reference neural TPP baseline.

AI.tldr: A neural temporal point process model that directly parameterizes the conditional intensity function using B-spline basis functions with neural network-predicted coefficients, enabling exact NLL evaluation, architectural flexibility, efficient parallelization, and natural smoothness regularization.
AI.motivation: Existing neural TPP models have limitations: they typically model the compensator rather than the CIF directly, impose architectural constraints, are computationally expensive during training due to sequential evaluation, and often require numerical integration for NLL evaluation.
AI.method: Proposes parameterizing the CIF as a non-negative combination of B-spline basis functions whose coefficients are predicted by a neural network. This enables exact evaluation of the negative log-likelihood without numerical integration while preserving neural architecture flexibility and allowing parallel training.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate improved computational efficiency and predictive accuracy compared to baseline neural TPP methods. The approach achieves efficient parallelization during training and supports CIF smoothness regularization through integrated squared second derivatives.
AI.conclusion: The proposed B-spline based neural TPP model successfully addresses key limitations of existing approaches by enabling direct CIF modeling, exact NLL evaluation, architectural flexibility, efficient parallel training, and built-in smoothness regularization, leading to better performance in both computational efficiency and predictive accuracy.

title: Naju: A Native Discrete State-Space Model with Independent Retention and Writing for Long-Sequence Memory
summary: Long-sequence memory tracking places two opposing demands on a recurrent state: near-lossless retention of stored bindings over long horizons, and active overwriting of stale ones. In our diagnostic suite, the strongest efficient baselines tend to solve only one side well. Continuous-time-parameterized state-space models (SSMs) such as Mamba obtain their discrete recurrence by zero-order-hold discretization of a continuous-time system; we argue that this detour is unnecessary for memory tracking and parameterize the discrete transition directly. Naju (Native Adaptive Junction Unit) factorizes the recurrent update, schematically $x_n = f_n\odot x_{n-1} + i_n\odot(B_n u_n)$, into an explicit discrete pole (a learned forget gate $f_n$), an independent write gain $i_n$, and input-dependent write/read maps. Since the sigmoid pole satisfies $0<f_n<1$, each frozen local coordinate is Schur-stable by construction, and the full time-varying recurrence satisfies a fading-memory/BIBO bound under uniform boundedness assumptions, with no stability regularizer. We formalize the key structural limitation of coupled designs: any non-expansive complementary single-gate recurrence ties the effective retention $r$ and write gain $w$ through $|r|+w\le 1$, so near-complete retention forces weak writing; decoupling $f_n$ from $i_n$ removes this constraint. Empirically, Naju is the only evaluated model that remains strong on both retention and overwriting at 4x the training length. Beyond the diagnostic suite, we evaluate Naju on WikiText-103 language modeling, Long Range Arena, and multi-query associative recall. Across these settings, Naju consistently combines strong long-range memory with competitive or superior performance, outperforming the Mamba baselines in the principal comparisons while remaining competitive with the Transformer and preserving linear-time, linear-memory scaling.

AI.tldr: Naju is a novel recurrent architecture that decouples retention and writing mechanisms to overcome limitations in existing efficient models for long-sequence memory tracking, achieving strong performance on both retention and overwriting tasks.
AI.motivation: Long-sequence memory tracking requires balancing two opposing demands: near-lossless retention of stored bindings over long horizons, and active overwriting of stale ones. Existing efficient baselines like Mamba/SSMs tend to solve only one side well, highlighting the need for architectures that can handle both retention and overwriting effectively.
AI.method: Naju (Native Adaptive Junction Unit) directly parameterizes discrete transitions without the continuous-time detour of SSMs. It factorizes the recurrent update as x_n = f_n⊙x_{n-1} + i_n⊙(B_n u_n), using: 1) an explicit discrete pole (learned forget gate f_n), 2) an independent write gain i_n, and 3) input-dependent write/read maps. This decoupling removes the structural limitation of coupled designs where retention and write gain are tied together.
AI.result: Naju is the only evaluated model that remains strong on both retention and overwriting at 4x the training length. It outperforms Mamba baselines in principal comparisons while remaining competitive with Transformers. It maintains linear-time, linear-memory scaling and achieves strong performance on WikiText-103 language modeling, Long Range Arena, and multi-query associative recall tasks.
AI.conclusion: Naju's decoupled design successfully addresses the fundamental trade-off in memory tracking by separating retention and writing mechanisms. This architectural innovation enables efficient long-range memory capabilities without stability regularization while preserving computational efficiency, making it a promising approach for sequence modeling tasks requiring both strong retention and active overwriting.

title: TOUR: A Trajectory-Level Unlearning Benchmark for Offline Reinforcement Learning
summary: Offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents are trained on fixed behavioral trajectories, which makes trajectory-level deletion important when selected data must be removed after training. Evaluating such deletion is difficult because a lower membership score can reflect trajectory removal, residual memorization visible to another attack, or policy collapse that destroys useful behavior. We introduce Trajectory-level memOrization and Unlearning in offline RL (TOUR), a benchmark that combines trajectory-level partitioning, matched non-member controls, retraining references, retained-performance anchors, and multi-attack privacy auditing. Across D4RL locomotion experiments and an exploratory AntMaze extension, TOUR shows that common deletion baselines have environment-dependent privacy-utility behavior. Retraining and fine-tuning often provide stronger retained-utility references than uniform GA+Refit, while TrajDeleter remains a useful comparator but is not uniformly stronger under the same audit. Reference-model, threshold, deviation, equivalence, action-error, representation-based, and query-limited attacks further show that a single likelihood-based membership score can overstate deletion quality. In the evaluated settings, conclusions about offline RL unlearning are therefore not stable under single-score auditing. They depend on matched non-member construction, retraining-relative calibration, attack family, retained utility, and explicit scope for diagnostic architecture or component-level evidence.

AI.tldr: TOUR is a new benchmark for evaluating trajectory-level deletion/unlearning in offline RL, showing that single-score auditing is insufficient and conclusions depend on multiple factors including attack types, non-member controls, and retained utility.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of trajectory-level deletion in offline RL is difficult because lower membership scores can reflect actual removal, residual memorization, or policy collapse. There's a need for comprehensive benchmarking to properly assess deletion quality and privacy-utility tradeoffs.
AI.method: TOUR combines trajectory-level partitioning, matched non-member controls, retraining references, retained-performance anchors, and multi-attack privacy auditing. Tested on D4RL locomotion experiments and AntMaze extension with various deletion baselines and attacks.
AI.result: Common deletion baselines show environment-dependent privacy-utility behavior. Retraining/fine-tuning provide stronger utility references than uniform GA+Refit. Single likelihood-based membership scores can overstate deletion quality, and conclusions are not stable under single-score auditing.
AI.conclusion: Offline RL unlearning evaluation requires multi-faceted assessment including matched non-member construction, retraining-relative calibration, diverse attack families, retained utility measurement, and diagnostic architecture evidence - not just single membership scores.

title: Reexamining zero-shot summarization: Empirical investigation of trustworthiness of LLM-summarizers
comment: 28 pages, Under review in a journal
summary:
Zero-shot summarization using Large Language Models (LLMs) has significantly advanced the abstractive summarization task by producing coherent and fluent summaries. However, underlying stochasticity of the large language models raises concerns about the stability and trustworthiness of the LLM-generated summaries. This issue has become increasingly important due to proliferation of LLM-generated summaries in educational settings, where students and researchers summarize complex academic materials in zero-shot manner.
  We propose a novel two-level diagnostic protocol for benchmarking LLM-summarizers based on the stability of the generated summaries. At the lower level, document-level stability analysis is performed over multiple LLM-summaries generated under controlled environment, and the stability coefficient is computed. Each generated summary is scored for semantic and factual alignment with the original document, enabling estimation of stability along more than one dimensions. At the next level, observations from a stratified sample of documents drawn from the corpus are consolidated to estimate the stability index of the LLM-summarizer, which is the proxy for its trustworthiness.
  Our empirical investigation of three LLM-summarizers across three genres of documents reveals statistically significant differences in the generation-level variability among LLMs across summary evaluation metrics. This study advances the LLM-summarization research by evidential recognition of the stability problem in LLM-summaries and motivates further research towards development of robust, reliable and trustworthy LLM-summarizers.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a two-level diagnostic protocol to benchmark LLM summarization stability, introducing stability coefficients and indices to assess trustworthiness of zero-shot summarization outputs.
AI.motivation: The stochastic nature of large language models in zero-shot summarization raises concerns about stability and trustworthiness, especially important in educational settings where students and researchers rely on LLM-generated summaries of complex academic materials.
AI.method: A two-level diagnostic protocol: 1) Document-level stability analysis with multiple LLM summaries generated under controlled environments, computing stability coefficients based on semantic and factual alignment; 2) Corpus-level stability index estimation by consolidating observations from a stratified document sample.
AI.result: Empirical investigation of three LLM-summarizers across three document genres reveals statistically significant differences in generation-level variability among LLMs across summary evaluation metrics.
AI.conclusion: The study advances LLM summarization research by providing evidence of stability problems in LLM summaries and motivates further research toward developing robust, reliable, and trustworthy LLM-summarizers through systematic stability benchmarking.

title: GlucoTune: A Unified Framework for Blood Glucose Preprocessing, Forecasting, and Benchmarking in Diabetes
summary: Preprocessing blood glucose time-series data is a critical yet often overlooked step in developing data-driven methods for diabetes management, particularly for type 1 diabetes. The lack of standardized preprocessing workflows and evaluation protocols hinders reproducibility and complicates fair comparison across studies. These challenges are further exacerbated by data-sharing restrictions, as privacy and licensing constraints often prevent the redistribution of preprocessed medical datasets. To address these limitations, we present GlucoTune, a comprehensive and extensible framework for reproducible experimentation with blood glucose time-series data. The framework standardizes the entire experimental workflow, from preprocessing to model evaluation, enabling reproducible experiments directly from the original datasets. Reproducible preprocessing is achieved through configurable pipelines defined in portable YAML configuration files, ensuring consistent data handling without distributing sensitive preprocessed data. Beyond preprocessing, GlucoTune provides a unified interface for implementing, training, and evaluating blood glucose prediction models. The framework integrates public datasets through standardized wrappers and provides a curated collection of state-of-the-art blood glucose prediction and general time-series forecasting methods, while remaining readily extensible to additional datasets, preprocessing strategies, and forecasting models. To promote transparent and consistent evaluation, GlucoTune includes a benchmarking leaderboard that reports results across datasets, preprocessing configurations, and forecasting methods, enabling systematic comparison of experimental settings. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GlucoTune through comprehensive experiments and assess its usability in a user study.

AI.tldr: GlucoTune is an extensible framework for reproducible experimentation with blood glucose time-series data, addressing standardization, privacy, and evaluation challenges in diabetes management research.
AI.motivation: The lack of standardized preprocessing workflows and evaluation protocols for blood glucose data hinders reproducibility and fair comparison across studies. Data-sharing restrictions due to privacy and licensing constraints further complicate research by preventing redistribution of preprocessed medical datasets.
AI.method: Developed GlucoTune framework with configurable YAML-based preprocessing pipelines that work directly from original datasets. Provides unified interface for implementing, training, and evaluating blood glucose prediction models with standardized dataset wrappers and integration of state-of-the-art methods.
AI.result: Created a comprehensive framework that standardizes the experimental workflow from preprocessing to model evaluation. Includes benchmarking leaderboard for systematic comparison across datasets, preprocessing configurations, and forecasting methods. Demonstrated effectiveness through comprehensive experiments and validated usability via user study.
AI.conclusion: GlucoTune addresses critical reproducibility challenges in blood glucose data analysis by providing a standardized, extensible framework that enables reproducible experiments without distributing sensitive preprocessed data, promoting transparent evaluation and accelerating diabetes management research.

title: EmoAgent-R1: Towards Multimodal Emotion Understanding with Reinforcement Learning-based Dynamic Agent Specialization
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance in multimodal emotion recognition (MER) tasks and lifted MER to a new level that is complex emotion understanding with advanced video understanding abilities and natural language description. However, existing MLLM-based methods often use a fixed prompt to perceive the emotions, ignoring the dynamicity and complexity of the emotion source in the multimodal inputs. To address these issues, we propose a novel Reinforcement Learning-based Dynamic Agent Specialization framework (\textbf{EmoAgent-R1}) to optimize the emotion recognition, reasoning, and generalization abilities of an MLLM with dynamic agent specialization based on reinforcement learning. Specifically, we first adopt a cold start strategy to endow an MLLM with preliminary emotion recognition, reasoning, and agent routing ability by training with synthetic answer-conditioned chain-of-thought data and agent routing data. Then, we further train the MLLM with reinforcement learning to perceive emotions in a two-step agentic workflow with agent selection and agent specialization. To effectively train EmoAgent-R1, we propose a novel Progressive Group-Relative Policy Optimization (P-GRPO) to combine group-based relative advantages with a PMI-inspired progressive token-level modulation to transform sparse rewards into fine-grained learning signals, mitigating the coarse-grained uniform credit assignment issue in GRPO. Extensive experiments on MER benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our EmoAgent-R1 in stronger emotion reasoning performance and improved optimization stability.

AI.tldr: EmoAgent-R1: A reinforcement learning framework that uses dynamic agent specialization in multimodal LLMs for better emotion recognition, addressing fixed prompt limitations with agentic workflows and progressive optimization.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLM-based emotion recognition methods use fixed prompts that ignore the dynamicity and complexity of emotions in multimodal inputs, limiting their ability to handle varying emotional sources effectively.
AI.method: 1. Cold start strategy: Train MLLM with synthetic answer-conditioned chain-of-thought data and agent routing data for preliminary emotion recognition and routing abilities. 2. Reinforcement learning-based training with two-step agentic workflow (agent selection and agent specialization). 3. Progressive Group-Relative Policy Optimization (P-GRPO) combining group-based relative advantages with PMI-inspired progressive token-level modulation to transform sparse rewards into fine-grained learning signals.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on MER benchmarks demonstrate superior emotion reasoning performance and improved optimization stability compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: EmoAgent-R1 successfully addresses the limitations of fixed-prompt MLLM approaches by introducing dynamic agent specialization through reinforcement learning, enabling more nuanced and effective multimodal emotion recognition with better reasoning capabilities.

title: Relative Value Learning
comment: Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026
summary: In reinforcement learning, critics typically estimate absolute state values $V(s)$, estimating how good a particular situation is in isolation. However, it turns out that only differences in value are relevant for control. Motivated by this, we propose Relative Value Learning (RV), a framework that learns value differences directly via an antisymmetric function $Δ(s_i, s_j) = V(s_i) - V(s_j)$. We introduce a pairwise Bellman operator and prove it is a $γ$-contraction with a unique fixed point equal to the true value differences, derive well-posed $1$-step, $n$-step and $λ$-return targets and reconstruct generalized advantage estimation from pairwise differences to obtain an unbiased policy-gradient estimator (R-GAE). Beyond theoretical results, we integrate RV with PPO and achieve competitive performance on the Atari benchmark (49 ALE games) compared to standard PPO, indicating that relative value estimation is an effective alternative to absolute critics.

AI.tldr: Relative Value Learning (RV) proposes estimating value differences directly via antisymmetric functions instead of absolute state values, enabling unbiased policy gradient estimation and achieving competitive performance on Atari benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Critics in reinforcement learning typically estimate absolute state values V(s), but only value differences are relevant for control. This motivates learning value differences directly to improve efficiency and theoretical properties.
AI.method: Proposes Relative Value Learning (RV) framework using antisymmetric function Δ(s_i, s_j) = V(s_i) - V(s_j) to learn value differences directly. Introduces pairwise Bellman operator (γ-contraction), derives 1-step, n-step and λ-return targets, and reconstructs generalized advantage estimation from pairwise differences (R-GAE) for unbiased policy-gradient estimation.
AI.result: Integrated RV with PPO and achieved competitive performance on Atari benchmark (49 ALE games) compared to standard PPO, demonstrating that relative value estimation is an effective alternative to absolute critics.
AI.conclusion: Relative value learning provides a theoretically sound and empirically effective alternative to absolute value critics in reinforcement learning, with proper contraction properties and practical advantages for control tasks.

title: Demographically-Informed Heat-Mortality Risk Curves via Risk Graph Neural Networks
summary: Estimating heat-related mortality risk is a core task in environmental epidemiology, typically addressed with Distributed Lag Non-linear Models (DLNMs); interpretable exposure-response surfaces fitted to temperature-mortality time series. DLNMs are effective but ignore demographic and geographic context, despite well-established relevance to heat vulnerability. We propose Risk Graph Neural Networks (RGNNs), a hierarchical GNN encoder that uses granular census features to optimise DLNM coefficient vectors, preserving interpretable risk curve outputs while substantially improving predictive calibration. Evaluated across 10 regions of England and Wales on two unprecedented heat years, RGNN variants maintain both lower point-errors and near-nominal uncertainty coverage during the 2022 heatwave where baselines collapse.

AI.tldr: RGNNs improve heat mortality prediction by incorporating demographic data into traditional temperature models while maintaining interpretable risk curves.
AI.motivation: Current DLNM models for heat-related mortality estimation ignore demographic and geographic context, which are well-established factors affecting heat vulnerability. This limitation reduces predictive accuracy during extreme heat events.
AI.method: Proposed Risk Graph Neural Networks (RGNNs) - hierarchical GNN encoder that uses granular census features to optimize DLNM coefficient vectors, preserving interpretable risk curve outputs while improving predictive calibration.
AI.result: RGNN variants maintain both lower point-errors and near-nominal uncertainty coverage during the 2022 heatwave where baseline models collapse. Evaluated across 10 regions of England and Wales on two unprecedented heat years.
AI.conclusion: RGNNs substantially improve predictive calibration over traditional DLNM models by incorporating demographic context while preserving interpretability, making them more robust for heat mortality estimation during extreme events.

title: Faster IndexTTS-2: Accelerating and Streaming Autoregressive Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech Synthesis on GPUs
summary: Autoregressive text-to-speech models achieve strong naturalness but suffer from slow inference due to sequential token generation, limiting their deployment in production applications that require low latency. IndexTTS-2 is a state-of-the-art autoregressive TTS model consisting of a GPT, a flow-matching Diffusion Transformer, and a vocoder. Despite its high synthesis quality, its inference speed barely reaches real-time without streaming or batching support. We present Faster IndexTTS-2, which accelerates all neural network components of IndexTTS-2 for production deployment on GPUs using NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM. Faster IndexTTS-2 also enables streaming synthesis for latency-sensitive interactive applications, and batched inference across all components to maximize GPU utilization. Experiments on the Seed-TTS benchmark for both English and Chinese demonstrate up to 5.0$\times$ speedup on the autoregressive GPT and 3.6$\times$ end-to-end, with minimal degradation in word error rate, speaker similarity, and naturalness. Our methodology provides a practical reference for efficiently accelerating similar autoregressive speech models on GPUs.

AI.tldr: Faster IndexTTS-2 accelerates the state-of-the-art IndexTTS-2 text-to-speech model using NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM, achieving up to 5x speedup on the autoregressive GPT and 3.6x end-to-end with minimal quality degradation, while adding streaming and batching capabilities for production deployment.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive text-to-speech models like IndexTTS-2 achieve strong naturalness but suffer from slow inference due to sequential token generation, limiting their deployment in production applications that require low latency. The original IndexTTS-2's inference speed barely reaches real-time without streaming or batching support.
AI.method: The authors accelerate all neural network components of IndexTTS-2 for production deployment on GPUs using NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM. They enable streaming synthesis for latency-sensitive interactive applications, and implement batched inference across all components to maximize GPU utilization.
AI.result: Experiments on the Seed-TTS benchmark for both English and Chinese demonstrate up to 5.0× speedup on the autoregressive GPT and 3.6× end-to-end acceleration. The accelerated model shows minimal degradation in word error rate, speaker similarity, and naturalness.
AI.conclusion: Faster IndexTTS-2 provides a practical reference for efficiently accelerating similar autoregressive speech models on GPUs, enabling production deployment with significant speed improvements while maintaining synthesis quality and adding essential features like streaming and batching.

title: Agree on the Model, Verify the Inference: GKR Protocols for HND-Based Transformer Inference
comment: 24 pages, including 4 pages of supporting information; 2 figures
summary: Outsourced Transformer inference exposes clients to model substitution and incomplete execution, while direct replay removes the computational benefit of delegation. We present GKR-HND, a registered-model protocol for verifying the polynomial backbone of Homomorphic--Nonhomomorphic Decomposition Transformers. The retained verifier checks the GKR transcript and registered-weight openings, but delegates expensive public evaluations to an assigned computation worker. Assuming an honest retained verifier and prover--worker non-collusion, the verifier accepts only when the worker's signed, request-bound response agrees with the proof claims. Experiments with pretrained HND models validate the proof path and the delegated public computation without dense-matrix replay.

AI.tldr: A protocol called GKR-HND for verifying transformer inference in outsourced settings, using registered-model verification to prevent model substitution and incomplete execution attacks while maintaining computational benefits of delegation.
AI.motivation: Outsourced transformer inference is vulnerable to model substitution attacks (using different models) and incomplete execution attacks (not running all computations), while direct replay for verification would eliminate the computational benefits of delegation.
AI.method: GKR-HND protocol uses registered-model verification for Homomorphic-Nonhomomorphic Decomposition Transformers. It involves the verifier checking GKR transcripts and registered-weight openings, while delegating expensive public evaluations to computation workers. The protocol requires an honest retained verifier and assumes no collusion between prover and worker.
AI.result: The protocol ensures verifier acceptance only when worker's signed, request-bound response matches proof claims. Experiments with pretrained HND models validate both the proof path and delegated public computation without requiring dense-matrix replay.
AI.conclusion: GKR-HND provides a practical solution for secure outsourced transformer inference that prevents common attacks while preserving computational efficiency through selective delegation of verification tasks.

title: Can Generative Recommendation Reach Cold Items? A Temporal Perspective on Semantic-ID Generation
summary: Semantic-ID-based generative recommendation represents items as sequences of shared semantic tokens, enabling token recombination beyond isolated item IDs. However, closed-world recombination does not necessarily imply temporal open-token cold-start induction, where new items enter the item catalog with unseen atomic tokens or weakly supported SID paths. In this work, we revisit SID-based generative recommendation under an absolute-time temporal protocol that separates seen and unseen targets and diagnoses the cold item reachability at the token level. Through seen/unseen-hit analysis, coldness taxonomy, and oracle-prefix probing, we show that current SID-based models can occasionally reach future items supported by observed tokens and prefixes, but struggle with unseen atomic tokens and unsupported SID paths. We further explain this boundary by interpreting SID generation as hierarchical semantic bucketing: early tokens select coarse semantic regions, while later tokens refine item-specific paths. These findings show that SID generation is compositional but not fully open-ended, and suggest future directions in more independent SID spaces, scoring-based interfaces, and dynamic textual context.

AI.tldr: SID-based generative recommendation models can recombine known tokens to reach some new items but fail with completely unseen atomic tokens or unsupported semantic paths, limiting true open-world cold-start capability.
AI.motivation: While semantic-ID (SID) based generative recommendation enables token recombination beyond isolated item IDs, there's uncertainty about whether this closed-world recombination capability translates to effective temporal open-token cold-start scenarios where new items introduce unseen atomic tokens or weakly supported SID paths.
AI.method: The study uses an absolute-time temporal protocol to separate seen and unseen targets, analyzes cold item reachability at token level through seen/unseen-hit analysis, coldness taxonomy, and oracle-prefix probing. It interprets SID generation as hierarchical semantic bucketing where early tokens select coarse semantic regions and later tokens refine item-specific paths.
AI.result: Current SID-based models can occasionally reach future items supported by observed tokens and prefixes, but struggle significantly with unseen atomic tokens and unsupported SID paths. The generation process shows compositional properties but lacks full open-ended capability.
AI.conclusion: SID generation is compositional but not fully open-ended, suggesting future research directions should focus on more independent SID spaces, scoring-based interfaces, and dynamic textual context to improve cold-start performance.

title: Automated Synthesis and Adversarial Validation of Executable Causal Research Pipelines
summary: While automated research systems promise to accelerate empirical analysis, they are prone to silent failures: instances in which analysis code executes successfully yet relies on invalid causal assumptions. We present the Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based Epidemiology Research Assistant (ARA), a framework that makes these failures visible by explicitly encoding causal design principles, study-specific assumptions, and methodological constraints. ARA integrates protocol construction, synthetic data generation, and adversarial validation into a unified pipeline. The framework translates natural language research questions into structured causal protocols and executable analysis code by first constructing a protocol and then generating synthetic datasets using Structural Causal Models (SCMs) with known ground-truth effects. This synthetic-data step can also support pipeline development when access to confidential data, such as medical data, is restricted. The generated analysis is then evaluated under controlled violations of identification assumptions. We evaluate ARA on the Automated Causal Reasoning Benchmark, assessing recovery of identification strategies, causal quantities, treatment and outcome variables, and consistency between generated code and approved protocol. Protocol construction and adversarial validation did not consistently improve numerical agreement with benchmark estimates compared with standard LLM-based generation. However, they changed the failure mode: instead of silently returning causal estimates, ARA often surfaced protocol concerns, diagnostic failures, incomplete inference, or downgraded non-causal interpretations. These findings suggest that validity-first automated science systems should be evaluated not only by answer accuracy, but also by whether they indicate when causal claims are unwarranted.

AI.tldr: ARA framework makes automated causal analysis failures visible by encoding causal design principles, generating synthetic data with known ground truth, and adversarial validation instead of silently returning potentially invalid results.
AI.motivation: Automated research systems are prone to silent failures where analysis code executes successfully but relies on invalid causal assumptions, creating misleading results without detection.
AI.method: ARA integrates protocol construction, synthetic data generation using Structural Causal Models with known ground-truth effects, and adversarial validation through controlled assumption violations. It translates natural language questions into structured causal protocols and executable code.
AI.result: Protocol construction and adversarial validation didn't improve numerical accuracy compared to standard LLM-based generation, but changed failure modes: ARA surfaced protocol concerns, diagnostic failures, incomplete inference, or downgraded to non-causal interpretations instead of silently returning causal estimates.
AI.conclusion: Validity-first automated science systems should be evaluated not only by answer accuracy, but by whether they indicate when causal claims are unwarranted, making failures visible rather than silent.

title: AttriMem: Attribution-Guided Process Feedback for Agent Memory Learning
summary: Effective memory is crucial for LLM agents, yet constructing it effectively remains challenging. A memory-construction policy decides what information to extract, store, update, compress, or discard as interactions accumulate. Heuristic memory methods rely on subjective, task-specific rules, which can misalign with downstream objectives and limit cross-task adaptability. RL-based methods, by contrast, learn from task feedback but mainly use outcome- or module-level rewards. These coarse signals indicate task success but cannot identify which intermediate memory contents support the final answer, creating a fine-grained credit-assignment bottleneck. However, constructing such process feedback is prohibitively difficult because intermediate memory decisions lack unique ground-truth targets, while the appropriate credit varies with the agent's uncertain reasoning trajectory and therefore cannot be specified in advance. We propose AttriMem, an attribution-guided process-feedback framework for learning memory-construction policies with RL. AttriMem augments the global outcome reward with local rewards derived from token-level contributions to the final answer. Experiments on long-horizon dialogue question answering show that AttriMem outperforms retrieval-based, heuristic, and RL-based baselines, generalizes across benchmarks and answer models, stabilizes RL optimization.

AI.tldr: AttriMem is an RL framework for LLM memory construction that uses attribution-guided process feedback (token-level contributions) instead of just outcome rewards, improving performance on long-horizon dialogue QA tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing memory construction methods have limitations: heuristic methods rely on subjective, task-specific rules that misalign with downstream objectives and lack cross-task adaptability, while RL-based methods use only coarse outcome- or module-level rewards that cannot identify which intermediate memory contents actually support the final answer, creating a fine-grained credit assignment problem.
AI.method: AttriMem, an attribution-guided process-feedback framework for learning memory-construction policies with RL. It augments global outcome rewards with local rewards derived from token-level contributions to the final answer, using attribution techniques to identify which memory contents support specific parts of the answer.
AI.result: Experiments on long-horizon dialogue question answering show that AttriMem outperforms retrieval-based, heuristic, and RL-based baselines. It also generalizes across benchmarks and answer models, and stabilizes RL optimization.
AI.conclusion: Attribution-guided process feedback (using token-level contributions) is an effective solution to the fine-grained credit assignment problem in memory construction for LLM agents, enabling better learning of memory policies compared to existing heuristic and RL approaches.

title: Filter Learning for Subgraphs: Algebras and Performance Risk Bounds
summary: Graph signal processing tasks that leverage spectral information typically assume access to the complete graph topology, which is often unavailable in practice. We propose a systematic framework for subgraph filter learning (SFL), where subgraph-supported operators approximate ambient graph filters under partial observations. We formulate SFL as a statistical learning problem in which optimal subgraph operators are inherently data-dependent. To address the difficulty of directly estimating such operators, we develop a subgraph filter algebra based on distance-aware Laplacian constructions, defining a structured and controllable class of filters for effective approximation. We further establish performance risk bounds under the least squares loss, quantifying how well the learned operator approximates the restricted ambient mapping.
