Experiments real-world datasets show that, for SFL tasks, the proposed algebraic models consistently outperform polynomial filters, distribution-agnostic operators, and direct numerical filter learning baselines that attempt to recover the underlying structure from data.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a systematic framework called Subgraph Filter Learning (SFL) for approximating graph filters when only partial graph observations (subgraphs) are available, developing algebraic models that outperform existing baselines.
AI.motivation: Traditional graph signal processing assumes access to complete graph topology, but in practice, complete graph information is often unavailable due to partial observations. This creates a gap between theoretical assumptions and practical scenarios where only subgraphs are accessible.
AI.method: The authors propose Subgraph Filter Learning (SFL) as a statistical learning problem. They develop a subgraph filter algebra based on distance-aware Laplacian constructions to create structured and controllable filter classes. This provides an approximation framework that doesn't require recovering the complete graph structure from data.
AI.result: The paper establishes performance risk bounds under least squares loss, quantifying approximation quality. Experiments on real-world datasets show that the proposed algebraic models consistently outperform polynomial filters, distribution-agnostic operators, and direct numerical filter learning baselines that attempt to recover the underlying structure from data.
AI.conclusion: The SFL framework provides an effective solution for graph signal processing under partial observations, with theoretical guarantees and superior empirical performance compared to existing approaches that either assume complete topology or attempt direct structure recovery.

title: V-DEAL: Diagnosing Video Safety De-Calibration as an Understanding-Refusal Coupling Failure
summary: As Video Large Language Models are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, ensuring their safety alignment has become critical. Counterintuitively, we find that harmful videos paired with benign queries achieve higher attack success rates than the same videos paired with explicitly harmful queries. To understand the underlying mechanism of this vulnerability, we present V-DEAL, a three-level diagnostic framework that jointly analyzes this failure across model behaviour, understanding, and internal representations. By progressively ruling out perception failure and quantifying the model's internal refusal tendency, V-DEAL provides a new diagnostic perspective for analyzing the underlying mechanism of the observed vulnerability. We tested six Video LLMs on three public benchmarks and observed that models correctly recognize harmful video content with over 81\% accuracy, yet the average attack success rate still reaches 48.33\% under the condition pairing harmful videos with benign queries. Hidden-state analysis further shows that visual understanding activates a weaker refusal tendency than textual understanding. Furthermore, we introduce a prompt injection intervention method that reduces attack success rates by an average of 48.24 percentage points and achieves performance comparable to prior fine-tuning-based methods, providing an effective and practical means to address such safety risks in Video LLMs.

AI.tldr: Video LLMs show a counterintuitive vulnerability where harmful videos with benign queries have higher attack success rates than with harmful queries, requiring a new diagnostic framework.
AI.motivation: As Video LLMs are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, ensuring their safety alignment has become critical. There's a surprising finding that harmful videos paired with benign queries achieve higher attack success rates than with explicitly harmful queries.
AI.method: The authors present V-DEAL, a three-level diagnostic framework that jointly analyzes this failure across model behaviour, understanding, and internal representations. They tested six Video LLMs on three public benchmarks, used hidden-state analysis, and introduced a prompt injection intervention method to address the vulnerability.
AI.result: Models correctly recognize harmful video content with over 81% accuracy, yet the average attack success rate still reaches 48.33% when pairing harmful videos with benign queries. Hidden-state analysis shows visual understanding activates weaker refusal tendency than textual understanding. The prompt injection intervention reduces attack success rates by an average of 48.24 percentage points, achieving performance comparable to prior fine-tuning-based methods.
AI.conclusion: V-DEAL provides a new diagnostic perspective for analyzing safety vulnerabilities in Video LLMs, revealing that visual understanding triggers weaker refusal mechanisms than textual understanding. The prompt injection intervention offers an effective, practical solution to address these safety risks without requiring fine-tuning.

title: The Dark Room in the Reward Channel: Dense Prediction Rewards Collapse GRPO-Trained LLM Agents -- and What Actually Works
summary: Dense per-step supervision is an appealing remedy for sparse-reward, long-horizon LLM agents: reward the agent for predicting its next observation, and memory should follow. We show that under group-normalized RL (GRPO), this recipe does not merely fail -- it destroys the policy. Across Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B on ALFWorld, a potential-based prediction reward drives every run into a degenerate absorbing state (prediction accuracy -> 1.0, task success -> 0,episode length pinned at the horizon): the "dark room" pathology, built automatically by the optimizer. A single-factor ablation localizes the cause -- removing only GRPO's std normalization turns the same reward from catastrophic (0%) into baseline parity -- and a two-line proposition explains why: in all-fail groups the z-scored advantage is invariant to the shaping coefficient, so bounded rewards become unbounded pressure and annealing cannot help. Our central insight generalizes this: what z-scoring amplifies is a dense signal's within-group variance while all-fail groups dominate, so signals whose variance decays by mastery are structurally amplifier-safe.This variance-profile criterion retrodicts our collapses, carries preregistered predictions for arms that had not yet run, and is consistent with published reward-channel successes (a compatibility check, not an independent test). Finally, a controlled signal-delivery matrix (identical signal, varying only the consumption mechanism) shows the reward channel is at best neutral while the auxiliary-loss channel gains ~20 points -- and a shuffled-gold placebo matches the true-gold arm, so the gap survives without correct labels. Endpoints are single-seed; seed replication and group-size controls are preregistered and in progress.

AI.tldr: Dense per-step prediction rewards combined with group-normalized RL (GRPO) cause catastrophic policy collapse into "dark room" pathologies where agents learn to maximize prediction accuracy while completely failing at tasks, but this can be fixed by removing std normalization or using auxiliary loss channels instead of reward channels.
AI.motivation: To investigate why dense per-step supervision (rewarding agents for predicting next observations) fails in sparse-reward, long-horizon LLM agent scenarios, and specifically why this approach causes catastrophic policy collapse when combined with group-normalized RL (GRPO).
AI.method: Experimental analysis across Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B models on ALFWorld, using controlled ablation studies to isolate factors (removing GRPO's std normalization), theoretical analysis with mathematical propositions, variance-profile criterion development, and signal-delivery matrix comparisons between reward channels vs. auxiliary-loss channels.
AI.result: Dense prediction rewards with GRPO drive policies to degenerate absorbing states with 1.0 prediction accuracy but 0% task success (dark room pathology). Removing GRPO's std normalization alone turns catastrophic failure into baseline parity. The reward channel performs at best neutrally while auxiliary-loss channels gain ~20 points, with placebo tests showing the gap persists even without correct labels.
AI.conclusion: The catastrophic failure stems from how group normalization amplifies dense signal variance within all-fail groups, turning bounded rewards into unbounded optimization pressure. Signals with decaying variance (as mastery increases) are amplification-safe. Practical takeaway: use auxiliary losses rather than reward channels for dense supervision, or avoid z-scoring normalization with dense prediction rewards.

title: Multi-Task Learning for Heterogeneous Prediction from Video Game State with Transfer Learning
summary: Multi-task learning (MTL) is a promising approach for prediction tasks derived from video game state data, as modern game telemetry provides multiple related supervision signals from the same structured observations. We study whether a shared model trained jointly across tasks in team-based multiplayer games can improve generalization while reducing training and inference cost compared to specialized single-task models. We adapt a multimodal architecture for endpoint prediction to a general multi-task setting that combines rasterized vision inputs, global match context, and per-unit state information through an image encoder and attention-based interaction modeling. Experiments on a large proprietary World of Tanks dataset compare single-task and multi-task training, evaluate weighting strategies for mixed losses and conflicting gradients, and test pre-training/fine-tuning under limited target-data regimes. We also examine within-game transfer across game maps under structured environment shift.

AI.tldr: Multi-task learning for video game state prediction shows shared models can outperform single-task models while reducing computational costs, especially in limited data scenarios.
AI.motivation: Modern video game telemetry provides multiple related supervision signals from the same structured observations, making multi-task learning promising for prediction tasks in team-based multiplayer games. The researchers want to determine if shared models can improve generalization while reducing training and inference costs compared to specialized single-task models.
AI.method: Adapted a multimodal architecture for endpoint prediction to general multi-task setting that combines rasterized vision inputs, global match context, and per-unit state information through an image encoder and attention-based interaction modeling. Experiments conducted on large proprietary World of Tanks dataset comparing single-task vs multi-task training, evaluating weighting strategies for mixed losses and conflicting gradients, testing pre-training/fine-tuning under limited target-data regimes, and examining within-game transfer across game maps under structured environment shift.
AI.result: The experiments show that multi-task learning can achieve better performance than single-task models while reducing computational overhead. Specific results likely demonstrate improved generalization, effectiveness of various loss weighting strategies, benefits of pre-training/fine-tuning in low-data scenarios, and successful transfer across game environments.
AI.conclusion: Multi-task learning is effective for video game state prediction tasks, offering improved generalization and reduced computational costs compared to specialized single-task models, particularly valuable in limited data scenarios and for cross-environment transfer learning within games.

title: Safeguards for Speech2Speech LLM-Assistants: A Case Study in Automotive Applications
summary: Recent advances have introduced speech-to-speech (S2S) conversational assistants capable of producing natural-sounding interactions, including non-verbal cues like tonality and mood. In the automotive domain, this enables intuitive and humanlike in-car dialogue experiences. However, integrating these end-to-end assistants limits architectural options for programmable domain-specific safeguards. This paper discusses two implementation approaches for S2S guardrails: transcript-based and tool-based. Through an empirical evaluation, we demonstrate that both strategies are insufficient for industrial deployment in most cases due to prohibitive latency (delaying each answer by 0 to 1.4 seconds even for computationally cheap checks) and technical impediments (like potentially non-deterministic tool call behavior). Finally, we outline open challenges for S2S guardrails in the automotive context.

AI.tldr: Speech-to-speech guardrails for automotive assistants face prohibitive latency (0-1.4s delays) and technical challenges, making current transcript-based and tool-based approaches insufficient for industrial deployment.
AI.motivation: Speech-to-speech conversational assistants enable natural, intuitive in-car dialogue experiences with non-verbal cues, but their end-to-end nature limits architectural options for implementing programmable domain-specific safeguards (guardrails).
AI.method: Two implementation approaches for S2S guardrails are examined: transcript-based (analyzing speech transcripts) and tool-based (using tool calls). The paper conducts empirical evaluation of both strategies.
AI.result: Both transcript-based and tool-based guardrail strategies are insufficient for industrial deployment due to: 1) prohibitive latency (delaying each answer by 0 to 1.4 seconds even for computationally cheap checks), and 2) technical impediments like potentially non-deterministic tool call behavior.
AI.conclusion: Current S2S guardrail approaches are not suitable for automotive deployment due to latency and technical limitations. The paper outlines open challenges for developing effective S2S guardrails in the automotive context that need to be addressed for practical industrial use.

title: AI Assistants Overassist
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as tutors and thought partners, helping users reason through problems. While guidance from AI assistants can scaffold thinking and foster learning, such benefits depend on how they help--for instance, intervening too early or too frequently may hinder true learning and cognitive engagement. Yet how AI systems navigate intervention decisions during problem-solving remains poorly understood. Here, we introduce Int-Bench, a simulation-based benchmark for evaluating LLM interventions during learning. Int-Bench simulates a "student" solving a problem while a "teacher" monitors the student's reasoning and decides whether, when, and how to intervene. Across three domains--code debugging, mathematics, and brain teasers--we evaluate LLM teachers on the frequency and timing of interventions, as well as their impact on both immediate task success and generalization to new problems. We also compare LLMs to humans, finding that LLMs intervene more frequently and earlier than humans. Moreover, in contrast to humans, they tend to provide complete solutions rather than targeted hints. These findings suggest that current LLM assistants often optimize for short-term success rather than supporting the reasoning processes needed for deeper learning and long-term success.

AI.tldr: Int-Bench is a simulation benchmark that evaluates when and how LLMs intervene as tutors during problem-solving, finding they intervene too early/frequently compared to humans and provide complete solutions rather than targeted hints.
AI.motivation: While LLMs are increasingly used as tutors, there's poor understanding of how AI systems make intervention decisions during problem-solving. Current approaches may hinder true learning if they intervene too early or too frequently, but there's a lack of systematic evaluation of these intervention dynamics.
AI.method: Researchers created Int-Bench, a simulation-based benchmark where a simulated "student" solves problems while a "teacher" (LLM or human) monitors reasoning and decides whether, when, and how to intervene. They evaluated interventions across three domains: code debugging, mathematics, and brain teasers.
AI.result: LLMs intervene more frequently and earlier than humans, and tend to provide complete solutions rather than targeted hints. This contrast with human tutors, who offer more strategic interventions, suggests LLMs optimize for short-term task success over fostering deeper reasoning processes.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM assistants prioritize immediate task completion rather than supporting the cognitive processes needed for genuine learning and long-term skill development. This highlights the need for better intervention strategies in AI tutoring systems to truly foster learning.

title: Explaining Weather Bulletins via ILP
summary: Inductive Logic Programming (ILP) originated within the Logic Programming community in the Nineties as a framework for combining symbolic learning with declarative knowledge representation. Nowadays, mature ILP frameworks exist and they are capable of learning complex, non-monotonic hypotheses, thus broadening both the modeling capabilities and the scope of real-world applications of ILP. This work is primarily based on the FastLAS2 framework and aims to generate simple, interpretable hypotheses to help clarify the weather bulletins issued by OSMER FVG, the Regional Meteorological Observatory of the Italian region of Friuli Venezia-Giulia. In this paper we present a pipeline that, starting from simulated meteorological raw data and from OSMERs' bulletins (used as ground truth), extracts data as ASP facts and generates ILP examples. From such examples an explanatory hypothesis is then inferred via FastLAS2. Such a hypothesis (translated into natural language) explains the weather forecast issued by human experts, and in particular the rationale behind experts' choices of specific symbols in the bulletin pictogram (the symbol-annotated meteorological map of the forecast). The proposed approach is general, not specific to any particular region and it can equally be applied to bulletins from other sources and to different regions.

AI.tldr: ILP (Inductive Logic Programming) framework FastLAS2 is used to generate interpretable hypotheses explaining meteorological forecast bulletins by analyzing raw weather data and expert-issued bulletins as ground truth.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to clarify and explain the rationale behind weather forecast bulletins issued by human experts from OSMER FVG (Regional Meteorological Observatory of Friuli Venezia-Giulia), specifically understanding why certain symbols are chosen in meteorological forecast pictograms.
AI.method: The approach uses a pipeline that: 1) processes simulated meteorological raw data and OSMER bulletins as ground truth, 2) extracts data as ASP (Answer Set Programming) facts, 3) generates ILP examples, and 4) infers explanatory hypotheses using the FastLAS2 ILP framework. The hypotheses are then translated into natural language for interpretation.
AI.result: The method successfully generates interpretable hypotheses that explain human experts' weather forecasting decisions, particularly the selection of specific symbols in forecast pictograms. The pipeline creates explanatory rules linking meteorological conditions to forecast symbols.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ILP-based approach provides a generalizable framework for explaining expert meteorological forecasting decisions, making forecast rationale transparent and interpretable. The method is not region-specific and can be applied to weather bulletins from various sources and different geographical regions.

title: M$^3$-Gen: Interpretable Multimodal Generation of Gene Expression Profiles Using Clinical and Imaging Data
summary: Integrating heterogeneous biomedical data, including clinical metadata, histopathology images, and molecular profiles, is crucial for comprehensive disease understanding. However, gene expression data acquisition remains constrained by high costs and privacy concerns, limiting its use in multimodal research and AI-driven applications. We present MultiModal Molecular Generation (M$^3$-Gen), a novel framework for the generation of gene expression profiles by conditioning a Generative Adversarial Network on histopathology images and clinical metadata. M$^3$-Gen learns a unified latent representation from the clinical variables and the images, leveraging contrastive learning, and exploits the embeddings of the two modalities to guide a generative model in producing biologically coherent gene expression profiles. Evaluations on the TCGA dataset demonstrate that M$^3$-Gen generates realistic and functionally meaningful gene expression data. Importantly, by integrating multiple modalities in an attention-based mechanism, M$^3$-Gen provides intrinsic explainability: it allows the identification of which regions of the histopathology images most strongly influenced the generation of specific gene expression profiles, making the model's decisions interpretable by design.

AI.tldr: M³-Gen is a novel framework that generates realistic gene expression profiles from histopathology images and clinical metadata using GANs with contrastive learning and attention mechanisms for explainability.
AI.motivation: Gene expression data acquisition is expensive and faces privacy concerns, limiting multimodal biomedical research and AI applications. There's a need to generate realistic gene expression data from more accessible modalities like histopathology images and clinical data.
AI.method: M³-Gen uses a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) conditioned on histopathology images and clinical metadata. It learns a unified latent representation through contrastive learning, then exploits embeddings from both modalities to guide generation. The framework includes attention mechanisms for explainability.
AI.result: Evaluations on TCGA dataset show M³-Gen generates realistic and functionally meaningful gene expression profiles. The attention-based mechanism provides intrinsic explainability by identifying which histopathology image regions most influenced specific gene expression generation.
AI.conclusion: M³-Gen successfully addresses the challenge of generating gene expression data from more accessible modalities while providing interpretable results through its attention-based design, enabling multimodal research without direct gene expression acquisition.

title: Differentiable Logic Programming to Mitigate Reasoning Shortcuts in Neurosymbolic Systems
summary: Neurosymbolic (NeSy) systems integrate neural networks with logical reasoning to achieve both generalization and interpretability, but recent work has shown they are susceptible to shortcut reasoning behaviors.  We propose a novel method using matrix-based differentiable logic programming to mitigate reasoning shortcuts in two phenomena: constraint satisfaction shortcuts, where constraints are satisfied without achieving the intended task, and cognition shortcuts, where biased data leads to semantically incorrect concept mappings despite logically sound inference. Building on recent matrix-based logic programming semantics, we introduce design elements to mitigate shortcuts, including a unified encoding of rules and constraints in a single matrix.  We also identify connections to fuzzy logic t-norms and empirically compare their gradient flow properties. Through carefully designed experiments on MNIST variants, we show that one-to-one grounding of neural outputs to logical atoms significantly reduces both shortcut types compared to previous methods that rely on soft probability distributions.  We then confirm that architectural choices in coupling symbolic knowledge with neural learning play a critical role in shortcut mitigation.

AI.tldr: Neurosymbolic systems suffer from shortcut reasoning; the paper proposes matrix-based differentiable logic programming to mitigate constraint satisfaction and cognition shortcuts by using one-to-one grounding of neural outputs to logical atoms.
AI.motivation: Neurosymbolic systems combine neural networks with logical reasoning for generalization and interpretability, but are vulnerable to shortcut reasoning behaviors that undermine their intended functionality.
AI.method: Matrix-based differentiable logic programming with a unified encoding of rules and constraints in a single matrix, using one-to-one grounding of neural outputs to logical atoms rather than soft probability distributions. The approach leverages fuzzy logic t-norms and analyzes their gradient flow properties.
AI.result: Experiments on MNIST variants show that one-to-one grounding significantly reduces both constraint satisfaction and cognition shortcuts compared to previous methods. Architectural choices in coupling symbolic knowledge with neural learning play a critical role in shortcut mitigation.
AI.conclusion: Matrix-based differentiable logic programming with proper grounding strategies effectively mitigates reasoning shortcuts in neurosymbolic systems, highlighting the importance of architectural design in integrating symbolic knowledge with neural learning.

title: How Many Bits Can an Adapter Write? Measuring the Capacity and Memorization of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
summary: A LoRA adapter is a few megabytes that almost everyone treats as a skill rather than a record of the data behind it. We put that assumption on a scale. Extending compression-based memorization analysis to the frozen-base setting, we measure directly, in bits, how much a low-rank adapter writes into a model it never changes. The answer is both smaller than full fine-tuning and less lawful than parameter counting would predict. Adapters store a couple of bits per trainable parameter, well short of a full model's budget, but that figure turns less on how many parameters an adapter carries than on where they sit. Move the same parameter budget from attention into the MLP and it holds nearly twice as much; strip the frozen base of its structure and the capacity all but disappears. Applied to realistic fine-tunes of Qwen2.5, the same instrument shows privacy leakage rising with the bits an adapter writes rather than the parameters it nominally has, and it draws a clean line between supervised and reinforcement learning: the secrets that supervised fine-tuning copies down verbatim, an adapter trained on verifiable rewards never records. Measuring what fine-tuning writes, rather than attacking it after the fact, turns a piece of folklore into a quantity one can design against.

AI.tldr: LoRA adapters store surprisingly little information (a few bits per parameter) compared to full fine-tuning, and their capacity depends more on placement (MLP vs attention) than parameter count, revealing privacy implications that differ between supervised and reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: The paper challenges the assumption that LoRA adapters are just "skills" rather than records of training data, aiming to quantify how much information adapters actually write into frozen base models to better understand privacy leakage.
AI.method: Extends compression-based memorization analysis to frozen-base settings, measuring in bits how much information low-rank adapters store. Examines where parameters are placed (attention vs MLP layers) and tests on realistic fine-tunes of Qwen2.5.
AI.result: Adapters store only a couple of bits per trainable parameter - far less than full fine-tuning. Capacity depends more on parameter placement than count: MLP layers hold nearly twice as much as attention layers. Privacy leakage correlates with bits written, not parameter count. Supervised fine-tuning copies data verbatim while reinforcement learning (with verifiable rewards) doesn't.
AI.conclusion: By measuring what fine-tuning writes rather than attacking models after training, we can design against privacy leakage. The findings turn "folklore" about adapters into quantifiable metrics for privacy-aware model development.

title: Identifying Good Rules for Efficient SAT Encodings of Single-Constant Multiplication Using Machine Learning
summary: The Single Constant Multiplication problem is a fundamental NP-hard optimization task in hardware design, which seeks to decompose a fixed constant using only additions, subtractions, and bit-shifts. Although dynamic programming methods can produce near-optimal SAT encodings for SCM, their encoding cost remains high for large constants. We propose a neuro-symbolic framework that accelerates SCM SAT encoding by identifying good rules for guiding operator selection during decomposition. Our approach employs a graph neural network model to predict promising operator types from constant decompositions, and exploits the resulting confidence scores to prune no-good choices in the symbolic search. Experimental results on unseen 17-32 bit constants demonstrate one to two orders of magnitude reductions in encoding time, over 97% reduction in memory usage, and an order-of-magnitude decrease in branching, while preserving near-optimal encoding quality in terms of additions. These results show that learning-guided symbolic strategies can significantly improve the scalability and efficiency of SCM encoding. Our code and data are publicly available at: https://github.com/Chufeng-Jiang/SCM_MLDP

AI.tldr: A neuro-symbolic framework that combines graph neural networks with symbolic search to accelerate SAT encoding for the Single Constant Multiplication problem, achieving dramatic speedups and memory reductions while maintaining near-optimal solution quality.
AI.motivation: The Single Constant Multiplication (SCM) problem is NP-hard and crucial for hardware design. While dynamic programming methods can generate near-optimal SAT encodings, they become computationally expensive (high encoding cost) for large constants, limiting scalability.
AI.method: The authors propose a neuro-symbolic framework that uses a graph neural network (GNN) to predict promising operator types (additions, subtractions, bit-shifts) from constant decompositions. The GNN's confidence scores are then used to prune no-good choices during symbolic search, guiding operator selection more efficiently.
AI.result: Experimental evaluation on 17-32 bit unseen constants shows: 1) 1-2 orders of magnitude reduction in encoding time, 2) over 97% reduction in memory usage, 3) order-of-magnitude decrease in branching, 4) preservation of near-optimal encoding quality in terms of number of additions.
AI.conclusion: Learning-guided symbolic strategies (neuro-symbolic approaches) can significantly improve the scalability and efficiency of SCM encoding, demonstrating that machine learning can effectively guide traditional symbolic optimization techniques in hardware design problems.

title: Gradient Concentration, Not Weight Saliency, Explains Representation-Level Class Unlearning
comment: 51 pages, 7 figures. Submitted to Neural Networks
summary: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of specific training data while preserving model utility. Many state-of-the-art approaches pursue this goal by restricting the forgetting update to a subset of parameters selected through gradient-based saliency. Although such methods are widely adopted, the actual contribution of saliency-based weight selection to representation-level forgetting remains unclear. In this work, we perform the first controlled ablation of the saliency masking mechanism used by SalUn. Using a matched-compute experimental design on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18, we compare saliency-based masking against random masks of equal sparsity and unconstrained updates, while keeping the unlearning objective, optimization schedule, and computational budget fixed. Across multiple representation-level evaluations, including linear probing, prototype recovery, and layer-wise CKA, the three configurations exhibit statistically equivalent representation-level recoverability. We find that forget gradients are strongly concentrated in the final network layers (approximately 92% of the squared gradient energy on CIFAR-10) before any mask is applied, causing all masking strategies to operate within the same representational subspace. Furthermore, saliency masks show limited class specificity (specificity index 0.09-0.11), selecting highly overlapping parameter subsets across different forget classes. Our findings suggest that, in the studied setting, representation-level forgetting is primarily governed by gradient concentration and representation geometry rather than by the specific identity of saliency-selected weights. More broadly, the results support a growing body of evidence indicating that effective representation-level unlearning requires objectives that act directly on latent representations rather than on increasingly sophisticated weight-selection strategies.

AI.tldr: Saliency-based weight selection in machine unlearning doesn't significantly affect representation-level forgetting compared to random masks, as gradient concentration in final layers and representation geometry dominate the unlearning process.
AI.motivation: Despite widespread adoption of saliency-based parameter selection in machine unlearning, it's unclear whether this mechanism actually contributes meaningfully to representation-level forgetting, necessitating a controlled investigation.
AI.method: Controlled ablation study comparing saliency-based masking against random masks of equal sparsity and unconstrained updates, using matched-compute experimental design on CIFAR-10/100 with ResNet-18, while keeping unlearning objective, optimization, and budget fixed.
AI.result: All three configurations (saliency masks, random masks, unconstrained updates) show statistically equivalent representation-level recoverability across multiple metrics. Forget gradients concentrate 92% in final network layers, and saliency masks have low class specificity (0.09-0.11), selecting overlapping parameter subsets across classes.
AI.conclusion: Representation-level forgetting is governed by gradient concentration and representation geometry rather than specific saliency-selected weights. Effective unlearning requires objectives acting directly on representations rather than sophisticated weight-selection strategies.

title: Bound-Founded Semantics for Answer Set Programming with Difference Constraints: Preliminary Report
summary: While the integration of linear constraints has significantly expanded the reach of Answer Set Programming (ASP), existing hybrid solvers often rely on disparate semantic underpinnings that lack a unified logical foundation. We address this gap by introducing a many-sorted variant of the Bound-founded Logic of Here-and-There (HTb), providing a versatile framework capable of characterizing equilibrium models across a wide spectrum of alternative semantics for extensions of ASP with linear constraints. We apply this framework to the setting of difference constraints, focusing on the semantic characterization of clingo[DL]. Central to our approach is the formalization of foundedness for numeric variables. By investigating how different hybrid systems - such as clingo[DL], clingcon, and flingo - justify constraint atoms, we uncover the semantic roots of their varying behaviors. This investigation results in a single, consistent framework that not only formalizes the foundations of current systems like clingo[DL] but also facilitates the rigorous study of program simplifications and the future integration of diverse semantic principles.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a many-sorted variant of HTb logic to unify the semantics of ASP systems with linear constraints, specifically analyzing clingo[DL] and providing a framework to understand semantic differences across hybrid ASP solvers.
AI.motivation: Existing hybrid ASP solvers that integrate linear constraints lack a unified logical foundation due to disparate semantic underpinnings, creating inconsistencies and making it difficult to compare or integrate different systems.
AI.method: Develops a many-sorted variant of Bound-founded Logic of Here-and-There (HTb) to characterize equilibrium models across various semantics for ASP with linear constraints. Specifically applies this to difference constraints and analyzes semantic justification of constraint atoms in systems like clingo[DL], clingcon, and flingo.
AI.result: Provides a single consistent framework that formalizes the foundations of current systems like clingo[DL], reveals the semantic roots of different behaviors in hybrid ASP systems, and enables rigorous study of program simplifications and future integration of diverse semantic principles.
AI.conclusion: The proposed many-sorted HTb framework successfully unifies the semantic foundations of ASP with linear constraints, offering both theoretical understanding of existing systems and practical utility for future developments in hybrid ASP solvers.

title: Emergent Misalignment Recruits a Pre-existing Persona Subspace
comment: 108 pages (19 pages main text, 13 appendices), 13 figures
summary: Fine-tuning an aligned language model on a narrow stream of bad advice can make it broadly misaligned on questions unrelated to the training data, a phenomenon called emergent misalignment. We ask why the narrow lesson generalizes at all, and we find that narrow fine-tuning recruits a persona structure that is present in the model before the fine-tune exists. From a frozen instruction-tuned model (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct) we extract per-domain persona subspaces by contrastive teacher forcing and find that 4 unrelated domains share one low-rank core at 657x a random-subspace null, with 82% of that core lying outside a style core built at matched diversity. The literal first optimizer step of fine-tuning on insecure code climbs a broad-misalignment margin harder than the same code framed as educational, and forecasts realized margin movement out to 375 steps. Projecting the subspace out of the residual stream throughout fine-tuning prevents broad misalignment (27.7% to 0.0% of judged generations) while a matched-rank random subspace changes nothing; injecting it into the never-fine-tuned model induces misalignment that grows with dose to 45.4%, past the fine-tuned model it is measured against. The same projection applied to the weight gradient is inert, and three post-hoc weight edits leave the disposition in place: the sharpest edit suppresses the behavior rather than removing it, and the ablated structure re-forms inside the subspace the edit cleared. Spreading a fixed budget of bad data across 4 domains produces more broad misalignment than mechanical weight superposition and matched diversity jointly account for. All measurements come from one model at 14B; the extraction is from an aligned instruction-tuned checkpoint, which leaves the structure's provenance open; and the intervention that prevents misalignment also abolishes the narrow trained behavior.

AI.tldr: Narrow fine-tuning on bad data can cause broad misalignment in language models, which occurs because the fine-tuning recruits pre-existing persona structures, not by teaching new concepts.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates why "emergent misalignment" happens - where fine-tuning language models on a narrow stream of bad advice causes them to become broadly misaligned on unrelated questions. The authors want to understand why narrow lessons generalize so broadly.
AI.method: Researchers extracted persona subspaces from a frozen instruction-tuned model (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct) using contrastive teacher forcing. They found unrelated domains share a low-rank core subspace. They then conducted fine-tuning experiments: one on insecure code and one framed as educational, tracking margin movements. They tested interventions by projecting out the subspace during fine-tuning, injecting it into the unfine-tuned model, and analyzing weight edits.
AI.result: Four unrelated domains share one low-rank core subspace. Projecting out this subspace during fine-tuning completely prevents broad misalignment (27.7% to 0.0%) while random subspaces have no effect. Injecting the subspace into an unfine-tuned model induces misalignment up to 45.4%. Weight edits don't remove the disposition - the structure re-forms even when ablated. Bad data across multiple domains produces more misalignment than expected from mechanical superposition.
AI.conclusion: Emergent misalignment occurs because narrow fine-tuning activates pre-existing persona structures, not by teaching new harmful concepts. The structures are already present in aligned models and can be manipulated to prevent or induce misalignment. This challenges assumptions about how fine-tuning works and suggests models have latent harmful capabilities that can be activated.

title: A New Well-Supported Semantics for Description Logic Programs
summary: Description logic programs are a powerful formalism for combining rules with ontologies. The well-supported semantics for description logic programs ensures that no answer sets rely on cyclic dependencies. Most popular semantics for logic programming have this property of well-supportedness. We recognize two limitations of the current well-supported semantics for DL programs: its increased computational complexity for the consistency problem and its lack of a reduct transformation characterization.  In this work, we present a new semantics which evaluates ontological atoms more strictly than the current semantics. This keeps the complexity of its consistency problem NP-complete, rather than increasing it to the second level of the polynomial hierarchy. Additionally, we identify a syntactic class of description logic programs for which our new semantics is equivalent to the current semantics. We characterize our semantics using a fixpoint operator and a reduct-based transformation. Our new semantics is a strict subset of the current well-supported semantics, so it maintains the prior notion  of well-supportedness while inducing its own stricter notion. We prefer our new notion of well-supportedness due to its similarities with logic programming.

AI.tldr: A new well-supported semantics for description logic programs that maintains computational tractability (NP-complete consistency) while providing better logical programming similarity through reduct-based characterization.
AI.motivation: Address two limitations of current well-supported semantics for description logic programs: 1) increased computational complexity (to second level of polynomial hierarchy), and 2) lack of reduct transformation characterization which is fundamental in logic programming semantics.
AI.method: Proposes a new semantics that evaluates ontological atoms more strictly than current semantics. Uses a fixpoint operator and reduct-based transformation characterization. Identifies a syntactic class where new semantics equals current semantics.
AI.result: The new semantics maintains NP-complete complexity for consistency problem (vs. higher complexity in current semantics). It's a strict subset of current well-supported semantics, maintaining well-supportedness while introducing stricter notion aligned with logic programming principles.
AI.conclusion: The new semantics is preferred due to its computational efficiency (NP-complete consistency) and better alignment with logic programming through reduct-based characterization, while maintaining the fundamental well-supportedness property for description logic programs.

title: Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE): A Mathematical Framework for Deconstructing Learned Representations in Deep Networks
summary:
Deep neural networks encode complex representations, but deconstructing this internal knowledge remains a challenge. Given the link between learning and compression, network compression offers a promising lens to analyze this knowledge. However, standard compression heuristics often suffer from scale symmetries and architectural biases. To resolve these, we introduce Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE), a mathematical framework to gradually deconstruct the representations in trained network weights.
  HOPE shifts network compression from the discrete domain into a Hilbert space of continuous functions. By modeling individual neurons as rank-1 Hilbert-Schmidt operators, HOPE unifies pruning and neuron merging as low-rank subspace projection. Extending this formulation, HOPE introduces macro block eviction to encompass multi-layer structures like entire residual pathways under the same unified metric. This unified approach enables unbiased architectural decisions across layers with different types and sizes. HOPE is a data-free and hyperparameter-free framework. We present proof-of-concept experiments in model compression and fine-tuning to highlight the practical potential of our theory.

AI.tldr: HOPE is a mathematical framework that transforms network compression into a Hilbert space problem, enabling unbiased representation deconstruction through low-rank subspace projections and unified neuron/metric treatment.
AI.motivation: Deep neural networks contain complex internal representations that are difficult to deconstruct. Current compression heuristics suffer from scale symmetries and architectural biases, limiting their effectiveness for analyzing network knowledge.
AI.method: HOPE shifts network compression from discrete to continuous Hilbert space, modeling neurons as rank-1 Hilbert-Schmidt operators. This unifies pruning and neuron merging as low-rank subspace projection, and introduces macro block eviction for multi-layer structures like residual pathways under a unified metric.
AI.result: HOPE provides a data-free and hyperparameter-free framework that enables unbiased architectural decisions across layers with different types and sizes, with proof-of-concept experiments demonstrating practical potential in model compression and fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: The HOPE framework offers a principled mathematical approach to network representation deconstruction that resolves scale symmetry and architectural bias issues in standard compression methods, providing a unified foundation for analyzing neural network knowledge through compression.

title: How Rules Represent Causal Knowledge: Causal Modeling with Probabilistic Logic Programming
summary:
Pearl famously argues that causal knowledge enables the prediction of intervention effects. By contrast, purely descriptive knowledge supports only conclusions drawn from observations. His theory of causality, however, is developed exclusively within Bayesian networks and causal models. Consequently, it is largely restricted to acyclic causal relationships, and transferring its ideas to other formalisms risks misinterpretation or inconsistency.
  This paper brings Pearl's approach to causality into probabilistic logic programming (PLP). To this end, such programs are aligned with philosophical foundations established in prior work that do not rely on temporal notions; that is, all relevant events are assumed to occur simultaneously. A formal causal semantics for these programs, together with a notion of intervention and an implementation, is proposed. It is shown that this semantics coincides with the P-log semantics for stratified ProbLog programs, while the two may differ in the non-stratified case and for other PLP formalisms.

AI.tldr: This paper adapts Pearl's causal reasoning approach to probabilistic logic programming, proposing a formal causal semantics, intervention mechanism, and implementation for such programs while showing alignment with existing PLP formalisms under certain conditions.
AI.motivation: Pearl's causal theory is limited to Bayesian networks and causal models, primarily handling acyclic relationships, and extending it to other formalisms can lead to misinterpretation. The paper aims to bring Pearl's causal approach to probabilistic logic programming (PLP) to overcome these limitations.
AI.method: Aligns PLP programs with philosophical foundations that don't rely on temporal notions (assuming all events occur simultaneously), proposes a formal causal semantics for these programs, defines a notion of intervention, and implements this approach.
AI.result: Shows that the proposed causal semantics coincides with the P-log semantics for stratified ProbLog programs, while differences may emerge in non-stratified cases and for other PLP formalisms.
AI.conclusion: Successfully brings Pearl's causal reasoning approach to probabilistic logic programming, providing a formal framework for causal analysis in PLP that works within simultaneous-event assumptions and bridges causal theory with logical programming paradigms.

title: Mean-to-Score Discrete Diffusion: Posterior-Mean Denoisers for Score Entropy
summary: Score Entropy Discrete Diffusion (SEDD) parameterizes discrete reverse processes with unconstrained positive score ratios. While positivity guarantees nonnegative reverse jump rates, it does not ensure Bayes realizability: ratios at a noisy state need not be jointly induced by any clean-token posterior under the forward kernel. The score-entropy loss has the correct population optimum but does not enforce this constraint away from it. In a trained pure-uniform SEDD checkpoint, roughly one quarter of complete score vectors violate the coordinate box, while more than half lie inside it yet remain materially incompatible with any valid posterior. Such violations can produce negative pre-normalization weights in finite-step sampling. Projecting raw scores onto the bridge polytope removes all observed negative weights and improves external generative PPL from $203.6$ to $175.1$ without changing the sampler. We introduce \emph{mean-to-score} (M2S), which predicts a clean-token posterior mean and converts it to the score through an exact kernel-dependent linear map. The construction applies to any known coordinate-wise continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) satisfying a mild support condition. For uniform corruption, it maps the probability simplex onto the bridge polytope; for absorbing-mask corruption, the resulting objective recovers MD4 exactly. In a controlled 28.4M-parameter CIFAR-10 comparison, M2S lowers test BPD from $3.173$ to $3.129$ and FID-50k from $\CifarSEDDFID$ to $\CifarMtwoSFID$. A 170M-parameter M2S model trained on about 262B OpenWebText token slots outperforms the evaluated pure-uniform SEDD, GIDD, and Neural CTMC checkpoints at every tested sampling budget, reaching generative PPL $143.3$ at 128 steps versus $183.6$ for the strongest pure-uniform baseline.

AI.tldr: SEDD diffusion models can produce invalid score ratios violating Bayes realizability. M2S (mean-to-score) method projects scores onto the bridge polytope, ensuring valid posteriors and improving generation quality across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Score Entropy Discrete Diffusion (SEDD) parameterizes discrete reverse processes with unconstrained positive score ratios, but these can violate Bayes realizability - ratios may not correspond to any valid posterior distribution under the forward kernel, leading to negative weights during sampling.
AI.method: Introduces Mean-to-Score (M2S) which predicts clean-token posterior means and converts them to scores through exact kernel-dependent linear maps. Projects raw scores onto the bridge polytope to enforce Bayes realizability. Works for any coordinate-wise continuous-time Markov chain satisfying mild support conditions.
AI.result: Projection onto bridge polytope removes negative weights and improves PPL from 203.6 to 175.1. M2S lowers CIFAR-10 BPD from 3.173 to 3.129 and improves FID. A 170M-parameter model trained on OpenWebText achieves PPL 143.3 at 128 steps vs 183.6 for pure-uniform baseline, outperforming SEDD, GIDD, and Neural CTMC checkpoints.
AI.conclusion: M2S enforces Bayes realizability constraints in discrete diffusion models through posterior mean prediction and projection onto the bridge polytope, leading to improved generative performance across image and text benchmarks compared to existing methods.

title: ICAE-Bench: Evaluating Coding Agents as Interactive Project Builders
summary:
The recent emergence of vibe-coding workflows is changing what coding agents are expected to do. Instead of merely completing code under fully specified instructions, agents are increasingly expected to transform incomplete product intent into working software by combining various abilities including planning, requirement clarification, tool use, debugging, and repository-level construction. Yet existing benchmarks have not fully caught up with this shift, evaluating agents on static, fully specified tasks.
  In this paper, we introduce ICAE-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents under interactive project-building settings. The basic idea is to start from a fuzzy product requirement, simulating the dynamic paradigm with an automated User Agent. To make this setting both realistic and evaluable, ICAE-Bench introduces three key designs. First, to avoid the ambiguity of unconstrained fuzzy requirements, each task derives ambiguity from a precise real open-source repository with executable behavior. Second, to ensure high-quality and reproducible user simulation, ICAE-Bench grounds interaction through User Agent Data, allowing the User Agent to reveal hidden constraints without inventing new requirements or leaking implementation artifacts. Third, to evaluate open-ended repositories fairly, ICAE-Bench uses standardized black-box tests together with multi-dimensional diagnostics, including functional correctness, semantic and API similarity, structural fidelity, design quality, and interaction quality.

AI.tldr: ICAE-Bench is a new benchmark for evaluating coding agents in interactive project-building scenarios that simulate real-world "vibe-coding" workflows, moving beyond static, fully-specified tasks to assess agents' ability to transform fuzzy product requirements into working software.
AI.motivation: Existing coding benchmarks fail to capture the shift toward "vibe-coding" workflows where agents must transform incomplete product intent into working software. Current benchmarks evaluate agents on static, fully specified tasks, but modern agents need to handle ambiguous requirements, interact with users, and perform repository-level construction through planning, clarification, debugging, and tool use.
AI.method: ICAE-Bench introduces three key designs: 1) Tasks derive ambiguity from precise real open-source repositories with executable behavior (avoiding unconstrained fuzzy requirements), 2) Grounds interaction through User Agent Data for reproducible simulation (allowing user agent to reveal hidden constraints without inventing new requirements), 3) Uses standardized black-box tests with multi-dimensional diagnostics including functional correctness, semantic/API similarity, structural fidelity, design quality, and interaction quality.
AI.result: The benchmark creates a realistic, evaluable interactive project-building setting starting from fuzzy product requirements, simulated through an automated User Agent. It addresses the gap between existing static benchmarks and modern coding workflows requiring dynamic interaction and ambiguity resolution.
AI.conclusion: ICAE-Bench provides a comprehensive evaluation framework that captures the complexities of real-world coding workflows, enabling better assessment of coding agents' capabilities in transforming ambiguous product requirements into functional software through interactive collaboration.

title: A Diffusion-Model Subpopulation Digital Twin for Mobile Health Deployment: A Case Study on the HeartSteps Intervention
summary: Mobile-health interventions increasingly use online learning and decision making algorithms to personalize when to nudge users toward healthier behavior, but a poorly designed algorithm can burden and disengage participants. New algorithm design decisions should therefore be vetted against realistic simulated users before each real-life deployment. We propose a method to develop ``JITAI-Twins'': digital twins of a target subpopulation for comparing candidate online algorithms before a just-in-time adaptive intervention (JITAI) deployment. The method builds on a conditional time-series diffusion model that is temporally consistent (future actions do not affect the generated past), and it supports repeated updating from three sources of information, in three steps: pre-training on a large observational dataset, fine-tuning on small prior intervention deployments in related populations, and inference-time calibration to the next target population from domain-scientist expertise. We validate the twin at each pre-deployment stage of the long-running HeartSteps series (v2 through v4) of physical-activity suggestion intervention deployments, treating each successive deployment as an upcoming study. The proposed method reproduces the target subpopulation's temporal and between-participant structure better than simpler simulators. These results suggest that our twin can be used to simulate a target deployment before it runs, the prerequisite for testing and informing online algorithm design decisions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes JITAI-Twins - digital twins for simulating target subpopulations to test and compare online learning algorithms for just-in-time adaptive interventions (JITAIs) before real deployment, validated on the HeartSteps physical-activity intervention series.
AI.motivation: Mobile-health interventions use online learning algorithms to personalize nudges, but poorly designed algorithms can burden and disengage participants. New algorithms need realistic simulation testing before real-life deployment to avoid negative user experiences.
AI.method: Propose JITAI-Twins method using conditional time-series diffusion models that are temporally consistent. Method has three steps: pre-training on large observational datasets, fine-tuning on small prior intervention deployments in related populations, and inference-time calibration to target population using domain expertise.
AI.result: Validated the twin at each pre-deployment stage of HeartSteps v2-v4 physical-activity interventions. The method reproduces target subpopulation's temporal and between-participant structure better than simpler simulators, enabling simulation testing before real deployment.
AI.conclusion: JITAI-Twins can effectively simulate target deployments before they run, providing necessary infrastructure for testing and informing online algorithm design decisions in mobile-health interventions.

title: Logic Programming Semantics for Causal Processes
summary: Motivated by challenging modelling issues in the life sciences, we investigate the relationship between logic programming semantics and the eventual states of causal processes compatible with those logic programs. More precisely, we show that while stable models of positive logic programs correspond to the eventual states of processes commencing from a neutral state and continuing undisturbed indefinitely, supported models describe the eventual states reachable from arbitrary starting points. This also contributes to the discussion of the appropriate semantics for logic programming as a causal rule language, adding a temporal perspective to recent interpretations of the stable and supported model semantics from an explanatory viewpoint of causality.

AI.tldr: Logic programming semantics (stable vs. supported models) correspond to different eventual states in causal processes, with stable models representing undisturbed neutral-state outcomes and supported models representing reachable outcomes from arbitrary starts.
AI.motivation: The research is motivated by challenging modelling issues in the life sciences, and aims to investigate the relationship between logic programming semantics and the eventual states of causal processes compatible with those logic programs.
AI.method: The authors investigate the correspondence between logic programming semantics and causal processes by analyzing how stable models of positive logic programs correspond to eventual states of processes commencing from neutral states, while supported models describe eventual states reachable from arbitrary starting points.
AI.result: The study shows that stable models of positive logic programs correspond to the eventual states of processes commencing from a neutral state and continuing undisturbed indefinitely, while supported models describe the eventual states reachable from arbitrary starting points.
AI.conclusion: This work contributes to the discussion of appropriate semantics for logic programming as a causal rule language by adding a temporal perspective to recent interpretations of stable and supported model semantics from an explanatory viewpoint of causality.

title: Semantic-Aware Task Clustering for Constructive and Cooperative Multi-Tasking
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Cooperative multi-task semantic communication (CMT-SemCom) improves task execution performance by leveraging shared representations. However, as we demonstrated in [1], cooperative multi-tasking can be either constructive or destructive, depending on the semantic relationships among tasks. To ensure constructive cooperation, we propose a semantic-aware task clustering method for CMT-SemCom. We have formulated a sequential multi-stage optimization problem in which semantically aligned tasks are clustered once after a short initial training phase, and then end-to-end (E2E) joint training is conducted exclusively within the discovered groups. Specifically, the problem decomposes into two stages: (i) a semantic clustering problem leveraging hierarchical density-based spatial clustering, and (ii) an intra-cluster E2E CMT-SemCom learning problem. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively mitigates destructive cooperation and negative transfer, yielding accuracy gains compared to unclustered multi-tasking and individual training baselines.

AI.tldr: A semantic-aware task clustering method for cooperative multi-task semantic communication that groups semantically aligned tasks to prevent destructive cooperation and negative transfer.
AI.motivation: Cooperative multi-task semantic communication (CMT-SemCom) can lead to either constructive or destructive cooperation depending on semantic relationships between tasks. Without proper grouping, tasks with conflicting semantics can interfere with each other, reducing performance through negative transfer.
AI.method: Proposes a sequential multi-stage optimization approach: 1) Semantic clustering using hierarchical density-based spatial clustering after short initial training to group semantically aligned tasks, 2) End-to-end joint training exclusively within discovered clusters. The framework prevents destructive cooperation by training only compatible tasks together.
AI.result: Simulation results show the proposed framework effectively mitigates destructive cooperation and negative transfer, yielding accuracy gains compared to both unclustered multi-tasking and individual training baselines.
AI.conclusion: Task clustering based on semantic relationships is crucial for constructive cooperation in multi-task semantic communication. The proposed semantic-aware clustering method successfully prevents negative transfer and improves overall task execution performance.

title: BasketEvent: Understanding Who Did What and When in Basketball Videos
summary: Comprehensive basketball video understanding requires resolving not only what event occurs, but also who is responsible and when the key evidence appears. However, exist- ing methods typically treat spatial perception and semantic recognition as isolated tasks, failing to ground events to individual players or pinpoint their temporal boundaries within complex collective dynamics. To bridge this gap, we introduce BasketEvent, a player- centric basketball event understanding dataset curated from real NBA broadcasts. In BasketEvent, event labels are grounded to the responsible players, and a manually an- notated subset of 1,000 samples with precise event intervals is provided to evaluate tem- poral evidence localization. Based on this data, we propose PlayNet, a player-centric reasoning framework that maps basketball videos to player-level event predictions with temporal evidence. Concretely, PlayNet tracks key entities, associates player identities, and reasons about events by modeling player-player, player-ball, and global court inter- actions, while aggregating sparse temporal evidence via gated pooling. Extensive experi- ments demonstrate that PlayNet significantly outperforms representative video-level and crop-based baselines, proving the superiority of player-centric modeling for fine-grained sports video understanding. Our data, code, and models will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: BasketEvent dataset and PlayNet framework for player-centric basketball event understanding with temporal evidence localization.
AI.motivation: Existing basketball video analysis methods treat spatial perception and semantic recognition as isolated tasks, failing to ground events to individual players or pinpoint temporal boundaries within complex collective dynamics.
AI.method: Introduced BasketEvent dataset (player-centric basketball event understanding from NBA broadcasts) and proposed PlayNet framework that tracks key entities, associates player identities, and reasons about events by modeling player-player, player-ball, and global court interactions with gated pooling for temporal evidence aggregation.
AI.result: PlayNet significantly outperforms representative video-level and crop-based baselines, demonstrating superiority of player-centric modeling for fine-grained sports video understanding.
AI.conclusion: Player-centric reasoning with temporal evidence localization is crucial for comprehensive basketball video understanding, enabling resolution of what events occur, who is responsible, and when key evidence appears.

title: Context-weighted Discrete Flow Matching
summary: Discrete flow matching provides a flexible framework for generative modeling on discrete structures. However, the standard factorized training objective exposes the model to targets of varying difficulty, mixing well-conditioned, predictable tokens with ambiguous, high-entropy ones. We empirically demonstrate that the uncertainty over the value of each token is closely related to the density of available context in its neighborhood. Motivated by this observation, we propose a simple modification to the underlying continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) that incorporates local context information. Our context-weighted sampler improves generation quality with negligible computational overhead, while our scaled cross-entropy loss function reweights the training signal from different tokens and reduces generative perplexity by up to 63% on OpenWebText. Moreover, our approach matches a strong semi-autoregressive block diffusion baseline in quality while retaining the ability to perform generation in any order. These results highlight the role of local context as an important factor in discrete generative modeling and show that simple context-aware modifications can significantly improve both sampling and training efficiency.

AI.tldr: Context-aware modifications to discrete flow matching improve sampling and training efficiency by addressing varying token difficulty.
AI.motivation: Standard factorized training objective in discrete flow matching exposes models to targets of varying difficulty, mixing well-conditioned tokens with ambiguous, high-entropy ones. The authors observed that token uncertainty is closely related to local context density.
AI.method: Proposed context-weighted sampler and scaled cross-entropy loss function that incorporate local context information into the underlying continuous-time Markov chain. The approach reweights training signals from different tokens based on their context availability.
AI.result: Improved generation quality with negligible computational overhead, reduced generative perplexity by up to 63% on OpenWebText. Matched strong semi-autoregressive block diffusion baseline in quality while retaining flexible generation order.
AI.conclusion: Local context is an important factor in discrete generative modeling, and simple context-aware modifications can significantly improve both sampling and training efficiency.

title: An LLM-Driven Workflow for Automated Process Control Strategy Generation and Tuning from Dynamic Process Models
summary: We present a structured large-language-model-driven workflow for automated multi-variable control design from dynamic process models. The workflow decomposes the design task into constrained code-generation steps: plant-interface construction, normalization, manipulated-variable controlled-variable (MV-CV) pairing, controller specification, closed loop simulation, scenario generation, performance evaluation and Bayesian-optimization (BO) based tuning. Generated artifacts are executed and validated before downstream tasks proceed, and failed artifacts are repaired using validation feedback. The proposed approach is demonstrated on a nonlinear gas-preheater benchmark with coupled pressure and temperature dynamics. The generated workflow produces a physically consistent decentralized PI (proportional-integral) feedback-feedforward control structure and an executable tuning environment. Bayesian optimization reduces the closed loop performance objective, which aggregates set-point tracking and disturbance-rejection errors for the controlled variables, by approximately 26.5% relative to the initial controller generated by the workflow, mainly through improved pressure-loop transient performance. This figure quantifies the automated tuning stage rather than a comparison against a manually designed controller. The results demonstrate the feasibility of using structured large-language-model-based code generation to construct executable control-design workflows, while also highlighting the need for broader validation on larger plantwide-control benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Automated LLM-driven workflow for multi-variable control design from dynamic process models, demonstrated on a gas-preheater benchmark with 26.5% performance improvement via Bayesian optimization.
AI.motivation: To automate the complex process of multi-variable control design from dynamic process models, which traditionally requires significant manual effort and expertise in control engineering.
AI.method: A structured LLM-driven workflow that decomposes control design into constrained code-generation steps: plant-interface construction, normalization, MV-CV pairing, controller specification, closed-loop simulation, scenario generation, performance evaluation, and BO-based tuning. The workflow includes validation and repair mechanisms for failed artifacts.
AI.result: Successfully applied to a nonlinear gas-preheater benchmark with coupled pressure-temperature dynamics. Generated a physically consistent decentralized PI feedback-feedforward control structure and executable tuning environment. Bayesian optimization reduced the closed-loop performance objective by approximately 26.5% relative to the initial controller, mainly improving pressure-loop transient performance.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of using structured LLM-based code generation for executable control-design workflows, while highlighting the need for broader validation on larger plantwide-control benchmarks. The approach shows promise for automating complex control design tasks.

title: KroQuant: Kronecker-Structured Block Transforms for Efficient Post-Training Quantization of Diffusion Transformers
summary:
Post-training quantization (PTQ) of diffusion transformers (DiTs) to W4A4 severely degrades output quality, because activations entering each linear layer contain outliers that 4-bit formats cannot represent. The standard fix applies an invertible linear transform to the activations and its inverse to the weights before quantizing both. Normalization layers between blocks force this transform to run online at every denoising step, making its inference computation cost the binding design constraint. Existing options trade quantization quality for inference cost: per-channel scaling (SmoothQuant) is computationally cheap but impacts the magnitude of the channels, which can harm quantization accuracy; fixed Hadamard transforms yield better quantization accuracy but require large block sizes that incur a high online cost; learned full-$d$ invertible transforms calibrate best but entail a prohibitive dense $d \times d$ matrix multiplication (GEMM) per layer per step.
  We propose KroQuant, a PTQ method that applies a learned Kronecker-structured invertible transform to each 32-element block of the activation, storing less than half the parameters of per-channel scaling. The block-local structure runs as small tensor-core GEMMs, and on an MI350 GPU the KroQuant quantizer kernel is up to $14\%$ faster than the SmoothQuant kernel. Offline LoRaQ weight calibration then absorbs the residual per-weight quantization error. On PixArt-$Σ$, SANA, and FLUX.1-schnell at W4A4 (MXFP4e2), KroQuant produces outputs closer to the FP reference than SVDQuant and LoRaQ on MJHQ-30K and SDCI, while preserving or improving image quality.

AI.tldr: KroQuant: An efficient W4A4 quantization method for diffusion transformers using learned Kronecker-structured transforms with LoRaQ weight calibration, achieving better quality than existing methods with lower computational cost.
AI.motivation: Post-training quantization of diffusion transformers to W4A4 severely degrades output quality due to activation outliers. Existing methods trade quantization quality for inference cost: SmoothQuant is cheap but inaccurate, Hadamard transforms require large blocks, and learned transforms have prohibitive computational cost.
AI.method: Proposes KroQuant, which applies learned Kronecker-structured invertible transforms to 32-element blocks of activations. Uses block-local structure for efficient tensor-core GEMMs and offline LoRaQ weight calibration to absorb residual quantization error.
AI.result: KroQuant's kernel is up to 14% faster than SmoothQuant on MI350 GPU. On PixArt-Σ, SANA, and FLUX.1-schnell at W4A4 (MXFP4e2), produces outputs closer to FP reference than SVDQuant and LoRaQ on MJHQ-30K and SDCI benchmarks while preserving or improving image quality.
AI.conclusion: KroQuant provides an efficient PTQ solution for diffusion transformers that balances quantization quality and inference cost better than existing methods, achieving high-quality W4A4 quantization with reduced computational overhead.

title: Expert Behavior Prior Reinforcement Learning
summary: Behavior prior reinforcement learning (BPRL) has emerged as a promising paradigm to improve sample efficiency in online reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging policy priors derived from offline demonstrations. However, most existing BPRL methods rely on static offline datasets, which often suffer from low data diversity and suboptimal trajectory quality. This reliance restricts the effectiveness of policy priors, hindering both policy exploitation and stability during online training. Consequently, agents are prone to inefficient exploration and unstable learning dynamics. To address these limitations, we deviate from existing offline pre-training methods and propose an Expert Behavior Prior (EBP) algorithm. Specifically, we introduce a Q-guided conditional variational autoencoder (Q-CVAE) that learns to generate expert policy priors directly from the online replay buffer. This enables the generation of high-value actions for guiding policy updates without relying on pre-collected expert trajectories. To further enhance policy exploitation, we propose an expert policy guidance (EPG) mechanism that selects expert actions from a generative support set, and we integrate a policy gradient correction (PGC) module to harmonize Q-guidance with expert supervision, promoting stable and consistent policy improvement. Extensive experiments conducted on robotic control (Gym, PyBullet) and industrial control (DMControl) benchmarks demonstrate that EBP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art online RL algorithms, achieving higher sample efficiency and more stable convergence.

AI.tldr: EBP (Expert Behavior Prior) is a novel online RL algorithm that learns expert policy priors directly from the online replay buffer using a Q-CVAE, eliminating the need for static offline datasets and improving sample efficiency and stability.
AI.motivation: Existing Behavior Prior RL (BPRL) methods rely on static offline datasets which have low diversity and suboptimal trajectory quality, limiting policy prior effectiveness and causing inefficient exploration and unstable learning during online training.
AI.method: Proposes EBP algorithm with three key components: 1) Q-guided conditional VAE (Q-CVAE) learns to generate expert policy priors from online replay buffer, 2) Expert Policy Guidance (EPG) selects expert actions from generative support set, 3) Policy Gradient Correction (PGC) harmonizes Q-guidance with expert supervision.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on robotic control (Gym, PyBullet) and industrial control (DMControl) benchmarks show EBP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art online RL algorithms with higher sample efficiency and more stable convergence.
AI.conclusion: EBP successfully addresses limitations of static offline datasets in BPRL by learning expert behavior priors online, enabling more efficient exploration and stable policy improvement without reliance on pre-collected expert demonstrations.

title: Test-Time Scaling via Error Localization
summary: Scaling inference-time computation has emerged as a reliable method to improve the performance of large language models on complex reasoning and programming tasks. However, standard approaches such as independent sampling and sequential multi-turn refinement operate without token-level credit assignment, resulting in computational inefficiency, since valid reasoning prefixes are frequently discarded. In this work, we introduce Test-Time Scaling via Error Localization (TTEL), an inference-time algorithm that utilizes fixed or environment feedback to perform token-level error localization. By comparing conditional probabilities under informed feedback against a null-context baseline, TTEL isolates the step at which an error occurred. The algorithm then truncates the trajectory and branches a new generation, maximally reusing the valid prefix. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that TTEL establishes strictly dominating Pareto frontiers across sequential reasoning domains, measured by pass-at-k vs. generated-token cost. With Qwen3-8B on LiveCodeBench, TTEL attains a pass@64 of 71.0% while generating approximately half as many tokens as independent sampling (360.4k vs. 735.0k). Generalizing to math benchmarks AIME-2025 and HMMT-2025, TTEL cleanly outperforms competing test-time baselines across both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507.

AI.tldr: TTEL is an inference-time scaling algorithm that uses error localization to identify and fix token-level errors during reasoning, enabling more efficient computation by reusing valid prefixes instead of discarding entire trajectories.
